div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL
The Question of Labour Representation. WORKMEN'S HOURS.

Mr. J. PODMORE presided over the monthly meeting of this Council which was held in Bold-street Wesleyan Schools on Tuesday evening: SHOULD HOURS OF LABOUR BE REDUCED ? The question of shortening the hours of labour in Warrington was introduced by Mr. Buckley who said he desired to obtain the opinion of Council on the matter. The question was a very serious oure lnd there were various opinions in regard to it, many trade unionists believing that a shortening of hours was un- necessary. Mr. Buckley advanced several reasons in favour of a reduction of working hours. He pointed , out that a man'shealth was injured when be had to work long hours in a badly ventilated place which for a con- siderable Epart of the day;had to be artificially lighted. Then again, when a man had worked ten hours in one day he had not sufficient energy to feel in a fit state to renew his employment next morning. Long hours also debarred men from indulging in recreation and improving their education by attending evening schools. He moved : "That this Council instructs the secretary to write to the Chamber of Commerce asking for a conference to be arranged between them and the Trades Council, to discuss the question of shortening the hours of labour; as to the advisability of it, and as to the best means of bringing it about.' Two trades which could be very easily dealt with at once were the engineering and building trades. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WARD seconded. The SECRETARY (Mr.F. Stott) said that considering the question was, as Mr. Osborne would say, somewhat revolutionary, they ought to give the delegates a month in which to think it over. He moved that the matter heladjourned for a month. In the meantime the dele- gates would bring it before their respective societies and report to the Council. If it were possible to obtain any reduction, however small, the Council ought not to leave anything undone to secure it. Mr. REDHEAD seconded. Mr. E. PLUSSTON supported and pointed out that they had it on the authority of Sir William Mather, who adopted tha eight-hours' day system at his engineering works, that the men did more work and there was greater satisfaction to employer and employed under those conditions. .

The amendment was carried. VIE TAXATION OF LAND VALUBS. The SECRETARY was appointed to represent the Council at a conference in connection with the Land Nationalisation Society to be held in Manchester on December sth. Mr. STOTT said he believed no system of fiscal reform or Protection would be,beneficial to the working classes of this country. He was of opinion that if any improve- ment I was to be brought about for the working classes of this country it would have to be done from within, not from outside. The unjust laud laws oppressed in- dustry to a great extent at the present time and rturredi- ate steps should be taken to remove that oppression.
M. rLINsTos AND 'ORFORD WilttD.

Mr. BUCKLEY presented a report of the proceedings at a meeting of the Labour Representation Committee on October 21st. He referred to the resignation of the chairmanship by Mr. Plinston. He regretted to have to refer to it because the decision come to was not unanim- ous. The subject was first introduced by a protest from the Independent Labour Party and the Cabinet Makers Society against Mr. Plinston having allowed himself to be nominated as a candidate in Orford Ward. Follow- ing that, a resolution was moved by the cabinet makers' delegate condemning Mr. Plinston's action, and calling upon hinrto resign his official position. It was one of those very regrettable incidents which sometimes occurred in the best arranged pardes, and perhaps the least said the soonest mended. (Hear, hear.) PROPOSED LABOUR CA'SDIDATE FOR WARRINGTON. , Mr. BUCKLEY called the attention of the Council to ,1 the conference of representatives of trade societies which wouldhe held en Thursdaydevening to definitely decide whether a labour candidate should contest War- rington at the next (election. There seemed to have been a difficulty in the minds of some trade unionists as to where the funds for Parliamentary representation would come from. At the meeting of the Labour Repre- sentation Committee the matter was satisfactorily explained. On the motion of Mr. PrxisTos, Messrs. Stott, Buckley and Barber, were anthorised to attend the con- ference on:behalf of the Council, and vote in favour of a labour candidate. The SECRETARY pointed out that they would prob- ably be able to secure a candidate whose expenses would be paid by a certain society. He liked men to pay for their politics. Some preferred to have labour politics without paying, and here was a grand oppor- tunity for those who held such views. THE EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CHILDREN. The SECRETARY read an exhaustive explanation of the Employment of Children Act which comes into force next year. It was pointed out that the local authorities would have the power to make special bye- laws prohibiting_ young children from selling articles in the streets. Mr. Stott said that quite recently he had seen children in Warrington,who were under eleven years of age, offering matches for sale late at night. The CHAIRMAN considered the Act Was a very good step. Mr. PLINSTON pointed out that the School Atten- dance Committee at the present time had to be satisfied before granting exemptions as to the beneficial results and the class of employment that the children would follow.

div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT,

TherQueen Victoria Memorial.—The Queen Victoria Memorial fund, now amounts to over £250,000 and some progress has been made with the decorative scheme which is to mark the site of the late Queen's statue, in front of Buckingham Palace. The memorial, when finished will make a great improvement to the mall, besides relieving the sombre front of the Palace. Upon the question when it is likely to be finished, no one would venture an opinion. As was the case with the Albert Memorial it will probably be many years before it is completed, though possibly as the work is to be carried out under the windows of Buckingham Palace, the King may insist upon it being pushed forward with- out the delay that characterised the erection of the Albert and most other Royal monuments in London. The largest Landowaers.—The .Dir.thess of Sutherland has been paying a visit to the island of Harris in the Outer Hebrides, which is famous for its homespun tsyeeds. The Duke and Duchess intend to spend the winter at their Sutherland seat, and though so far North and on the East Coast,' Dunrobin Castle is quite the reverse of bleak and cold. It stands on a ;iatural terrace above the sea, and the most ancient part of the Castle is over 600 years old, having been built by the second Earl, named after him—Dun Robin. The Duke of Sutherland is by far the largest landowner in the Kingdom, possessing some 1,176,000 acres in the county from which lie takes his name, but his father owned in addition some 150,000 acres in Rosshire, which now belong to the Countess of Cromartie, the niece of the present Duke. The Duke of Sutherland also has a mag- nificent seat at Trentham in Staffordshire, and the 30,000 acres he owns in the Midlands are of more value to him than his vast estates in Sutherlandshire. The French Grace Darling.—lt would be singularly unlike the French people if they did not make a national heroine of Rose 11•614, who swam out in the raging surf, and saved a boats crew off Ushant. In one respect that feat surpassed the famous exploit of Grace Darling,who went with her father in a small boat to the help of some ship wrecked sailors, whereas Rose 114r‘ went out alone, on her perilous mission of rescue. She is a poor fisher- woman, unmarried, and forty years of age, so that she bas not the youth which, in the case of Grace Darling, contributed so largely to the outburst of enthusiast,. It was in 1838 that the whole country was moved by thill heroic act of Grace Darling. A public subscription was raised, to which the treasury gave £5O, and a sum of money was invested for her benefit, but she died at the early age of 27 of consumption. Rose Here is to receive a decoration, and a special reward from the Minister of Marine, and it is likely that better days are in store for her than in passing her time in picking up shellfish on the rockyshore of Brittany. Pandering to the Vices.—Paris is just now afflicted with a mania for " treasure hunts" and "guessing zompetitions." Most of the minor papers, and many of the more reputable ones, are offering their readers opportunities for gaining large sums of money. All they have to do is to discover hidden tokens in the public parks or squares, or to rightly guess the number of a certain bank note, or the number of grains of corn in a bottle or so on. As might be expected, the chance of gaining prizes has a great fascination for servants, clerks, shop girls, and others, and large numbers spend their spare time in attempts to solve these puzzles. Women and girls are even more taken up with this mania' than men, and this is perhaps why a large shop- keeper has decided to start what can only be called a new form of gambling. He las announced that on a certain day each mOnth,the whole of the money taken, will be returned to his, customers who keep, and can produce their bills. The particular day is stated in a sealed envelope, but is, of course, kept secret until the end of the month, the idea being to attract customers each day, with the hope of obtaining their purchases far nothing. Tailors and Braid.—Braiding is a form of trimming much employed by leading tailors just now, an item calculated to please the great majority of women. It is invariably, a most effective form of ornamentation, yet one about which one need feel no anxiety, concern- ing the weather. Moreover, if one is painfully thin, the clever tailor can so arrange the braids. that the wearer looks quite substantial and, more important still, he can, by following just opposite methods, ap- parently reduce the proportions of the too-abundent andi‘(idual considerably. The broad soutache, or military braids are,needless to say much more desirable and satisfactory wear than the old gold and silver varieties,which,like the rich and costly passementeries, need care taken of them. A Too-popular Trimming.—Second and third rate dressmakers and tailors, are dotting smell tassels all over their gowns, coats and wraps, witha fine 'disregard for the rule that a trimming to be a success must appear to be useful, as well as ornamental. Furriers also,would seem to have a too great regard for the tassel. To quote one example, many of their long stoles are finished off with huge specimens, and such wraps recall vividly to mind the old fashioned flat bell pull, with which we were at one time wont to adorn our walls. Probably no other trimming needs more careful arrange- ment tthan the tassel, as when this appears in an im- possible position, the effect is often ridiculous. liThe Silk Bolero.—The knitted silk bolero is having a wide vogue for morning wear. This is donned over a quite short walking skirt, which it exactly, matches in colour, the vest being of face cloth or suede, lightly worked with coloured embroidery. These boleros are exceedingly cosy, and provided the vest and collar are warmly lined, no coat will be necessary, save in the coldest weather. Many home workers, whose knitting leaves something to be desired, are crocheting the boleros., when the effect is, if anything more chic still. An Eccentric Idea.—There have always been plenty of people ready to join any leader with eccentric ideas on the subject of religion. A modern example is afforded by Zion City which is stated by Mrs. Dowie to be "a paradise on earth." It is not at any rate a paradise for smokers, for one, of.the rules is that both tobacco and alcoholic drink must he given up. Marriage is per- mitted, but on this subject Mrs. Dowie is reported to have said :—" There must be no unnecessary bother about it no prolonged courtship and flirting, and that sort of thing ; we expect the man to pop the question straight." It ill strange iadeed that people should be found willing to allow others to regulate such matters

FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Fringe is much used. this season as a trim- ming and ranks so high in popular estimation that it is even emplreyed as a finish to certain furs, the fringe in. this instance being made from the tails of the animals whose skins are employed ia the.. construction of the garment The ,effect is very good, especially on a
itself

fur cape. For vs-oorttn and heavy material dresses the heavier Tiviak-es of fringe are preferred, such as troche.t thread, while others again are of metal beads or :are tipped with coloured beads. For .evening wear nothing gives such a pretty :finish to a dainty toilette as a fringe of crystal .or irridescent beads, while for a richly flowered brocade dinner gown silk fringe ma,kes 4n ex- cellent .trimming. have seen some vedj chic

div.head: COMVOIITABLE COAT.
div.p: A COMVOIITABLE COAT.

fringes of -silk on which a pattern is printed, the result being -very charming. Others again are of shot silk, • the two contrasting tones. being skilfully blended. 'at floral patterned silk fringe, makes a striking trimming to a black or -white cloth costume, especially when grills or flounces are employed on the skirt andl edged with: the fringe which in turn, to prove 'effective, Should be finished off •at the top by a narrow ruching of silk 4ar velvet ribbon. A deeper silk fringe is usually employed on the bodice.

We have 'now to devote much of our atten- tion to outTcloor garments; And my sketch shows a very comfortable coat which is also exceedingly smart. it is made in the Russian blouse style, and is 9!ightly pouched -over the band. slack velve: 4s used in this instance for the coat lined with quilted silk, but fur or even an imitation moleskin would loOk very nice. The collar is of embroidery' and is finished at either point by a head and fur tails. The style is rather out of the common, but is very stylish. The fur par excellence this season is mole- skin, with the result that the price of- these tiny skins has, greatly gone up and, Places -them out of reach of any of those who are not possessed of a very liberal dress allowance. There is nothing really so very attractive about this peltry, -upon whom Dame Fashion smiles so affectionately, and many others which are at present neglected are really much more becoming if less fashionable. Neither is

div.head: SMART TOQUE
div.p: A SMART TOQUE

moleskin a mode which will long remain in vogue, and I should therefore counsel those who are at present in doubt as to what fur to select to invest in something which will not date itself and will therefore prove a more satisfactory purchase. The smart toque sketched is of ermine and is of quite the latest shape. It is trimmed simply by a handsome aigrette caughtt by an orna- mental cabuchon. Worn with a necklet and muff of the same fur, it makes a charming finish to a black or dark red toilette. • Fur is much used for hats and toques, and is in the French models oftep trimmed with lace or even tulle, while often natural looking flowers are likewise used as a trimming, although there seems something incongruous about the intermingling of these materials. There are some very cosy fur wraps which are suited to a slender figure. These are very much like the old- fashioned cross-overs, a deep cape over the shoulders with crossing ends extending round the waist to the back of the figure. A very charming wrap of this kind I recently saw was worn with a grey cloth costume and ,was made of chinchilla, that most becoming,

div.head: AN AFTERNOON BLOUSE
div.p: AN AFTERNOON BLOUSE
EY MARY HOLLAND,
Author of "The Diamond Shoe Buckles," "Our Seaside Adventure,' "Annette," "Morro Castle," ttc.

nelphine Aveling stood looking ateratiny .OVel tea on aright June day. The cottage garden ran tight down to the coast, ending a strip of sandy bead' from which a low stone all divided the ultivated portion of the garden.. 'Great bushes of fuchsia and myrtle grew beside the stone wall, and belphine, standing sainiaSt these, queen among her -subjects, was to the eye of -man the .fairest iflower of

but unprofitable fur. The little opening at the throat was finished off by a cravat of fine lace with long ends, while a big bunch of parma violets was fastened at the point of the V. A toque likewise of chinchilla gave the requisite .touch, together with a muff of the same fur trimmed with lace and also boasting a bunch of scented violets. These furs could be copied less expensively in imitation grey astrakan.

"My birthday! lEightem ! Oh, for a year or Iwo—only that—Of freedom. Then I 'could do it,, ,perhaps—but there might be someone else by that time. Oh!" with a shrug and a smile that had no :joy in it, "it's better done and over. He must know—he cannot think for an instant that I, a girl,
can love, im that was, r mannold•enough to be my father!" • • •
Delphine'had lived this simple life in the cottage on the coast ever since she could remember.

The cottage, which belonged to Lord Granton, was let to Mr. Avelino' at a nominal rent. Had his pride 'permitted, Mr.e'Aveling could have had the house rent-free, for Lord Granton was an enthusiastic admirer of his talents, and was eagerly desirous of assisting in a substantial manner the man whom he considered poverty had lost to the world. Mr: Aveling's writings had been known to Lord Granton icing before the two gentlemen were personally acquainted, for the man of study had taken the pretty seaside cottage during the absence of his landlord.

Lord'Granton had returned home after years of I travel -some eight years ago. He had immediately sonata the friendship of his tenant; and though 'fifteen years the junior of Mr. Aveling, his interest in the 'researches of his new friend' nom made him a welcome companion to the recluse. For the last two years, however, Miss Rachel Aveling's quick perception had discovered to her a -stronger motive in Lord Granton's visits. He was more frequently found'in the garden or drawing- room now than in the study. During these two years another change, too, had been gradually and painfully making itself known in the household. Mr. Aveling's health was rapidly failing. A chest complaint, developed from a slight beginning, was quickly gaining ground. The doctor, from gently hinting at the necessity for change from this bracing eastern coast, now began openly to declare that unless a trip to Algiers, Egypt, or the Cape 'were taken, he would not answer for his patient's recovery. And how that change was to be procured—this was the -problem for Rachel Aveling and her niece. The problem could have been easily solved had Lord Granton been permitted to take the matter into his hands. He would have sent or taken the invalid away without delay. But Mr. Aveling would not accept charity. Then Lord Granton, • speaking gently aside to Miss Aveling, but looking the while at Delphine, said, quietly: "If I might but have the right—the right of a son." And Miss Aveling, responding to the half- question in his tone, said: "Perhaps you could, if you tried." Her next step had been to tell Delphine that in her hands lay her father's hope of restoration, whispering to the girl her belief in Lord Granton's love for her, a love he was too modest to hope would be returned. A hundred remembrances came floating back to Delphine, confirming her aunt's suggestions. Yes, he loved her, and, if he spoke, as he would soon,. no doubt—to-day, perhaps—she must accept that love for her dear father's sake. The conversation with her aunt had taken place in the morning. When it was over Delphine had run into the garden to think, and to cry out against

her fate. She heard a step on the crisp sand, quickly coming nearer, from the direction in which lay Granton Castle. Lord Granton generally. came by way of the beach, leaping the little wall and coming up the garden to eater the house by one of the long windows in the drawing-room. Delphine's heart beat more quickly, yet she fancied she did not recognise the step. In another instant a man came in sight, but—and she gave a sigh of relief—his was not the figure of Lord -Granton. Is he came nearer, Delphine saw that this was a young man, tall like Lord Granton, but more erect. As he caught sight of Delphine, he lifted his tweed cap, and with a bright smile greeted the girl. "Miss Aveling, I hope ?" he cried, stopping at the foot of the wall. "May I leap this formidable barrier? I come, fully accredited, from Granton Castle." Delphine laughed—a, laugh of unfeigned joy. "I ought to tell you who I am," he began, but Delphine broke in upon his explanation. - "I know before you speak. You are Lord Gran- ton's Victor,' the model of youths in general, and the pattern of nephews in particular." The young man's face clouded over. "I suppose my uncle has been making me *ridiculous to you ? " he said. "By no means. But he cs—and with cause— exceedingly proud of his soldierly nephew. I assure you that you stand only second in his affections to—" The girl stopped short, blushing in confusion. The conversation with her aunt flashed back upon her mind, giving a new significance to the words she had all but spoken. "Yourself," said Victor, laughing. "I know all about you, Miss Aveling. My uncle has adored you since you could walk; and if, I am the model of young men, you are his paragon among women." Delphine joined happily in the laugh. • "Where do you come from ? " she asked. "Lord Granton did not speak last night of expecting you." "I came down !Ton him like the wolf in the night, only not so brightly accoutred as the Assyrian. lam the bearer of a message and a parcel for' you, Miss Aveling, and, as I am informed that this is your birthday, I beg to have the honour of adding my congratulations to those of my uncle. Lord Granton has been so unfortu- nate as to slip his knee this morning, and will be unable to walk for a day or two. He therefore desires me to make his apologies, and to ask you to accept his gift from the hands of an unworthy substitute." "Lord Granton is far too kind," murmured Delphine, blushing, as she saw from the shape and size of the parcel that her present was contained in a jewel-case. . The present consisted of two pretty bracelets, half bangle in form, each set with gems. One had a diamond star in the centre, the other con- tained threepearls of exceeding beauty. Victor Mainwaring took each of the girl's pretty hands in turn, and slipped a bracelet round the slender wrist. "They look prettier now," he said, holding out her hands; and then his look glanced upwards to her dimpling face, and rested there until Delphine withdrew her hands in haste, and turned away, blushing, to gather a spray of fuchsia. . "I remember now," she said, her voice trembling slightly, "that I admired some gold bangles a . girl was wearing who stayed at the Vicarage. He must have heard me. I wish he would not be so kind. You must tome in now, and see my father' and aunt," she added, turning to Victor. "Need I? Not yet, surely?" he said, plaintively. "It is so pleasant here. I had no idea Wythe was such an enchanting place. Don't you admire Granton Castle, Miss Aveling ? " "It is certainly fine, but gloomy, I think," she said, with a little shudder. "It only wants a woman's presence.” Delphine shook her head. Victor looked at her keenly. "It needs something more, then?. I doubt if my uncle understands women. Miss Aveling, you wish to see the world ? You don't want to be mewed up here all your life? " "No, indeed. I often wish— But what makes you say that ? " She looked curiously at him, even with a little awe, as if lie were in some degree a seer. "I understand girls—that's all. Nature may be very charming, and study very attractive—l know all your accomplishments, I assure you, Miss Aveling." "Don't!" cried Delphine, putting out her hand deprecatingly. "Very well, I won't," answered Victor, taking her hand. "But girls want dances, parties, new dresses and—lovers." DelPhine gave a little start. The colour rose in her cheek. She drew her hand away quickly. How this young man read her thoughts! To her simple mind, it seemed as if he possessed wonderful intuition. She sprang up from the low wall on which they bad been sittine.

Lord Granton 's hurt knee kept him prisoner for longer than he had anticipated. Every day Victor found his way to the cottage garden. When he could walk, Lord Granton had been there one evening when Victor and Deiphine had arranged tea out of doors. He watched them flitting backwards and forwards, making a pretence of requiring some slight assistance from each other. He saw Delphine's quick blush and glad smile whenever Victor called her by. her Christian nene as he had done since the second day of his acquaintance with the girl. He saw, as 11', quietly sat by, many signs that made him feel __Us opportunity had gone by for ever. He,could not bear the pain at first. So he stayed away, and made plans whereby Mr. Aveling should still, through the instrumentality of his daughter, gain the required change." If Victor and Delphine loved each other, there was no reason why they should not be married immediately. One evening a mote came to him. "Dear Lord Granton,—l am so sorry; it was all roy fault! Your nephew, in clambering down the cliffs to get me some Parnassus grass, fell and sprained his ankle. The doctor says there is no need for anxiety, but Mr. Mainwaring cannot, of course, walk. Aunt Rachel says I am to tell you we will nurse him carefully, and you must come to-morrow and see him. —DELPIIINE. Well, here was the climax. Victor would play the invalid for a day or two. Delphine would, in her pretty way, play the nurse. Before Victor returned to the Castle these two would be engaged. So thought Lord Granton. When Victor was visited by his uncle next day, he was fulfilling that gentleman's expectations almost literally. The injured foot was resting on cushions; the invalid, proppedo up with more cushions, was supposed to be playing draughts with Delphine, who was sitting on a low chair close to him. "Hullo, Uncle Gerald! Come to see how much of an impostor I am ? " "He's not an impostor at all, Lord Granton. His foot is badly hurt. You know it is, Victor." The name, slipping out unconsciously, made Delphine blush, but Lord Granton feigned an admirable indifference. He paid but a short visit. "Shall I send the carriage round, Victor ? " he asked; "we must not inconvenience Miss Aveling too much." "Miss Aveling is kind enough to say I don't give her so very much trouble, uncle," said Victor; "and really I am afraid I couldn't even limp as far as the gate to-day. Perhaps till-morrow." Next morning, Delphine gathYred a moss-rose bud, , and came and put it' in Victor's coat. She knelt . beside Him, to fasten it securely. As she did so, his arm passed round her, and he drew her close, whispering: "Kiss me, Delphine." For an instant the girl hesitated. "Kiss me," he said again, and she no longer resisted. She bent over him and pressed her sweet lips on his forehead. "Kiss me on the lips," he commanded. But, blushing at having bestowed the first caress, she rose quickly, saying: "No, no." She felt some- thing was wrong. In all the love stories she had read, tho lover gave the first kiss. Now, she had given without receiving. "0 Victor What have I done ? " she cried, tears starting to her eyes. "You have had your first lover, that's all, child," laughed Victor. "I wish you would kiss me again and again, Delphine. You have the sweetest lips of any woman I know!" Crimson with shame, the girl listened to these words. What did he mean? Why did he not say more? Why did he not ask her now, as all lovers did in novels, to be his wife? Just then the door-bell rang. Distressed and agitated, Delphine rushed from the room, almost falling into Lord Granton's arms on the threshold. With a quick word of apology, she passed him. "I'm afraid I came at an unlucky moment, my boy," he said to Victor. But Miss Aveling entering, he explained that he had driven down on the chance of his nephew being able to return with him. "I hear the new people have come to Mount Eden. You said they were friends of yours, I think? A Mrs. Montresor, her daughter, and 3 large party, Fowler tells me." "Any men ? " asked Victor, anxiously, sitting up. "I fancy he said a good many. I don't remora.. ber. I suppose you'll have to call ? " "Of course. lam constantly at the Montresors' when lam in town. She is awfully rich; the daughter is a great heiress, and an uncommonly handsome girl.' "I suppose she is the Ida Montresor ' one sees such a fuss made about in the papers," remarked Miss Aveling. "Yes. Well, uncle, if you think you can give me an arm, I'll try to reach the carriage. I'm sure 7'm tremendously grateful to you, Miss Aveling, ior all your kindness. I shall call and thank you when I am over this." "I will call Delphine, if you are really going," said Miss Aveling, looking rather perplexed. "Where can she be ? " "Your niece has a bad headache to-day, I'm afraid," said Victor. "Pray don't disturb her." "You will certainly see him here again very soon, foot well or not," remarked Lord Granton, looking very arch. Then they went away, and Delphine, looking from the window, knew not what the meaning was of the sudden fear that seized her. The headache that Victor had feigned for her had come in truth, and she was thankful to spend the day in her darkened room. In the evening she heard Lord Granton come, in the accustomed way. Her window was open, and she heard him say to her

aunt: • "Victor insisted on driving to Mount Eden this afternoon. The carriage returned without him, with a line to say he was over tired, and that Mrs. Montresor had insisted on his remaining. I must go and call on her to-morrow, when the carrriage goes for Victor." I fortnight passed and Victor did not return. Lord Granton, coming 'every night to the cottage, expressed great and ever greater surprise at his nephew's protracted visit. He saw with a stricken heart Delphine's pale and weary face. 3rie day when they were alone together, he said: "Have you heard from Victor,Delphine ? " She shook her head. "I do not expect to hear from your nephew," she answered, a shade of defiance in her tone. What could Victor mean? Lord Granton dared not ask the girl what had paSsed between Victor and herself, yet he could not but believe that , his nephew had behaved in such a way towards.: Delphine as to justify her and her relations in expecting him to make her an offer of marriage. Lord Granton said no more, but next day he drove over to Mount Eden to see his nephew. lie was ou tueearaen terrace. From a window, he could see his nephew sitting under a wide-spreading cedar at the feet of Miss Montresor. His head WR B resting against her side. Her hand fondled his hair and caressed his brow. Suddenly Victor looked up and 'caught sight of his uncle standing in the window. 'He isprung up, said a laughing word -to Ida, kissed her cheek, and strode quickly across the lawn. Springing up a flight of stone steps be stood a minute later before his uncle. "Welcome, Uncle Gerald," he said, extending his hand with a frank smile. "You have come just at the right time to offer me your • congratulations. Ida accepted me last night." Lord Granton drew back his hand. "I hardly understand you," he said. "I was under the impression'that you were as good as engaged to Miss Aveling." Victor opened his eyes. To Miss Aveling ? Oh, Delphine, do you mean ? Well, that is rich, uncle ! Why, I regarded that young lady as your exclusive and entire property." Lord Granton's face grew dark. "And therefore you went day after day to see her? To make love to her? You took advantage of a young girl's innocent trust in you to amuse yourself in trying to engage her affections. You abused the hospitality of her relations by taking, the opportunity their kinddess offered you to—to-0 Victor, that one of my own blood should be such a dastard!" Victor laughed aloud. " How dare you, sir! How dare you!," Lord Graaton's voice was raised in loud anger—his face was white with passion.

My last sketch shows an aiternoon blouse of washing silk trimmed with lace. It is made in a very pretty style and could be worn with a coat, an impossibility with some of the very elaborate designs. Blouses are now worn eithtr in white or cream or in a silk which matches as closely as possible the colour of the skirt worn with it. This is a change from the violent contrasts of a few seasons ago. Taffetas is a favourite material for blouses and is much tucked and drawn and further ornamented by lace applique. The little turn- over lila. collars make a pretty finish to the throats of a morning or afternoon blouse, and these.can be easily made at home out of one of the pretty lace bordered handkerchiefs one can so readily obtain in any good drapers fot a few pence. The collar is made by cutting oft one side about an inch wide which is tacked into a plain band of cambric and forms the turn-over collar, while the remainder of the handkerchief is neatly pleated, the edges hemmed and tacked* under the centre of the band. •

No, thanks, I must tt getting oefore I sell illrs. Montresor and tell her what sort back. How the time has gone! I supper you are of man sll eha 1 accepted as her daughter's &'great deal in the garden, Miss Aveling ew husband." . 'Yes, especially on these fine days." "Mrs. Montresor is a woman of the world. She "Good-bye "—taking her hand. "May I come would hardly understand a man in your position again—to-morrow? " with a petitioning look in his playing champion to a village maiden. Really, handsome dark eyes. Uncle Gerald, I thought— Oh! "Yes, if you care to," Delphine's colour rose For Lord Granton, after turning sharply to him. again. "But you must eome in next. time and see with a threatening gesture, had as quickly turned papa and my aunt.", . wain. Ida Montresor had entered, and was gazing He sprang to the beach, lifted his cap, and was at him in astonishment. Lord Granton faced her gone. for a moment. "Ask my nephew 'to relate what has been passing between him and me, madam. If after that recital you still wish to marry him, I can only say I pity you from the bottom of my heart." With these words he left the room and was gone. Victor broke into a low laugh. . "rs your uncle a little odd, Victor ? " asked the young lady. . 0 "On one -subject, apparently," said Victor, laughing again. And then he proceeded to give his fiancee an amusing account of his uncle's infatua- tion for a rural beauty, and his jealousy at Victor's having shewn some little admiration for the good looks of his inamorata. 111.

Lord C4ranton drove home in a very uncomfort- able state of mind. He felt he had come off badly in the interview with his nephew, his show of temper only disabling him in the presence of the young man's cool self-possession. And—how was he to tell Delphine ? As he drove 'past the white cottage, she was standing at the gate in the act of closing it. She saw him, and be called to the coachman to stop..
Delphine opened the gate and put her hand out to him. - ,
..... "You have something to tell me.?: she said, looking in. his face.

"Yes , child." . "Shall we go into the garden ? " asked the girl. "As you please, my dear." She led him to her favourite seat under a bower of roses and honeysuckle. Then she said, lifting her eyes calmly to his: • "I know what you aro going to say, and I know, too, that you dread saying it. Your nephew is going to marry Miss Montresor." Lord Granton-started and looked anxiously at the girl, so pale and yet so calm. "How did you know, Delphine ?" "I was told of it just now at the Vicarage. The vicar had dined and slept at Mount Eden last night. But it was not a surprise to me. For on,. thing, I had a dream. ,But, more than that, -"I have seen things in their true light lately." "What do you mean, child ? " • "Yes," she went on. "I was foolish and romantic. And, ,worse than that, I was rebellious and ungrateful. 'When: he came with his words of .flattery and of insincere love, I was so happy that I forgot everything. • I let him master me. It seemed so—so sweet—to have a lover of my own age, so handsome and so—just what my fancy had painted." The blushes were dyeing her cheeks, her slender hands wrung each other in nervous agitation. Lord Granton bent`tenderly over her. "My dear little one, spare yourself. yourself and inc this pain ? " .She looked up at him through her tears " You ? " she said, wonderingly. "You should be glad, because now you know how—how worth- less I am I " He took her band.
Why givo

"Delphine, nothing that could happen to you could ever lessenrby one jot or tittle your worth in my eyes. I had had the vanity to think I might win you for my wife.- I meant to come on your birth- day and ask you if you could give me some of the love I craved. The night before, my sister's son, Victor, came and took me by surprise. He seemed to me a splendid fellow, so high spirited and hand- some. I said to myself: How would it be if Delphine accepted me out of pity, and afterwards —too late—met one like him ? ' I dared not risk such a disaster. So I made the most,of my slight injury and sent him nto you. When I saw him and you together, I congratulated myself that I had made the experiment. You and he seemed to be made for each other."

Delphine shook her head. "No; I see it now. He is a man of the world— cruel, selfish. You could not understand such an ' one. Child, how can I atone for the suffering I have brought on you ? " "Dear Lord Granton, why will you blame your- self? You thought, as you always did, only of the good of others. Aunt Rachel had told me that morning of—.-of—what you proposed. You wanted to help papa and all of us. And I—l meant to say Yes. But I only meant to do so as a duty— for papa's sake. Then—when he came—l forgot everything but My own selfish wishes." "It was only natural." "Ah I I have paid for it with the price of my own pride and self-respect. When he left and saw he did not mean- to come back, the pain of the mortification was what I felt most. I know from that that I did not really care for him as I fancied I did while he was here. But oh! the bitter, bitter shame of it! He actually—" She covered her face with her hands, while between .the slender fingers Lord Granton could see that her face was again suffused w,ith blushes. "Delphine, you must not allow yourself to suffer so much. If—if, as you say, he did not win your best love, be happy for that much. Let him not cost you one other thought, one other pang." "You are right, right!" she cried, springing up. "I shame myself the more by dwelling on my shame." "And you will let me be your friend as before, my child?" "I do not deserve your friendship," she said, sadly. Then with a sudden impulse she seiied his band, pressed it to her lips, and fled indoors. A week later Mr. Aveling received a letter from the Research Society asking his acceptance of a yearly pension of two hundred pounds, as a mark of the high esteem in which he was held by the members. As the society was in the habit Of granting these -pensions to members whose work they deemed of especial value, Mr. Aveling accepted the offer in the spirit in which it was made. In reply to his letter of acceptance, he received a further communication from the secretary saying that a gentleman greatly interested in the work of the society had offered to defray the expenses of a trip to Egypt, of som.! member specially qualified to elucidate an antiquarian difficulty at that time greatly exercising the minds of the learned society, and asking Mr. Aveling, as one notably fitted for the mission, to undertake the journey. Delphine was quick to see who was the originator of these proposals, but as her father remained in happy ignorance of being the recipient of any special favour she kept her own counsel and deter- mined to thank Lord Granton in private for his generosity. , • She was further confirmed in her suspicions by Lord Granton's offering, upon hearing the news, to accompany her father on the trip. When she thanked him, with tears in her eyes, he answered laughing that she was a great deal too "deep," but he read in her look and manner that which filled his heart with a new feeling of hope —a hope that some day Delphine might love him tor himself.
Standing one June morning, as she had stood a year ago, Delphine is watching for the codling of one whom now she looks for with joyful expectation. _ .

Her face has regained its foriner radiance, but there is upon it afresh sweetness and tenderness. • She hears the step at last, and shyly advances to greet the new-comer. Lord Granton sees her, and a glad light over- spreado his handsome face. Lightly he leaps the little boundary and is at her; side, taking in his own the outstretched hands s fair girl-love. "Were you looking for me, Delphine ? " he asks, listening with tender anv;ety for her answer. "I am always lookisyi tor you now," she says, softly, yet so that his ear catches every syllable. "My darling! My lose! You love me, Delphine ? You are glad ,to see me?"

"Glad?" ' The one word, the look that goes with it, are enough. Deluhine is clasped to his heart. Lord Granton knows now, at last, that she is his—his very own. By-and-bye, .when she whispers "yes" in answer to the question : "And you will be my wife?" he asks further, though he knows the question is unnecessary and only for his own gratification: , "Do you say.' yes' for duty or for love?" - And she whispers: "For love, only for love ! I think," she adds, Tory softly, "that I have loved you always, though I did not know it."
[THE END. 1

Nothing of the kind has never taken place in this country before, for, while goods engines have been supplied by American firms, no British rail- way has ever before acquired from abroad an express passenger loco,- - The fame of
THE COMPETITIVE ENGINES.

the De Glehn four-cylinder compound engine is expected to be fully maintained by "La France." This engine has ten wheels: a four - wheeled bogie, four coupled driving wheels, and a pair of trailing wheels under the Belpaire fire-box. There are four cylin- ders : two high-pressure, placed outside the frames, and two low-pressure, arranged inside the framing under the .smoke-box. The re- markable feature about the De Glehn system of compounding, which is believed to be the secret of its success, is that the engine pos- sesses the advantage of being workable as a four cylinder simple engine whenever circum- stances render such an operation desirable; further, it is claimed that practically any rates of expansion can be obtained as the running dictates.

div.head: OUR ROYAL VISITORS.
div.p: OUR ROYAL VISITORS.

The visit of the King and Queen of Italy to England next week is being looked forward to with no small interest. It is the first State visit to Windsor since . the German Emperor and Empress were entertained there in 1899, and guat preparations are being made. In the first place, an imposing naval welcome will be given to their Majesties, who will be brought from Cherbourg to ,Ports- mouth on the Victoria and Albeit, escorted by the flagship of the Channel Squadron and -some cruisers. Landing at Portsmouth on Tuesday, they will proceed direct to Windsor by special train, where they will be met by King Edward. There will be a State dinner and a dramatic performance by Sir Charles Wyndham and Miss Mary Moore; and the .daytime will be occupied in shooting over -the famous royal preserves. On Thursday the King and-Queen of Italy will pay a visit to London, arriving at Paddington in the :forenoon. The whole route is to .be gaily -decorated in their honour, and they will drive -to the Guildhall via Oxford. Street and Hol- born.

div.head: CIVIC LONDON'S EVENT OF THE YEAR.
div.p: CIVIC LONDON'S EVENT OF THE YEAR.

Though Lord Mayor's Day is sail by some .to excite less and less interest eve:y year, the annual civic function this year, on Monday last, was accorded no less enthusiam than has ,been evident or the past .four or five years. 'The old barbarous • splendour, however, is 'suffering extinction, gradual but unmistak- able, this year's show being more monochro- matic than ever before. The function really .consisted of a Volunteer display (among whom %were the smart "Rough Riders" of London), .and the Lord Mayor's banquet, always im- Tortant owing to the distinguished chata.ccer :of the guests. While the speeches were in -progress dancing in the library commenced, and continued until a .late hour. The new Lord Mayor, .Aid. Sir J. T. Ritchie, does not go into residence at the Mansion House until it has undergone cleaning, redecorating, and partly this operation which is to cost this year over -E,600. Alderman Sir James Thompson Ritchie was born at Dundee in 1835. In due course he became a partner ALD. SIR J. T. RITCHIE, MISS RITCHIE, LORD MAYOR.. -.ESS.

Sir James was founder of the London Jute Association, and was for twenty-eight years chairman of the society, retiring only this year. He has been identiiied with the municipal work of the Corporation for the past twelve years, having been elected Alderman for the Tower Ward in 1891. In 1894 the .Lord Mayor sustained a sad loss by the death of his wife. Conse- quently, the office of Lady Mayoress will be filled during the coming year by his eldest unmarried daughter. Miss Ritchie. Alderman Sir John Knill, one of the sheriffs, •is a mem- ber of the firm of John -Knill & Co., wharf- . ingers and warehouse .keepers. THE NEW MEMBER FOR CHORLEY. div.head: KINETON TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE KINETON TRAGEDY.

The terrible tragedy which has just taken place at Compton Verney, Lord Willoughby cle Broke's beautiful house 'in Warwickshire, will be a grave warning against idle flirtation, as jealousy seems 'to have been at the root of the crime. Annie Devall, the head laun- drymaid, a fine and pretty girl, was engaged to

Walter-Cciuzens, of Chippenham, a labourer ; but after she had been a little while at Comp- ton. Verney, which is let to Herbert Smith,the bank- er, she jilted him, because, as she said, she could not stick to • one man. Last week Couz- ens came over to see her in the afternoon, and in the..even- ANNIE DEVALL, ing they again THE MURDERDD GIRL. met. That night the girl did not return to the house; and out side the house on the lawn there were signs of a terrific struggle. By these her body was traced to a ditch, and she was found murdered and fearfully mutilated. Couzens had, in the . meantime, disappeared. He took train to London, and thence to Swindon. From there he went to Wootton Bassett, where he had supper and-went to bed. Two hours later he was arrested by the police, who had tracked him very cleverly. He was brought up before the magistrates at Kineton and formally re- manded.

div.head: ARMENIAN VENDETTA.
div.p: THE ARMENIAN VENDETTA.

It is many long years since London had such a sensation in its midst as that afforded by the Armenian Vendetta in Peckham. The actual neighbourhood is in a state of terror, and all Armenians are going about under police protection. This terrible blood feud is between the Hentchakists and the Alfarists, two Armenian secret political societies, of which the former has been formed with the abject of freeing Armenia from the rule of Turkey. The Alfarists are pro-Turkey, and it is rumoured that that country is financing the assassins. The first move in the tragedy occurred in Switzerland a few weeks back, when a prominent Hentchakist was stabbed. M. Sagouni went over to minister to him and investigate the circumstances, and upon his return the week before last he was shot on his own doorstep in Nunhead Grove. The assassin got clean away, and was not heard of until last week, when he shot two other

div.p: RTER S 01

PECKHA NI RYE,

Hentchakists, Grigorian and Izmiriam, in Peckham Rye. A third Hentzhakist, Kara- petian, escaped ; this time, fortunately, the murderer did not again escape scot free, but was bowled over by a man called Jarvis, who ran out of a side passage. Jarvis with great bravery possessed himself of the murderer's revolver after a struggle. Then the murderer, whose name appears to be Yorgie Yangie, drew another revolver from his pocket and shot himself, sitting on the pavement. In all cakes the shots were instantaneously fatal.

Prestwich, went to him and laid information for bigamy against the prisoner, who was then passing as Dr. Her- bert Part, of Golborne. An arrest was at once effected. Mrs. Ellen Part stated to him that she was married in January,l9oo. Her husband only stayed with her ten days and then sailed on a boat for New York. On a second voyage on August 11, 1900, he died, and was buried at sea. In proof of this she produced a certifi- cate which she had received from Dr. Herbert Part's brother stating that he had died on a Transatlantic steamer. On a communication being received from Mr. W. J. Part, of NVarrington, that gentleman came to Manchester and was shown two photographs. One of these, which was the prisoner, he failed to recognise, but the other he at once said was a photograph of his brother,the late Dr. Part. Doubts being thus raised as to the identity of the man in charge; the Superintendent asked him if he had any statement to make. REMINISCENT OF TICHBORNE. He at once made the emphatic state:light "I am Dr. Herbert Part, and 'gay practiced at Bank House, Golborne. • I fttriediEllen Kershaw in January,49oo, and I left her'tendaYs after marriage. I went asVship's doctor, andduthig•the se,cond voy- age I concocted a story with'theviirser and steward to put me ashore at New Yoric-efid cable home the news of my death." At Leigh the Superintendent di46overed that prisoner had been to the County Court and claimed moneys be- longing to the late Dr. Herbert Part. He caused a large number of people to come from, Golborne, Warrington, and Liverpool,together with the'brother of the late doctor and the chief engineer of the vessel, who happened to be in Liverpool. Prisoner was con- fronted with all these people, and the whole of the'men after putting a large number of questions, absolutely refused to believe that he was the real and rightful Dr. Part. The Superintendent himself asked about forty questions, to which he gave inaccurate replies. Asked what was the year of his birth, he gave a date altoget- her different from that of Dr. Herbert Part. One woman however, identified the smaller photograph, and shook hands with the prisoner, and became very sentimental. He-picked out the right man for his brother, and sub- sequently said, "It is my brother," spoke to him al Jack, and said, "You rememoer me." "Jack" dis- believed him altogether. EXTRAORDINARY CONFESSION. Whenitold thnt investigations would be made as to his movements in January, 1900, thv prisoner made the following extraordinary confession:— " I am Dr: Hubert Part, but not the Dr. Herbert Part who practised at Bank House, Golborne. I was in Liverpool when Dr. H. Part, of Golborne, returned from his first voyage. I met him at the Bee Hotel in Liverpool: Ife was talking to some men about his being at sea as a ship's doctor. They asked me if I would join them in a drink, which I did. Dr. Part told me the boat he had been on and said he was married and wanted to escape from his wife. Thenhe told meabout his brother. What I have learned about the family- I have got from the girl. I ought to say that Dr. H. Part gave me his card giving his address Bank House, Golborne, "I was born ill Adelaide on April 21, 1866. My father was-a retired farmer. I first caff:e to England about eighteen years ago. T had plenty of money and so did!nothing. I commenced practising as a doctor at New York. It is about four and a half years ago since I came to England the last time. I did nothing till about 15 months ago when I came to Pinder and Johnson, doctors, Great Clowes-street, Salford. I qualified as a doctor in New York, but never in England: I practised as a doctor at Pinder and Jobnson's, and whilst I stayed at Prestwich with my wife I prescribed occasionally for people; but I did not pat up my name plate. I also practised as a doctor at La Page's, in Salford, and the last place I was at, was D. Chapman's, Vine-street, Hulme. "When my wife brought Mrs. Herbert Part, of Golborne, tome and charged me with having married her, and said T had committed bigamy, I admitted it to her, and said they-could do their worst. I thought my wife would'not take action against me. " I declare to you: now, and confess that I never married Ellen Kershaw, of G3lborne, as stated, and what I said respecting that and being Dr. Herbert Part was untrue. I never married anyone but Alice Ford, who is my lawful wife. ladmit, also, that when I put the letters L.R.C.P., L.R.C.L., and L.F.P.S. after my name I had no right to do so." Upon this the bigamy charge was withdrawn, and prisoner was charged with an offence against Mrs. Ellen Part, ?f Golborne, by impersonating her husband. LOVE LETTE'RS FROM GAOL. Another extraordinary feature of the case was the letters which the prisoner, before the exposure, wrote to both women. Supt. M‘Kenzie read a letter of seven pages addressed to Mrs. Ellen Part beginning "My dearest wife," and ending "Your own true loving husband, H. Part." The letter invited Mrs. Part to come across to pristiner's house, and she did so. The letter was couched in the most affectionate language. Whilst in goal he wrote letters to both women, styling both '; His dearest wife,' and concluding the letters. "Believe me still your ever loving husband,H. Part." Prisoner was further charged under the Medical Act of 1855, with falsely pretending to be a physician and surgeon, and obtaining registration by a false repre- sentation. In answer to that charge prisoner said: "I am not on the English register, I know." Whilst with Drs. Pinder and Johnson, Higher Broughton, he met Alice Ford, of Prestwich, and married her in December, 1902:

"T have no doubt at all," said the Superintendent. "that he is a rank impostor, and I know he is a most consistent and confirmed liar. One can scarcely con- ceive the pain, annoyance, and expense caused to the relatives of the late Dr. Part." THE DECEIVED "WIFE." Mrs. Ellen Part was then called, and stated that her husband left her in January, 1900, after only being married ten days, and that she had never seen him since. On receipt of prisoner's letter she went to his lodgings and met him. He represented himself to be her husband, and she believed him, thinking that no one else would' be able to tell her the things that he did. The Stipendiary: Did you honestly believe him to be your husband? Witness: Yes. She stayed at prisoner's rooms until next morning. Prisoner was remanded until next Tuesday. He made an application for bail, but the Stipe'ndiary promptly refused it. His wife and Mrs. Ellen Part, who during a portion of the proceedings sat next to one another in front of the dook, left the court together.
SIX MONTHS FOR A RUNCORN BLACKLESTER.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Friday Henry Cooke, Fryer-street, a well-known character and blacklister, was charged on remind with having been drunk in High- street on the 4th,. also with having attempted to ob- tain intoxicating liquor in Runcorn on the Sunday. P.C. Oakes proved the first charge. The evidence on the second was that the prisoner entered the Holyhead Harbour Inn, the George and Dragon Inn, and the Masonic Arms Inn and asked to be supplied with drink. He was refused at all the places. He admitted that what drink he had had he got in IVidnes. He was bound over in £lO and two sureties of £5 each to be of good beinviour for two months, or in default to go to gaol for six months. He went to gaol.

div.head: WANTED: MORE BABIES.
div.p: WANTED: MORE BABIES.

in recent years so many gloomy predictions have been made concerning the decline in the birth rate in Groat Britain, that it is quite refreshinglto find that John Bull has still left a remnant of sturdy sons and daughters possessing the faculty of perpetuating their species in a degree not one whit less than the most prolific of their ancestors.

To the Lincolnshire Agricultural Society we are in- debted for this inspiriting discovery. At their Annual Exhibition held recently in Lincoln, prizes were offered to the labourers who had brought up and placed out the greatest number of children. The first prize was awarded to Thomas Honght, of Tealby, Market Rasen, with a record of 19 children born, 17 brought up and 12 placed out, Other competitors had families of 16, 15. 1-1, 13 and 12, there being altogether ten entries for . the prizes offered.

That large families, such as these, should still be common in rural districts, at a time when the birth rate is steadily declining in the great centres of industry and commerce, is but another proof of the damaging I effect of city life and air upon the national health and vitality. One eminent authority declares that of per- sons city born and bred, who have attained the awe of thirty years, not more than one in every ten is free from indigestion in one or the other of its varied forms. When we consider how the body is starved and poisoned and the vital functions impaired by this scourge of modern life, we cannot be surprised at any shrinkage in the birth rate or deterioration in the national physique. To stop this ruinous loss of vital- ity and restore the national stomach to its former efficiency is an object worthy the support of every true patriot. Fortunately no time need be lost in experiments. In Mother Seigel's Syrup we have, at hand, a digestive tonic that exerts a cprative and stim- ulating influence upon the debilitated organs of diges- tion, which fully justifies the position it has held for , thirty-five years as the national remedy for indigestion. To tens of thousands of tortured dyspeptics it has brought comfort, health and renewed vitality. One of them—Mr. W. Nicholls, of Whitehall Mansions, Arch- way road, Holloway, N., says - "At one time every- thing rate, and especially the things that I most relished, seemed specially designed for my torture. After every meal the pain and discomfort in my body and the sense of fulness and oppression at the chest were most distressing and wearisome. Coupled with this were constant retching and the frequent vomiting of an acid fluid. It didn't much matter what or how little I ate, my stomach seemed utterly utteq_ual to its task and I suffered in consequence. Though I regulated my diet and tried all manner of medicine, I gained no perman- ent relief until I had recourse to Mother Seigel's Syrup and that went right to the root of the malady. in a very short time, under its influence, I could eat whatever was set before me without fear of pain or distress, and felt brighter and more buoyant than I had done for months. if by any chance, anything that I eat disagrees with me, a few doses of Seigel's Syrup invariably puts me right again. As a digestive tonic T consider it has n 9 equal and my own experience and observation justify me in strongly recommending it to all who are cursed with indigestion ora weak stomach." Abounding vitality and buoyant healthfulnes such as follow the use of this tonic of fruits, roots and herbs, are the surest antidotes to dwindling birth rates and national decay.

UNITED 13.t.ND Si HoeE.—The second public meeting of the session in connection with the Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath Band of Hope was held in Ebenezer Chapel on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. In the unavoidable absence of the Presi- dent the chair was occupied by Mr. Joseph Mounfield, who set forth the benefits of total abstinence. An address was delivered by Mrs. Simpson, of Warrington in which she appealed to all present to help those who were suffering through intemperarne. A good programme had been provided, consisting of recitations by Jane Harmer. Mabel Proud. Mary E rle, May Vernon, Florrie Lowe, Elith Cole, Evelyn Beet, Annie Broadhurst, Lillian Hall, and Masters James Lloyd, H. Earle, A. Bailey and S. Jones. Masters G. Arthur Whitfield con- tributed an organ solo. Selections were given on the auto harp by Mr. W. Wood,and songs by Master Stanley Jones, Miss Winnie Jones, Miss Rotighsedge, and Mr. J. Roughs.edge. On the proposition of Mr. H. Brereton, hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Simpson and all who had contributed to the programme. Master Whitfield, Miss Woods, and Mr. A. 11.Dunn,accompanied the various musical items on the organ.

div.head: REMARKABLE CASE.
div.p: A REMARKABLE CASE.

Very few men are alive to-day who have been so near death's door as Mr. Robert Rodgers, Quarry Buildings, Blackridge, Linlithgowshire, Scotland. Mr: Rod gars had Diabetes. He describes thesymptoms as follows : " I was always hungry, and terribly thirsty, my back pained me and when I sat down it was only with the greatest difficulty that T could rise again. My teeth became loose and my gums bled. I used to have a fluttering around my heart, soreness of the bowels,pains between my shoulders and through my hips, so that I could hardly lie in bed. T lost sixteen pounds in six weeks and I was so weak that I could hardly crawl about."
He is at work now and explains how the remarkable change has been brought about in these words:—

"I consulted several doctors and took a deal of medicine, but nothing did me any good, until I com- menced using Dodd's Kidney Pills. They gave me great relief from the start. They did wonders for me and as soon as I found they were doing me any good, I left off all other medicines and took Dodd's Kidney Pills until was completely cured. T an back at my work and I enjoy the best of health without a trace of the old trouble."

It is Drink! We spend about £180,099,030 w-yOolr upon it.

Is there any remAy ? S nue countrie forbid; its. sale. You cannot do that here. Preach temperance, say some; start cone-houses, say others. The main- stay of tile evil is the modern pubfic-house, no lbriger, the old tavern providing.f n• the way-farer good cheer,. but shrunk into a,thinicing-bar, the sourea of vice.atull

div.head: crime.
div.p: crime.

"Away with it,": cries ,th alnhitioiijst, "by local veto." But in those•areas where it is the greatest evil, where the people are most wedded to their drink, the result would disappoint us, and where temperance predominates. the evil is less paramount, while the outcry. of deprived publicans and hard-hit brewers would split the welkin and delay reform: "Appeal t the Licensing' Justices to reduce their number," cries the temperance advocate. But if the Justices will not act you cannot tuake them, and they shrink from sacrificing comparatively innocent publi- cans to a theory of numbers, without which no drastic reduction can be made.
.The bad elem3at3 of the m )(len' pusie-hpa3e3 are :hese :
1. The quality of the drink supplied. 2. Undetected and constant evasions of the law regulating the traffic. •
-3. Deice s for the promotion of the trade. 4. Insecurity of the tenure of the publican. 5. Practical exclusion of the sale of other com- modities than drink.

If you could cure or minimise these evils you would strike a sounding blow for temperance. The law treats the licensed holder as the substan- tial person interested in the licence. He is alone responsible for the conduct of the house. He must be constantly on the premises. To him the Justices look for the keeping of the law. To him the monopoly for a year is granted. This is wide of the truth. The tied-house system is all but universal. The real seller is not the publican but the brewer. The brewer owns the house and in substance the fittings and goodwill, and sup- plies the drink. The publican is a mere caretaker. He must not go into the market like any other retailer and buy the best that offers. He must buy of the brewer, and of him only. As particular breweries own the public-houses in whole districts, it follows that no one in those districts can bay any drink but) that which they choose to supply. All healthy com- petition is removed. Monopolies produce bad goods. This kind of monopoly produces bad drink. It is difficult indeed for a publican to please the brewer and obey the law. He is liable to dismissal at short notice if he does not adequately "push the trade." The customer must drink, or out he goes. Every temptation lies before him to induce.the public to con- sume the drink. He and the brewers anxiously count up the pints. If they fall short of what the brewers think ought to be sold, a more " active " publican is placed in charge. Consequently the publican breaks the law —he sells to drunken men, he gets up games and clubs and similar devices to prom )te the sale of drink, he sells substantially naught else, for naught else in- terests the brewer.

The result is the widespread dem )ralisation of the publican and the public. Can this be checked without rousing the opposition which the abolition of the licence must entail, with- out outstripping public opinion on the matter?

• I think -ii cc—an-. My dvice is this. Abolish the tied house. This, at . all events, as a first instalment of reform, leaving qpen further changes to be made as public opinion ma! permit. I woul7i not alter the discretion which the law gives to the Justices as to taking away the licences which now exist. But I would make it compulsory for the Justices, in granting fresh licences or ' renewals, to be satisfied that the tenant to whom the licence is granted for the year cannot be removed by his landlord during the period of the licence except for non-payment of rent, or breach of covenant to repair, &c., after due notice of breach, or for mis- conduct endangering the licence which he holds.

This would 'mean that from every tenancy agree- ment all covenants restricting the source of purchase, or inducing the tenant to restrict his- source of purchase by reduction of rent if he purchases from a particular source, or requiring him to purchase a given amount, should be _deleted. In a word, no covenant should be permitted fettering him in any way in the purchase of the goods Which he retails. Also I would require the Justices to be satisfied that the tenant is not made the mere creature of his land- lord by other means, such as being compelled to pay a 'sum by way of interest on mortgage or as rent, which' the legitimate profits of the trade cannot afford, so as to enable the landlord to eject him—nominally because of non-payment of the interest or rent; really because he has not bought from him, and bought

. enough. In fine, the Justices should be bound to satisfy themselves that the tenant is in the position of any . other shopkeeper, where the landlord has no interest beyond the maintenance of that, premises and the pay-; meat of the rent. Further, to protect the publican, where, at the close of the year or at any time during the continuance of the licence, an application for the transference or renewal of the licence is made to the Justices. I would make it compulsory for the Justices to be satisfied that the outgoing tenant is being removed on the ground of misc induct in the management of the house, or for reasins wholly un- connected with the amount of drink sold or the source from which it was purcltased. I knew that these changes would add considerably to the work of the Justices, but I feel sure that it is • work which they would willingly and loyally perform in the discharge of their. important public duty. I Certainly this proposal falls far short of some of 1 the measures which have been urged. It falls short of what I myself should approve. But it is a step in the right direction, and is on the lines of least resistance. Until you have the publican in a position of independence you have no hold ;on him. He has not.sufficient interest in his trade to dread removal from it. It being the brewers' house ' and he the mere caretaker, be goes along from hand to mouth, and the Justices have no real terrors for such as he. The brewers have more dread, lint they can always pacify the Justices if anything is discov- ered by presenting to them a fresh applicant with a ' clean bill of health, to whom the Justices transfer the licence; and the game begins again. • The brewers will oppose this change, but the pub- licans and all their customers will welcome it. !Divide et imp,ra ! It will tend to make the drink of better quality, and to make it to the vital intereSt of every publican to conduct his trade as respectably as. such a trade can be conducted. •

div.head: WEAR AND TEAR OF CITY LIFE.
div.p: THE WEAR AND TEAR OF CITY LIFE.

Why do so many of our City men look so sickly ? Because they drink too much tea, and when they are fagged out cannot take more substantial and nutritive food. The system thus gradually becomes weakened and debilitated ; there is no relish for food, no energy for work, and the whole of the ph3 sical and mental con- dition becomes seriously deranged.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
FIRST DIVISION.
WARRINGTON v. OLDHAM.

The engagement between these teams at Wilderspool on Saturday drew a crowd of about 6,000. There was plenty of excitement about the contest, both teams being in the running for the championship. A win for either meant a considerable advance. Unfortunately Warrington were without Fish, who had not been work- ing, and Edmunds filled the vacancy. Oldham were at full strength. Teams and officials: Warrington—Hallam, back; Edmunds, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Harris, three-quarter backs; Mahoney and Davies, half backs; Morrison, Boardman, Thomas, Jolley, Lunt. Edmundson, Swift, and Naylor, forwards. Oldharn—R. L. Thomas, back; SpottiswoOde, Tyson, P. Thomas, and Civil, three-quarter backs; Dixon and S. Lees, half 'backs; Fritter, Ferguson, Topham, Wilkin- son, Jardine, Wright and Kelley, forwards. Referee. Mr. F. Kennedy, Broughton. Touch judges, Messrs. Graham, St. Helens and Lee Leigh. Dickenson ki,cdced off' andjSam Lees 'ran to centre. Davies] had a kick charged down by Sam Lees, who passed to Dixon. Fortunately for Warrington the latter knocked on when a score was almost certain. Davies soon afterwards broke away, and an excitinc, dribble followed, which cowered a good length of the field, Spottiswoode eventually saving from a good run along touch. The game had been wonderfully even, and for a long time the ball was scarcely ever more than a dozen yards from the centre. Morrison made a daring save from a dribble, and soon afterwards a round of passing by the Warrington backs ended in Edmunds being held near centre. Dickenson took a pass at full speed, but un- fortunately stumbled and fell. The first bit of good play was by Oldham. Sam Lees breaking away from a scrum- mage gavethe pass to Tyson who:gave it to Spottiswood,• who got over only to find that be had stepped in touch in evading Hallam and was brought back. The next minute Davies was penalised for off-side. Ferguson took the kick but missed an easy goal. Warrington now warmed up, and smart following up by Harris caused Thomas to be brought down at his own quarter flag. 'Exciting play followed and dribbling by Davies, Edmunds, and Mahoney sent the ball in touch at the corner flag. Harris got over at the opposite corner after good passing but he had knocked an, and the try was therefore disallowed. Davies was at this point playing a splen- did game, and broke away, and tackled Thomas close to the line. From the following scrimmage Dickenson hadan unsuccessful drop at goat, and also failed at a penalty kick. Half-time: Oldham nil, Warrington nil. Turning round, Warrington forced the pace, and Thomas's charge was frequently in danger. Successive clearances were made by Civil and P. Thomas, whilst a particularly fine effort by Spottiswoode was certainly deserving of a tangible return. Warrington, however, again attacked tenaciously, and a couple of fine kicks by Hallam harassed' the Oldham defence. Suddenly the venue was changed, through the medium orDixon, who kicked past Hallam, and Tyson racing up at top speed, scored the winning point of the day. Warrington attacked strongly during the remaining portion of the game, but nothing more was scored though Dickenson was only a yard short at the corner from Isherwood's kick, and the game ended as follows :—Oldh am 1 try (3 points), Warrington nil.

div.head: RUNCORN V. BRA DFORD.
div.p: RUNCORN V. BRA DFORD.

At Runcorn. Faulkner and Deakin took play to the ; Bradford quarter, where a round of passing almost ended in Price crossing. The Bradford forwards then I rushed past the centre, and Sinton scored. The visiting 1 forwards were now asserting themselves, and their ; backs indulged in some fine passing. Half-time score: 1; —Bradford, one try; Runcorn, nothing. Restarting, the whole of the Runcorn backs handled the ball, Dutton being tackled by Sinton. Tall kicking took play to the Runcorn quarter, and exchanges landed the ball to Sinton, who scored at the corner. IVlosby's kick fell short. Again passing gave Sinton a chance which he accepted, hut Mosby's kick again failed. Butterworth picked up at the feet of the Bradford forvxarcls and raced away, but Dunbavin intercepted his pass and threw to Dechen who scored. Mosby kicked a goal. Result : Bradford, one goal and four tries (14 points), Runcorn, one goal, (two points). _BROUGHTON RANGERS v. WIDNES.I The fimt-match this season between these clubs was played on the Rangers' ground before a moderate num- ber of spectators. From start to finish the Rangers showed such superior form. that Widnes in the end were beaten .by twenty-five points, and it was solely due to the fine work of Tilley that the score was not even larger. The Widnes backs had no idea of com- bination, and the few individual efforts which were inadi, were easily frustrated by the strong tackling of the home backs. In the lirit five minutes Wilson and Hogg scored a try. A similar movement a few minutes later enabled Hogg to again cross the line, whilst Wilson also scored a try, and at half-time the Rangers led by nine points tolnothlng. It was in the second half that Widnes were so hopelessly overplayed, and , Widdowson ran in two brilliant tries, from which S. James kicked two goals. Other tries were obtained by Hogg and Harry, neither of which were converted, and a very one-sided game ended :—Broughton Rangers, two goals and seven tries (25 points); Widnes, nothing.

div.head: HULL. v..IIUNSLET.
div.p: HULL. v..IIUNSLET.

Owing to the late arrival of Hunslet the start fig t6a game at Hull was delayed forty-tive minutes The game • was of an even character. Carvell scored' smartly for Hull, the place kick failing. Then Hull' played up strongly, the. forwards doing good work. They did not score again, however, and at half-time Hull led by three points to nothing. Resuming, Hunslet scored, Goldthorpe placiO the goal. The play was keenly con- tested. Hunslet were stronger forward, and played a good defensive game, the result being :—Hunslet, one goal and one try (five points) ; Hull, one try (three points).

div.head: SALFORD v. HUDDERSFIELD.
div.p: SALFORD v. HUDDERSFIELD.

This match was played on the Salford ground, before a good attendance of spectators. The first half of the game was well contested, but in the second half Salford wore down their opponents, and eventually won by a margin of thirteen points. The opening stages were, evenly contested, but at length Huddersfield were pena- lized, and Lomas placed a goal fore Salford. Then the visiting forwards controlled the scrummages for a short time, and Larrard gave Deerean opening from which he scored a try. Salford took up the attack, but were repeatedly driven back by the fine work of Walton. From a loose dribble, howover, Buckler scored a try,and at half-time Salford led by five pointstothree. Salford had by far the best of the game in the second half, and Williams, Preston, and Lomas scored tries one of which Lomas improved. Final score :—Salford, two goals and four tries (16 points) ; Hadderfield, one try (three points).

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
0 LIMIAAI A" v. WARRINGTON "A."

The Warrington team sustained a defeat on Saturday when they met I.oldham " A" at the Watersheddings. From the outset the Oldham backs displayect a superior- ity which was most marked, and after Gardner had been grassed nearthe line, Sellars scored from the succeed- inglpack, and Hopwood placed a goal. Warrington allied slightly, but the attack was not maintained, and anotherexcellent display of running and passing cul- minated in Gardner beating the 't pposition. Oldham kept np the pressure, and in quick succession Lewis and Gardner crossed the Warrington line, both tries being converted. Oldhani led at the- interval by 18 points to nil. During the second half the game was more even, and after Carpenter had placed a penalty goal, Gardner raced in for his third try of the day. Warrington did not relax their energies,and after Cooke had placed a penalty goal, he dropped one. The final score was: Oldham, four goals five tries (23 points); Warrington, two goals (four points.)

div.head: LIVERPOOL'S GREAT CATIIEDRAL.
div.p: LIVERPOOL'S GREAT CATIIEDRAL.

Liverpool Cathedral Committee on Tuesday decided to proceed at once with the construction of the main fabric. to seat 3,500 people, at a cost of £240,000. The Cathedral, it is stated, will be the largest in Great Britain. The new mammoth offices of the Royal Insur- ance Company in Dale-street could be accommodated within the ebthedral nave, and the tower of the same building, which is a landmark for miles around, would come inside the tninsept cross of. the Cathedral when completed.

The Bishop of Liverpool has received £207 is. from the Rector of Wigan, vice-chairman of the Wigatt Ruri- decanal Cathedral Committee, to whom this sum has been handed by the ex-Mayor on 'resigning office, as the result of the Mayoral appeal. It is to be desired`that the chief magistrates in our larger centres may see their way to take. similar action.
