div.head: EXAMINERS
div.p: THE EXAMINERS
NOVEMBER 14th 1903.

THERE is no end to the RETALIATION. dilemmas'of the Unionists,who can scarcely feel grateful to Lord HUGH CECIL for his ingenious attempt to show that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has not mastered the principles of Mr. BALFOUR'S pawphlet. This pamphlet is, of course, the one in the left-hand pocket, the other having been suppressed after its unsuccessful appearance at a Cabinet Council. Mr. BALFOUR and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, as their famous correspondence made plain, are certainly under the impression that the surviving pamphlet is a bond of unity between them. Lord HUGH CECIL thinks differently. He undertakes to teach these two eminent persons what they really mean. We should say that much the , simpler course, in the interests of Free Trade, is to say that they mean the game thing, which all Free Traders must strenuously oppose. But that is the way of the Opposition, and not LORD HUGH CECIL'S way He and MR. WINSTON CHURCHILL have to cling to something or other which will not detach them altogether from the bulk of their party. It is a most uncomfortable position, and resembles nothing so much as the famouti trick of the Indian jugglers, who throw a rope into the air and thou climb it. LORD HUGH has discovered that MR. BALFOUR'S pamphlet is quite reconcilable with Free Trade. The Prime Minister does not propose a general tariff, which is protection, but only a tariff in " special cases" and LORD HUGH thinks this is a legitimate development of COBDEN'S ideas. He also thinks apparently that while it would be sound Free Trade to put a retaliatory duty on a very perverse foreigner, it would be intolerable Protection to give the IColonies the benefit of a preference. It really looks as if the suggestive commentary of the " Times " had caught the essence of Lord HUGH'S singular doctrine. "Free Trade exists betwee n

this country and another, in respect of a given article which both can produce, only when the I Customs duties imposed upon that article in the two countries are equal. The essence of the thing is equality of impost, and it is an accident whether the equality is nothing equal to nothing, or ten equal to ten, or twenty equal to twenty." The beauty of this will be best appreciated by an illus- tration. If the foreigner puts 20 per cent. on our goods, and we put 20 per cont. on his, then we have Free Trade according to Lord HUGH CECIL. Thus, in Mr. BALFOUR'S immortal words at Sheffield, where Lord HUGH dissented entirely, "tariff attacks will be met by tariff replies." .Is this what the Free Trade Union meant by its Birmingham resolution that the Bricish Govern- ment has a right to propose retaliatory duties in certain cases? If SO, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN must have regarded the Free Trade meeting in his stronghold much as a spider in the centre of his web regards the appearanee of a fly on the circum- ference. He must be eager to see more meetings of the same ingenuous kind. Such an interpreta- tion of the pamphlet in the left-htnd pocket must fill Mr. BALFOUR with parental joy. If a countervailing duty is real Free Trade, why boggle at a general tariff? Why hunt for shadowy distinctions between fair Ind unfair competition? • Mr. WINSTON CHURCHILL gh,es us a just and eloquent account of the benefits the country has derived fro'u free imports. But how can this be reconciled with the theory of retaliatory duties in " special cases " ? Are the free imports in the special cases no benefit to the country ? If they are, why check them ? and if they are not, what becomes of Mr. CHURCHILL'S demonstration ? There can be no such thing as a special case, which is to have an economic treatment all to itself, while the rest of our trade is conducted as before. We have to stand by the principle of free imports or drop it; there is no middle way. Arguments designed to prove that whereas Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S policy is fatal, MT. BALFOUR'S may be cautiously accepted for the sake of some shred and semblance of unity in the Conservative ranks, are rather wsaker than moonshine. Lord ROSEBERY quoted the other day a letter which described the effect of the fiscal commotion on the household budget of the poor. While Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is Calculating the farthings which the poor will save under his scheme, the grocer in a small country town is putting up his prices. Would he put them down again when he found that it was only the pamphlet in the left-hand pocket that was coming - into operation? -Would retaliatory duties, strictly confined to special cases, check this tendency of small groceries to rise in the market ? It is notorious that when the price of any commodity in widespread use is enhanced, the extreme sensi- tiveness of all the rest makes them follow suit. That is the practical lesson before us, and it is worth more than all the theorising of bewildered Unionists.

The Mayoral and aldermanic vacancies have now been filled, and, we hope, to the satisfaction of the townspeople. Alderman Bolton is fully conscious of the responsibility he has undertaken, and with that loyal support he is entitled to expect, he should have no difficulty in maintaining the best traditions of the Mayoralty during his year of office.

Councillor Pierpoint has at last become Alder- man Pierpoint. The appointment tempts one to remark: "after many days," for Mr. Pierpoint has been a candidate previously, and if he had been fairly treated would have been an Alderman years ago. It is a curious and pleasing coincidence that the new Mayor and the new Alderman should each obtain the honour on the 21st anniversary of his entering the Council. We only regret that our Conservative friends-, at the last moment enueav- oured to prevent Councillor Pierpoint celebrating the attainment of his municipal majority so fittingly. They have seldom done a more ungracious thing in the history of local patty politics, and they richly deserved the snub which the Council, by its decisive vote ad- ministered. There are at present just eight Tory I Aldermen out of nine, and though the retiring. Alderman Mr. F. W. Monks WAS a Liberal, the Sankey Street Secret Conclave endeavoured to so I pull the strings that the whole nine wards should be presided over by a Conservative. This suddenly hatched plot failed, and its originators well de- served the castigation which fell unsparingly from the lips of Alderman Pierpoint and Councillor Tinnion. Politics in the Council chamber are at all times to be deprecated, and we are sure the people of Warrington will condemn the reintro- duction of party strife by the Conservatives.

A labour candidate for Warrington is practically assured. At their meeting on Thursday the Labour Representation Committee, representing some three thousand Warrington Trades Unionists, unanimouslytagreed to invite Mr. Alexander Wilkie, of Newcastle on-Tyne, to contest the borough in the Labour interest. Mr. Wilkie's con- sent, and that of his Society, are confidently ex- pected, as he was present at the meeting. Liberals and Conservatives alike are thus face to face with a new .condition of things in Warrington, which demands very serious consideraton, particularly from the Liberals. It is unfortunate that there has not been that rapprochement bet seen Liberal and Labour which we have on several occasions advocated. Their interests are very largely identi- cal, and for both to select candidates to oppose a sitting Conservative is not only absurd but it is putting a premium on the:chance of the Conservative to beat both. Such an event as that at Barnard Castle, where the Labour candidate, Mr. Hender- son beat Liberal and Tory, is unique, and not at all likely to be repeated at Warrington. In our opinion neither Libzlral nor Labour candidate can win Warrington without united support from both parties. The position of affairs is somewhat com- plicated by the action of the Labour Representation Committee. Mr. A. H. Crosfield has been in the• field since the last election, when he was defeated, and we think,in all fairness to him, to themselves, and to the man they desire to support,the Labour leaders should have approached Mr. Crosfield before taking any decisive step. There will have to be co-operation and concord to ensure success, and it is not too late for the two parties to meet and agree upon some course of action against their common Conservative foe.

"It is easier to hang a man than to obtain a conviction stgainst a publican,'' was the striking remark we heard after the conclusion of the abor- tive prosecution for permitting drungenness, at the Police Court on Monday. In Warrington at any rate, the sarcastic observation approaches very near the truth, for publicans who have been haled before the local bench h ive generally come through the ordeal better than they had any reason to expect. In Monday's case, the defendant ad- mitted the offence for which he was summoned. The police evidence showed that a man had been found " speechlessly " drunk on the licensed premises of the Roebuck Hotel, drinking whisky and tea from a glass. A clearer case of permitting drunkenness could hardly have been imagined, and the police were entitled to suppose that a conviction would be recorded. The bench, how- ever, dismissed the case on payment of costs, though, as we have pointed out, the offence was admitted. A verdict such as this is equal to "Not guilty,but don't do it again,"and we are afraid the Warrington . magistrates have earned an un- enviable reputation for such equivocal decisions.
We are getting quite accustomed to Municipal Elections in Warrington. Two more contests are impending. They are to be decided at an early

date and will take place together. One vacancy ig caused by the retirement of Councillor Upson in Orford Ward and the other by the elevation of Councillor William Pierpoint, (who represented Bewsey Ward) to an Aldermanic seat. Alraady the air is filled with rumours of possible candidates. One thing is certain and that is that Mr. F. Stott intends once again to contest Orford Ward, as a Labour candidate. It would have been a gracious act on the part of the political parties to have , allowed Mr. Stott a walk-over, if only as a reward for his gallant fight on November fid.The Labour party is at least.entitled to one representative in the Council Chamber; and we do not think a better man could have been chosen as a labour representative than Mr. Stott. The Gonserva- tives, it seems, are determined to contest the seat and it is rumoured that their candidate is to be a publican. Without wishing to cast any reproach on representatives of " the trade," we still think there is already a more than sufficient number of them in the Council Chamber. Mr. Stott wil! win this time, we are sure, and if he beats a publican candidate we shall be additionally pleased to con- gratulate him.

The proposed tramway from the present terminus at Wilderspool to the Square at Stockton Heath is at last well within sight. A start has been made this week in connection with the scheme by the demolition of the old cottages near the Mulberry Tree, and the whole of the route from the Square to St. Thomas's Church will shortly be widened. The crossing of the swing bridge which spans the canal pre— sents engineering difficulties but it is anticipated that these will be overcome. In case of dispute, I the matter will have to be submitted to the Board of Trade but it is to be hoped that the scheme will be carried through without their interven- tion, and that the trams may be run- ning to the Square by midsummer next year. This is the first venture by tla Corporation in running trams outside the Borough and unlPss the increased support extended to the new system is such as to repay the enterprise of the ratepayers of Warrington it will probably be the last. There are mans residents inside the Borough who hold the opinion that their conveni- ence with regard to trams ought to have been consulted before attending to the wishes of those who do not pay Borough rates. The residents in Lovely-lane and Padgate-lane will have a double grievance if the Stockton Heath line is not a financial success. `42,1=1P

Once—na. O-re the Board of Trade returns have supplied welcome material for the advocates of Free Trade. Our exports for October shew an in- crease of £750,000, and as our coal exports have somewhat fallen off our exports of manufactured goods have augmented to a still greater extent. All our principal industries—iron and steel, cotton, woollens, leather goods, and so forth—shew the same gratifying tendency to expansion, those very industries which, according to Mr. Chamberlain, are steadily decaying. What renders the figures still more noteworthy is that in many classes of goods the shipments to the Colonies have fallen off. Thus Australia and Cape Colony are,buying boots and shoes in diminished quantit:es, in the one case as the result of the new Commonwealth tariff, and in the other owing to the reduced garrison. When the returns for the completed year are published it will be seen that the increased Colonial consumption of British goods during recent years has been checked, and that another of Mr. Chamberlain's theories respecting the course of foreign trade has been exploded.

The administration of the Inebriates Act. so far at least as:power of committal to reformatories le concerned,is not yet in a fully-developed condition. The Act has only been working for a compara- tively short time, and its operation has been pre- judiced by a variety of circumstances over which the authorities have had no control. Magistra-es have shewn themselves willing to give prisoners the benefit of thelchances of reform offered under the Act, but their action has constantly been hampered by the inadequacy of the accommodation at the disposal of the authorities. This difficultAY is one which will disappear in course of time/ and the more rapidly as the good effects of detentl.oo begin to be more widely known. Other difficulties in connection with the institutions themselves and their inmates abound, and one of the most fruitful sources of complaint from thu.se who see to the working of the reformatories is the indisposition on the parc of the com- mitting authorities to order detention for a sulE" cient period to produce the most satisfactory re- sults. It is abundantly proved by the experience of these first years' working that short sentences are of no use in the work of 'reclaiming the habitual inbriate. The majority of people sent to reformatories are persons who would require the longest possible sentence,the reason being not that they should be necessarily detained for the whole of the period, but that if released on licence the inebriates might, should they give way the second time to drink,be taken back to the reforma- tory and given a second chance by serving the rest of their sentence. Trio whole question of the. methods of dealing with inebriates is a comPl.i- cated and difficult one, and can only be solved 10 the school of experience.

An Army Chaplain's Experience. An interesting lecture on " The Boer War" was delivered in St.''Barnabas' Schools on Monday evening by the Rev. T. H. Powell, organizing secretary to the additional Curates' Society N. W. District.) The rev. gentleman acted as chaplain to the field forces in South Africa during) the late war and the narration of his experiences, including his capture with one of the 17th Lancers, sentence to death, and escape, was followed with keen interest. Lantern views taken from the lecturer's own photographs were thrown on the screen. There was a good attendance and the proceeds will be devoted to home missions. Suspension of a Football Team. At a meeting of the Warrington and District Foot- ball Association held on Thursday evening, a serious report by Referee J. Bibby against the players of the , Stockport Half Holiday Club, at Warrington, on October 29th, for misconduct was dealt with, at the request of the Stockport and District F. A. During the progress of the game the referee had occasion to order off the field of play a player of the name of Comston, for using foul language, but he refused to leave, and the referee appealed to the Captain of the Stockport club. Sheeham. to assist him in getting the player off, but the Captain insisted that Comstan should not go off, and the referee therefore stopped the game, when he was subject to insulting remarks by all the team. Mr. Harvey, the Chairman of the Association, who was a spectator at the match, '(rave ,evidence in support of the referee's statement, when it Was resolved that Comston, be suspended for 1 month "Sheeham, the captain until the Ist of January 1904. and that the club be suspended for 14 days. All suspensions to date from Friday the 13th November. Child's Sad Death.

Coroner Brighouse held an inquest at the Police Station on Saturday afternoon on the body of John. Fothergill, four years of age, son of Samuel Fother- _gill, insurance agent,„ 4, Fotherg,all-street.—The eviden.ee showed that very early on the prevfous Wednesday morning, the child came into his sick mother's room and obtained a bottle containing Whisky, some of which he drank. His father put him to bed again, thinking he would sleep off the effects. He thought the child had drunk a sthall quantity of the whisky. There was originally sixpennyworth in the bottle, but some had been spilled on the floor. Mr. Fother,ill went to work, and later in the day was told that the child had fallen downstairs. Dr. Ander- son was called in, but the child died at one a.m. on Thursday. The doctor stated that death was due to alcoholic poisoning' the result of drinking the whisky. A verdict of " Death from misadventure" was returned.—The foreman of the jury, Mr. Whittle congratulated the Coroner upon his having been elec- ted a member of the Southport Town Council. A GOOD RESOLUTION.—Wear ALF TAYLOR'S Wonderful Boots.—Advt. Some Lower Forms of Life." • Tdis was tha subject of an interesting lecture delivered baforo the members of the Warrington Field Club on Friday by Mr. F. W. Monks. The ,chair was occupied by Mr. T. May, F.E.T.S. In the to limited leisure of a very active life Mr. Monks has devoted attention to certain branches of miscroscopic work, and a portion of the fruits of his labours was lout before the members of the Field Club in clear and simple language. He dealt principally with the Hydra zoa the group which includes such forms as the jelly fishes on the one hand and the fresh water hydra on the other. Starting with a brief statement of the relations of these anim tls amongst themselves and to higher forms, he passed to the consideration of their structure and habits,and dealt at some length with their modes of reproduction, which in many of the species involves an alternation of generations ; a fixed asexual form giving rise to a free swimming sexual from,which in turn produces eggs from which .grow the fixed asexual organisms. The Subject was beautifully illustrated by a series of admirable lantern slides, some of which had been prepared by the lecturer, who was warmly congratulated by several speakers during the subsequent dissussion, in which the President, Mr. Charles White, and Mr. L. Green- ing took part.

div.head: Warrington Draughts League.
div.p: Warrington Draughts League.

A meeting of the league Committee was helct last Monday evening. The Hon See. (Mr, D. Plinston) re- ported that six teams, including:four works teams.have •entered the League Competition for the new" Cup" offered by Mr. R. A. Naylor, and that there were prospects of several more works teams entering if the rules could be altered so as to place the new clubs on an equal footing with the old league clubs in regard to playing strength. After some discussion a list of about a score of the strongest players in the town was dawn up, and it was agreed that no club should be allowed to play more than two of these player's in any league match, thus levelling up the playing strength of the teams in the new competition and placing them all as nearly as possible on an equal footing. After the conclusion of the ordinary business. Mr. Dunn (the Chairman) handed to Mr. Plinston a handsome dressing case, -which had been subscribed for among the members of the old League, as a slight recognition of the ser- vices he has rendered to the League and the game in Warrington,as the hon. secretary of the League during -the last six years.—Mr. Plinston, though taken by surprise, responded with a few appropriate remarks, expressing the pleasure he felt at this token of, their esteem. The meeting was then adjourned. The Committee will meet again next Monday evening, the 16th inst., at 8 p.m.. at the rooms of the Warrington C. and D.C., Market-street, Warrington, and all dele- gates from the works and clubs intending to enter the competition are invited to attend. - - -

St. John's Literary Society. The members of St. John's Literary and Social ociety held their usual fortnightly meeting in the church schoolroom on Wednesday evening, the Rev, J. L. Milne, B.D. in the chair. The Rev. John Gunnell, of Penketh, gave an address on" Old Saws" <proverbs). He explained that. the word was of Anglo-Saxon origin, and that a " Saw " or proverb might be described as a pithy sentence, giving forcible -expression to some practical (truth, rDr. Johnson's -definition beimg "a short sentence frequently repeated ,(by the people." One was struck by the vast number' ;of t.hese old saws in their common speech. A great many were found in the Bible, and their presence gave a charm to Bunyan's writings. One reason why 'the common people heard Jesus Christ so readily was because he used common speech and proverbs. There was an endless variety of those saws, and they dealt With every phase of human life. It was this variety that rendered their classification so difficult.. Mr. 'Gunnell quoted a very great number of old sayings of different kinds, indicating, in a highly interesting manner, their probable origin, and showing how they -threw considerable light on life in Old England in :days long gone by.—On the motion of the Chairman, Mr. Gunnell was accorded a hearty and unanimous vote of thanks for his address, which had been listened to with great attention by those present.

LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER the CLOCK, BRID GE-STREET.—Ad7t- tante's " Divine Comedy." Mr. Philip H. Wicksteed, M.A., continued his course ,of lectures on " Dante "in the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening. In discussing "the Divine 'Comedy," he said the comedy contained a great deal -that was allegorical in the strict sense of the word, 'but included in it there was much that was typical ;and symbolic, The literary subject of the poem was -the state of souls after death but the allegorical sub- ject referred to man making the evil or the good 'choice. The lecturer explained that Dante's view of the state of souls after death was not that men were to get what they gave in this life but to get what they -chose here. Hell, in Dante's view was simply the ',defeat of the man who made the evil choice. Hell, he held, was already inherent in the evil choice itself: Dante's essential conception of hell was "let the wicked man have the thing that he chooses." In re- ferrinr, to Dante's ideas of repentance, the lecturer stateethat Dante held that to repent was not to shrink from the consequences of sin, but to loathe the thing 'Which he once chose and strive to dissociate himself from the thing to which be had been committed. When Dante told them he had seen hell, purgatory and heaven, he meant that he had seen the nature of sin, the nature of penitence and the nature of bliss. In Dante's hell the soul was still impenitent. When Impenitent sin was allowed to make its own atmos- phere the result in Dante's opinion was Hell. A public leeting promoted by the Warrington Liberal Association will be held in the Parr Hall on Tuesday evening, the 24th inst. The occasion will be rendered more than usually interesting by the fact that the Earl of Crewe and Mr. Henry Broadhurst, MP., will deliver addresses. Mr.- C. E. Parker will, preside and will be supported by a number of well- known local Liberals. Tramway Offices Broken Into.

The Tramway Offices in Cairo-street were broken into early on Wednesday morning but nothing of any value was stolen. The safe was tampered with but fortunately could not be opened. The depredators had entered the premises from the rear, breaking a pane of glass in order to open one of the windows. They also removed a panel from a door which barred their way into the offices.

div.head: FISCAL PROBLEM.
div.p: THE FISCAL PROBLEM.
" Bassani° " and Mr. Edwin Woods.

"0 wad some power the giftie gie us" "To see oursel's as ithers see us," "It wad fra mony a blunder free us, And foolish notion." Sir,—l see that Mr. Edwin Woods, the man who is so busy that he has neither time or inclination for con- troversy, has made a farther great sacrifice in this respect by trying his hand at oratory and extinguishing all his combatants by one master stroke. I hope and have no doubt his readers would duly appreciate this mighty effort and would see very good reason to agree with Mr. Woods when he says that his opinions are not based on knowledge acquired in the school of economy, but, they may be pardoned if they think that he might make some acquaintance with the roughest rudiments of economy before he sets himself up as an authority on it. Mr. Woods began by describing myself and those who have given expression to the same train of thought under a "nom de plume," as "Snakes in the grass.' I admit that he would at least be at home here, and shall not contest with him for supremacy in this elevating role. It will be remembered that he had made the wonderful discovery that if he bought 1,000 tons of German wire rods (and in this he acknowledges with amazing frankness that he was the chief of sinners, which would be properly appreciated, though the fact had long been common knowledge) he thereby robbed the British workmen of the labour of producing 6,500 tons of material. I ventured to ask him a few what would have] been very simple questions to anyone who had the most rudimentary knowledge of the subject,but Mr. Woods did not answer the questions. Why? Your readers must decide for themselves.—Yours &c., BASSANIO.• November, 12th, 1903, MR. EDWIN WOODS AND THE IRON TRADE.

div.head: Reply by a Practical Man.
div.p: Reply by a Practical Man.

Sir,—My attention has been called to a letter from Mr. Edwin Woods of Warrington, in which he gives the imports of iron or steel into this country for 1902 as 1,131,000 tons, and works out (evidently to his own satisfaction), what an invaluable gain it would be to the workmen if, by a protective tiriff, this had been excluded and worked up in this country. I neither "hive time lor inclination for newspaper correspond- ence," but such almisleading statement, especially from one who calls himself a practical business man, can not go unchallenged. Mr. Woods assumes too much in his assumption that the whole of these imports if excluded by tariffs (which vvould have to be prohibitory in order to prevent their purchase b 3 English manufacturers) would have been produced in this country, and one has certainly a right to expect some intelligent analysis of figures from a practical man. ANALYSED.

Oar imports of iron. and steel in 1902 were 1,170,667 tons, but analysed they woitlft work out as follows : Pig iron 223,138 tons ; eliminating Swedish pig—a high- priced speciality—and a small lot of 10,000 tons from America, which somebody was foolish enough to pay £5 us, per ton for, we have 155,595 tons at an average price of £2 13s. per ton. Does any manufacturer re- gret this, when, owing to our large exportation of pig iron-1:102,835 tons, at an average of £3 4s. 9d. per ton --the finished iron trader was seriously luindicapped with the high price of his raw material? It would have been a God-send to the finished manufacturers had they been able to secure quadruple .that amount. Puddle bars, 3,700 tons, at £6 16s. 4d. per ton, is another Swe- dish speciality which we were bound to obtain —to our advantage. Bars, angles, bolts and rods account for another 171,015 tons, at an average of £6 Os. 2d. per ton; but, again, eliminating a few high- priced specialities, we have included in this 136,773 tons at £5 14s. per ton, mostly landed in Newport (Mon.) as the raw material for their growing sheet and tin-plate industries, the exports of which show large increases resulting therefrom, fmging employment for thousands, who would otherwise have been idle. Iron and steel scrap shows an import of 38,958 tens, at £2 15s. 4d. per ton—also of great benefit to the purchaser. Unwrought steel accounts for 280,990 tons, at an aver- age price of £5 Os. Bd. per ton ; but, here again, we must eliminate the high-class speciality, a tariff on which would only penalise the buyer, and restrict trade leaving 266,916 tons at £4 10s. 7d. per ton.

—to our advantage, and his loss. Girders, beams, joists, and pillars account for another 127,208, tons at £6 9s. per ton, the bulk of which comes from Belgium,of which they make a speciality. If it were the practice to "stock " girders in this country to any great extent,and if our engineers and builders had not so many fads as to specifications in home products, while taking the stock of the Belgian we migkt have produced some portion of these, but the exact amount is debatable and proble- matical in the absence of exact particulars. Nails and screws account for 44,171 tons at £l2 2s. 3d. per ton. I know too•little about this branch to offer an opinion, though Mr. Arthur Chamberlain, the greatest screw maker perhaps,protests strongly against any Protection whatever, and as one of the largest manufacturers of these commodities he ought to know his own trade.

as I understand it, is a tax on food stuffs and finished goods, will not increase the cost of living, is certainly from experience on this side, very strange. The ques- tion, I see from thelpapers, has led to a great deal of discussion and in some places comparisons are made with this country. Thinking that a few facts would help, by enquiry I have ascertained that the cost of living, since 1896 or since the present high tariff was put on imports into this country, has increased from 20 to 30 per cent. The Republican party admits of an increase of 11 per cent., but for political purposes tries to represent that this is all. The workingmen have in some cases had a small increase in wages, but nothing like an increase of 20 per cent. It is not a fact that they have had an increase equal to the increase in the cost of living. Here is a large country which grows all its own food stuffs and mines all its raw materials, but with a tariff the' cost of living increases. What would England do when as we all know, all her food stuffs and raw materials must be bought outside, if a tariff is imposed ? .Is it probable that the producers are going to pay it? From the above illustration it appears to me that the people pay it here. You can draw your own conclusions as to who will pay in England. Again, the colonies are being thrown b3fore the people so much that the effect is striking. But do the public understand the sentiments of these colonies? Take Canada for instance. In many of its papers one can read of the favour such a tariff receives, but at the same time is it to be taken for granted that she will stop her present rapid development of iron, steel and coal? From expressions in these same papers I doubt it. Canada is progressing by leaps and bounds and the time is not far distant, when she too will want a place in the markets of the world. Are they going to throw over these fine commercial prospects and simply pro- duce for English manufacturers? Again I doubt it, and expressions by their public men support my doubts. In what way can the change be effected, whereby England shall maintain her commercial supremacy? Undoubtedly there are many, but one striking illustra- tion which bears on this in many ways and whichl came across the other day in looking through the leading journal devoted to the iron and steel trade will suffice. The article was entitled :

"BRITISH MANUFACTURERS HANDICAPPED." It says :—"England has been sharply criticised for her want of enterprise as we understand it in this country, but there are two aspects of every question and some very good reasons for the course of English manufacturers are given by one of them who is apparently familiar with his subject from every point of view, as it affects the obstacles in the way of adopting new methods. In an article entitled "The inspection of materials" in the "Engineer," London, a manufaoturer says" : Theljournal then reproduces the article above- mentioned, which deals with the specifications English makers have to adhere to, and points out at the same time how these handicap them. It (the journal) after- wards'says "it is, perhaps, unnecessary to follcrw the writer further in his arguments, which is a long plea along certain lines. Its frankness and candour are remarkable, but without intending to criticise it adversely, it seems to us rather a special plea for seine branches, and does not wholly explain the want of enterprise which characterizes British industries. Large commissions visit us and are given the freedom of our shops without reservation. The members composing them are experts them- selves and can understand, or rather see, without comprehending in some cases how we turn out double and more, than they do in a given time. Then the Commissioners return and report that boasted superiority is a sham and that if perchance our tonnage output is greeteis occasionally, it is inferior in quality and workmanship than their own, and they adhere more firmly to the way their fathers walked. We have no quarrel with this method of meeting competi- tion, because it does not compete, and the writer of the article reviewed fails to recognise this weakness of his countrymen ignoring it wholly.' And yet it is a very prominent factor in the argu- ment of commercial supremacy. This is not an occasional happening with commissions; year after year delegations visit us and go through the same routine without profit to them of any kind, for they , have followed their plans for hundreds of years, I and will not, even if they were so constituted that they could abandon them. There are no bugaboo , specifications in this line of business to affright them, simply a change of machines and methods, but these are unchanging in Great Britain. It is first in the minds of all who read what is going on in the world of trade,that an American contractor who had large buildings toerect in England, offered them to resident builders with the stipulation that the work was to be completed within twelve calendar months, but was met with the assertion that it was not possible to do it under five years. Thereupon the American manager built them himself, with the aid of native labour, in the timestated. Naturally, this would be expected to serve as an object lesson and one worthy of emulation; but it did not, for only a few weeks ago the same spirit of delay and inaction prevailed on another building and every sort of obstinate hindrance was opposed to prevent the American contractor from sueceeding. Here again is an example of century old prejudice in regard to trade procedure; it matters not that loss and delay attend the operation of them; they are traditional and that answers the whole argument from the English point of view. In any event how- ever annoying and restrictive specifications may be, they do not cover all the issues in the indictment brought against England's neglect to keep step with progress in arts, but charges in this direction have been brought so often that they have become unin- teresting,and We shall not repeat them here." The above criticism is one of many on English methods and also on the reports of commissions, one es- pecially which was brought over last year.llFor myself, I think it bears directly on the future of England, and as one who has had exceptional opportunities of judging both English and American methods, I cannot help but coincide with this. It is quite possible that English people are sick and tired of hearing of American methods and systems, and one feels afraid to venture on the subject further. We are however living in an ivre when production must be made at the lowest pos- sible cost, human brains and enterprise must always be on the alert for new methods and ideas. This they re- cognise to a very marked degree on this side, but in England it seemed to be recognised only to a small extent. T. know of American machinery being taken , over to England and workmen put to work on these machines but with nothing like the success attained here. Why is this? Do American workmen treat English machinery in like manner? Not a bit of it. We can then only assume that it is prejudice, and here , I think is one of the chief reasons why up-to-date methods arenot further advanced at home. The sooner both employer and employed in England throw off this prejudice, the .better it will be for the country. We must remember that althr,ugh it is hard to beat English made goods, Eno.- land is not the only country, and that although the American tool may not be so perfect, it is able to do the work required at a much lower cost. In a certain trade which is one of Warrington's largest industries, and which I am well acquainted with, the tonnage rate difference, or difference in the rate per cwt. paid for wages in certain stages, is 100 to 200 per cent higher at home than in this country, but the men receiving these low rates of pay, are able to earn considerably more per week than the same class of workmen in England. This difference being so great, people can be excused for showing a want of credulity, but when the figures show it to their faces and they cannot be refuted, it is quite natural to expect them to accept statements which are made in perfect good faith. rhe answer is however, that it has never bean done in England and therefore it never can be done. . -

_ One of the things which workmen must exorcise from their minds is the idea that labour saving machinery will throw some of their fellow men out of work. If they care for their country's future, this must to some extent be done. Another thing they should endeavour to do, is to raise those who are fallen in drink and so raise the standard of a brighter and hotter life. Drink is universally known as the curse of England. Is it to remain so? I hope not. Many other things may be brought into the national life at home, to make England what it should be. It rests not only with the workingmen, but with their employers and unions. It finally devolves itself upon all those who make the fight with the idea that England is only one out of many. With improved methods and machinery and without taxation. they can compete successfully with the rest of the world. Hoping I hive not presumed to lunch on your space I am yours etc., (Signed) ANDREW B. RATHBONE. Palmer, Mass. U.S.A. Warrington P.S.A.

div.head: EMMANUEL CHURCH.
div.p: EMMANUEL CHURCH.

Annual Sale of Work. For many years the members and congregation of the Emmanuel Church, Warrington, have held an annual sale of work in order to enable them to get sufficient funds to meet their financial needs. In an appeal for assistance, the churchwardens (Mr. Thomas Allen and Mr. Henry Dickens) and Mr. George Norman(secretary), state that "the Church is supported by voluntary con- tributions but these need to be supplemented by the proceeds from an annual sale. Throughout the year many willing workers have spared neither time, labour, nor money, t,o make the sale of work a success. The need of a movement like that of the Reformed Episcopal Church becomes increasingly great, and we' are confident that to all lovers of a sound Protestant Evangelical Faith, this appeal will not come in vain. For many years past, friends have rallied round us and given very valued assistance. The knowledge of their past generosity gives us confidence in asking for further ' help. We feel sure that the sympathy so kindly extended to us hitherto will be granted again this year. The past year has been one of especial difftcultt Many valued workers have been taken away by death—chiefest of all, our much beloved incumbent, the Rev. A. D. Gee. But through much discouragement our workers have been faithful to the highest interests of the church." The stalls had been effectively set out in the large room and there was a refreshment and tea room in addi- tion. The stalls and stallholders were as follows : Congregational Stall.—Mrs. Norman and friends. Warden's Stall. —Mr. S. Allen, Mr. W. H. Dickens and friends. Sunday School Stall.—Mrs. A. Gandy and friends. "Endeavour Flower and Fruit Stall.—Miss E. Heald, Miss Hodge, Miss Carriage, and friends. Children's Stall.—Miss Booth and friends. Refreshment Stall and Tea Room.—Mrs. E. Allen, Miss Lees, Mrs. A. Landon, Mrs. Minards and friends. THE OPENING CEREMONY. SPEECH BY COUNCILLOR DODDS.

A number of friends gathered to witness the opening ceremony which was performed by Councillor Dodds. Dr. T. W. BOWMAN, of Liscard, said the friends con- nected with the Emmanuel Church had done him the honour to ask him to be their minister for the day. (Laughter.) He very gladly accepted the office as he considered it a very great honour and al privilege to be in their midst on an occasion which he hoped would be aus- picious. He rejoiced to think that although they were still suffering from the loss of their dear pastor they were working earnestly together in doing a good work for God. He hoped the future of the Church would be still more blessed and more prosperous than the past and that under the pastor whom they would call bye and bye they would have a glorious career of spiritual success in this town. (Hear, hear.) They were not assembled to talk about the spiritual interests of the Church but about its material interests. He found that the financial needs of the Church necessitated the holding of a sale like that every year. He supposed that was due to the fact that they had no endowment, and that they were not composed of a very rich com- pany of believers.' By means of the present sale it was hoped to raise £lOO and he trusted they would exceedltheir anticipations. There could be no doubt that a church like the Reformed Episcopal was very much needed. Sacerdotalism was making great strides and in many centres it was increasingly successful. It was necessary that in every large centre there ought to be churches of the reformed episcopal denomination to hold up the bainer of evangelical truth. They had done so in the past and he hoped they would be more suc- cessful in the future. He was exceedingly glad to know they had Councillor Dodds with them that day and they were exceedingly obliged to him for his generosity in giving them a handsome donation of £5. (Applause.) Councillor DODDS, who had a hearty reception, said it was not the first time nor the second that he had been there in connection with that annual function. He might almost call it a "hiardy annual." (Laughter). It was a privilege to be amtngst them and if he was in- vited to come again he did not think he would refuse. (Hear, hear.) He missed one or two familiar faces that afternoon. He was sorry when the Rev. E. T. Reed left the town, because after all he was a man of nigh character and of culture and was not afraid or ashamed to speakthis convictions on any questions, popular or otherwise. In these days we needed to have men of that kind amongst us. (Hear, hear.) He was grieved to hear of the death of the late pastor,Mr. Gee,a gentle- man whom he did not knovi personally. He was told they were to have another pastor ere long and he hoped that "{under his direction, the church would be even more prosperous and successful than in the past. They were doing one great work—the work for which the Reformed Episcopal Church was founded —to keep aloft the flame of Protestantism in this coun- try. (Hear, hear.) He was sure they were doing that and he was also glad to hear that they were not for- getting that there was a work to do amongst the people. They were working to some extent to uplift the people by caring for their moral elevation. (Hear, hear.) That was a worki which must not be overlooked. If they did the work for which they were specially adapted and did not forget also to work amongst the masses of the people and spread those principles of religion and Christianity which they all believed in, he was certain there was a great future for that church. In the Name of the Trinity and the Unity he now declared the sale of work open. (Applause.) The services of Councillor Dodds were acknowledged on the proposition of Mr. A. GANDY. Dr. BOWMAN stated that subscriptions amounting to nearly £2O had been received'already, including one of £lO from Miss Woods and another of £2 from Mr. Ziba Armitage, Councillor DODDS proposed a vote of thanks to Dr. Bowman and the sale of goods then commenced. The result of the first day's sale was £l2 17s. 10d, THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. "THE INIQUITOUS EDUCATION ACT." The sale was again openea on Thursday. The Rev. ROWLAND PARKER, of Tuebrook, in intro- ducing Mr. Joha Griffiths, of Warrington, to open the 'sale, thanked him for his presence, and proceeded to state that while they as members of the Reformed Church of England had a reformed prayer book they did not exist as a church simply because they had a liturgical service, or because of the alteration of a few phrases of the prayer book with a saoerdotal tendency but for something far broader. They existed to uphold the Protestant evangelical truth in the Christian church and while they recognised that that truth could be sup- ported and upheld by the Nonconformists still the Non- co nfo rmistslwere hardly in a position:to meet the needs of the evangelical portion of the Church of England when ritualism was introduced into the Parish Churches. Hence it was that the Reformed Church stepped in, and as they were churchmen and churchwomen driven oat of their churches they just had their services on the true old evangelical lines and supplied the needs of those who could not join in the ritualism and sacerdotalism which was advancing every day all round about them. Beyond this they were able to stretch out a hand of brotherly friendship to those who did not have quite the same services as themselves. They recog- nised that they existed for fellowship with all evangelical Christians and their ministers were allowed to preach in Nonconformist pulpits and Non- conformists in the pulpits of the Reformed Church. There was nothing more conducive to the welfare of the Christian cause than to see Christians of all denomi- nations working together without any jealousy or jarring amongst them. In a passing allusion to Mr. Chamberlain's fiscal proposals, he expressed the opinion that the average man had a difficulty in deciding what was absolutely best for the country. He was con- vinced that there were other matters of greater im- portance than the fiscal policy. (Hear, hear.) There was the iniquitous Education Act which they wanted to see swept away. (Hear, hear.) He believed that education ought to be national and not denominational and then it would be fair and right to everyone. (Hear, hear.) Some considerable reform was needed. There were thousands of people who were passive resisters, and whether they were passive resisters, rightly or wrongly, they could but see that the Education Act must be an injustice in some way to a certain portion of the com- munity, and while it remained thus something must be done to remove it. He would advise them to turn their attention and give their support to those who were pre- pared to uphold the Protestant constitution of our country. There were many other things calling for attention, including the question of temperance, which was of vital impo:tance to the nation. In conclusion, the rev, gentleman expressed his sympathy with those present in the trials they were going through as a church: An esteemed churchwarden, Mr. Dickens, was unable to be present through illness. He hoped they would 1:1Q guided by God in the selection of a new pastor and that success would attend their efforts. (Applause.) Mr. GRIFFITHS said he supposed he ought to be orthodox and say he was pleased to be there and to have that opportunity of meeting Christian friends of another church. (Hear, hear.) He did not like Christian service of that kind because it brought one before the public. Personally he preferred to do Christian work ' silently and quietly. He thought there was a dearth in Warrington of Free Churchmen to do this kind of work. That ought not to be so in an industrial town like Warrington, and'although they were passing through a period of trade depression, still he thought there was a vast amount of wealth even amongst the men con- fleeted with the Free Churches. A portion of that wealth ought to be at the command of the Chris- tian Churches of the town for the moral and social improvement of the people. (Hear, hear). He was glad they had a gentleman amongst them on the previous day whose sympathies were with the Free Churches of the town. During the past few years, Mr. Dodds had been very generous in his help to the free churches. There was no reason why they should not have other men animated by the same spirit. (Hear, hear.) He had pleasure in declaring the sale open. Mr. Griffiths services were acknowledged en the pro- position of Mr. Bibby. Thursday's proceeds amounted to £26 Os. 21d. YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS:
Last evening the sale was re-oPened-I;:V.th(Tßev. JOHN! YONGE. The nroceedings were presided over by the Rev. W. H. 'I7AvLoR, of Eccles, who referred to the

(growth of ritualism and Romanism 'and the need for work such as was carried on by that Church. The Rev. JOHN YONGE said he wished to express what te believed was felt by their churches throughout the own and that was the very great sympathy they felt with the friends at Emmanuel Church in the dark season through which they had recently been passing. They had el6cted a new pastor, and he had commenced his work and was winning his way to the hearts of the people when suddenly the great Head of the Church took him to his reward in heaven. They hoped God in His mercy would guide to them a man after His own heart to build them up in all that was good and lead them on in their great work. The rev, gentleman ex- pressed himself in agreement with the remarks of Mr. Taylor in regard to the spread of ritualism and R omanism.
On the motion of Mr. ATHERTON a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Rev. John Yonge and Mrs.

div.head: RAILS.
div.p: RAILS.

The small parcel of 2.421 tons of tyres and axles, at £l4 9s. 7d. per ton, is a fleabite to our total make. It would be interesting to see Mr. Woods try to disprove the statement that these imports so far have been of the greatest benefit to us, and greatly enhanced our trade, of which the bulk of them form the raw material. Now we come to rails. Our imports have been 48,171 tons, at an average price of .26 18s. 2d. per ton, by the side of which I place our exports of rails over the same period of 581,334 tons at an average price Of £5 Bs. 9d. per ton. I leave Mr. Woods to inquire from the mem- bers of the rail ring in this country why and how it came about that they let slip that odd 4,800 tons at £6 18s. 2d. per ton. There only remains now the classes of material designated by the Board of Trade" unenumer- ated," which in 1902 was 228,715 tons at £l2 12s. 3d. per ton. Were it possible to analyse these we should prob- ably be able to fully account for these purchases , abroad—or the bulk of them. Our own unenumerated export I are 140.883 tons at £2l 9s. per ton. Both undoubtedly include many specialities. On what grounds or basis does Mr. Woods therefore, claim that prohibitive tariffs would have increased our trade to this amount, and how will Mr. Woods explain the fact that with decreasing prices in our manufacture and increased imports of what are largely semi-raw material,l our iron and steel profits for 1902 were £6,600,263, as against £3,211,884 in 1899-1900, though our prices had very much receded in the latter period? I leave his fallacies regarding machinery to those having a more expert knowledge than myself in that direction, confi- dent that his assertions in that direction have no more basis than in those relating to iron and steel • but generalising and assuming without proof in a matter of such importance is too common in the present con- troversy, and I cannot sit idly by and see working men confused and misled into Protective fallacies having for their object the creation of vested interests and monopolies from which we are now unhappily suffering too much already.—Yours faithfully, JAMES COX, (gen. Sec. of the Iron and Steel Werkers Union).

div.head: Darlington, Nov. 12th, 1903. Mr. Hugh Bell on Protection, and the
div.p: Darlington, Nov. 12th, 1903. Mr. Hugh Bell on Protection, and the
Iron and Steel Trades.

Sir,—The question of the iron and steel industries is of such local, as well as national importance, that I trust I will notbe thought to occupy too much of your space in noting some points man article in the October number of the"lndependent Review" by Mr. Hugh Bell This may be of interest to the people of Warrington,and all the more so, when some local manufacturers, in the different branches of the iron trade, are making such efforts to secure support to the proposals of Mr. Chamberlain.

Mr. Hugh Bell occupies a higli position in the Iron Trade in the North of England,and speaks with author- ity. In his article he lifts the discussion on to broad lines of national policy, and avoids sectional and selfish issues. Mr. Bell seems to recognize a development in the iron trade which will result in British capital and labour being employed more than hitherto in working up the material into more finished products, and thinks it possible, that more and more, we will import iron in the early stages of its manufacture, and that capital will naturally flow into the channels where it is probable most labour will be employed and most profit obtained The writer deprecates artificial measures, such as tariffs to divert the application of capital from the sphere, which it is naturally finding to be most profitable, into spheres which are only made profitable at the expense of other classes of the community. Mr. Bell says :—" To some small extent there has been a shifting of activity from the making to the utilization of unwrought steel; but the labour thrown idle in the former occupation has been more than made good by the additional labour required in piling on more and more labour in the production of the finished article."

My next quotation bears outivhat I have thought about many of the manufacturersl6ho are crying out for Protection, but did not care to say in case it should be thought to have local and personal application, and as such might be considered offensive. "Protection is an excellent thing for the conservative or inefficient manu- facturer; for it enables ehini to cover up his backward- ness at the expense of the consumer. On close investiga- tion we shall find, that much of the bitter cry of the iron trade comes from men who have not been able to keep themselves in the front rank of progress, and to whom it seems simpler to ask for Protection against the foreigner than to set their own houses in order." The strongest point in Mr. Bell's paper is in the form of a quotation bearing on the question of 'dumping" and is from a recent report of Mr. F. Oppenheim, British Consul-General at Frankfort-on-Main. This shows how the syndicates sold their raw material, and half finished goods' abroad at low prices, so that the home industries which worked off such raw materials, &c., were severely handicapped. He points out that cases had occurred in which finishing manufacturers had to decline orders owing to the exorbitant prices of raw material, and the orders passed subsequently to Holland, Belgium and England. "Thus this German material is to be had much cheaper abroad than it can be had at home, yet the home customer makes from such German material (half finished goods), and as this material was purchased at a greatly reduced cost, the foreign manu- facturer can sell his goods considerably cheaper than the German. Thus it 'follows that the German export of half finished goods is rapidly driven up, while the export of finished goods recedes— a state of affairs altogether contrary to the best economicinterests of the country, as it is most beneficial to the country at large that the exported goods should contain and represent as much national labour as pos- sible. The exports of machines, e.g., benefits national labour more than the export of iron bars,yet ironbars, while they cost home customers 95 marks delivered at the Rhenish-Westphalian works, were exported during the month of September for 80 marks, or even 72 marks f.0.b."

—lt is strange that while dear raw material is shown to handicap German industry in its higher branches, we should find any British manufacturers contending that it is a national loss to take advantage of the cheap material.

We are told by a German writer Edouard Bernstein in the November issue,l"lndependent Review," "That seven hundred manufacturers and merchants engaged in the cutlery and implement industry,whichhas its centre in Solingen, last spring petitioned the Reichstag in the matter. They were wnling to forego all protection for themselves, if only they might buy their raw material at the price of the world's market. This was no isolated case. Manufacturers in others of the metallurgical trades have explained in the Reichstag the harm done them by the duties on iron and steel, but, knovving well the political power of the ironmasters, have been con- tented to ask higher protection for their own goods. Had the latter petitions been granted, the evil would have been increased. Another stage of manufacture would have seen its cost of production raised still further." With these facts in view,it is not surprising that we should find such industries in Germany depressed, their hours of work longer, wages lower and their spendingipower less. These are facts which no protectionist, or retaliator, can get over, and is one on which the Warrington exponents, who clamour against German "dumping" and long for Protection, keep a discreet silence. This is the system which Mr Chamberlain would have us adopt, and Mr. Chamberlain is the great triumph of the work of Natura. or to puts it in Mr. Robert Pierpoint's Words, when in an unusual burst of oratory he says "Nature has been in travail, and has at last produced a man." Looking at this prodigy from the same point of 'view as Mr. Pierpoint, i.e., in the light of the proposed fiscal policy (and apart from Mr. Chamberlain's past services to the country,which I have always recognized,) it seems to me a pity Nature went to all this trouble if she could produce nothing better. Mr. Bell's article concludes with the following strenuous words :—"What the remote futufe may have in store for us, I will not endeavour to foretell ; but I venture to assert that, though changes at least as great as those I have described may be repeated under the eyes of living men, he is not born, nor his father, nor his grandfather,. who will see the British iron trade displaced from its proud position,provided only that we succeed in saving it from the false frieiids who would offer it a protection which it spurns. Let those en- gaged in it, alike employer and employed, co-operate in maintaining its progressive character ; let the State provide facilities for the scientific training of the officers, and suitable education for the rank and file of the great regiment, leaving them otherwise as free from legislative trammels as is consistent with the common weal; and I for one will look to the future of the trade with the same undaunted confidence with which I have witnessed it pass through the storms of the past half century."
CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh. November 12th 1903.

div.head: TEMPERANCE CAUSE.
div.p: THE TEMPERANCE CAUSE.
MEETING IN WYCLIFFE MEMORIAL
BUILDINGS.
Interesting Addresses.

Gratifying success attended the meeting promoted by the Temperance Committee of Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church held in the Memorial Buildings, Edgeworth-street, on Wednesday evening. Mr. George J. Brown presided over a large gathering, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. eS. Hughes, Mr. J. Owen and Mr. F. Morrell (secretary). The CHAIRMAN said he remembered that in years gone by Wycliffe Church had a very good temperance organization with which he was connected. He was glad 'to see from the large attendance at the meeting- that the organisation seemed to have been resuscitated and to have taken a fresh lease of life. It the temperance workers of that associ- ation would only take up an aggressive work, the chances were that they would do considerable good not only in the immediate locality but in the to-m. Accord- ing to his view, no church was complete in the circle of its organizations that did not include a temperance society. He would go further and say that no minister of religion, no matter to what sect he might belong, completed the circle of his obligations if he did not ,1 from time to time speak out against this greatest, most persistent and most over-powering enemy of the working-classes of the country. (Hear, hear.) Some people looked upon temperance societies as being incap- able of doing either very much good or very much harm. They told the members that when they had said and done all that they could, men would still continue to drink. That, to .tais mind, was one of the strongest arguments in favour of the existence of a temperance society. The object of temperance organizations was to try to assist those who had not got the - moral strength to resist the temptation when standing alone. Experience had shown them that the captive of strong drink in time frequently became the captive of other vices. What a great help it would be to the active temperance workers if they knew they had at their backs their fellow Christians, who, if they could not actually put their hands to the plough and help them in their active work, ,might at any rate give them their consistent example and their prayers. He was not at all inclined to take a gloomy outlook on the question, although people said temperance workers were not making much headway. There was an opinion in this country at the present time which was ripe for legisla- tion and some reform of the liquor laws, and if they could only find some strong statesman who would be willing to bring in some drastic Bill for the curtailing of the power of the brewing interest he (the speaker) thought that statesman would be very largely, supported. That would undoubtedly be a great advance, but per- sonally he, Telt that no legislative action could effectually deal with the drinking curse. It seemed to him that the only way of abolishing drunkenness was by Gospel temperance work. (Hear, hear.) He was sure all present believed that when drink had firmly got hold of a man nothing but the Gospel could save him. Mr. Brown proceeded to refer to the proposals of the National Defence League. That body, he said, argued that the time had come when every young man should become at any rate "a compulsory volunteer." Great stress was laid upon the fact that, the physique of our men was deteriorating, and the argu- ment was that military drill would have the effect of stopping that deterioration. There was a great deal to be said in favour of military training, but he thought he could discover some other reason for the decline of the physique of our men. The largest proportion of our soldiers were drawn from the cities and large towns, from men who had lived in squalid surroundings, in insanitary conditions, with the public house close to their doors and easy of access. What could military drill do to men who had ruined themselves and were ruining themselves by the facilities afforded to them for drinking? The speaker urged up- on his hearers the duty of being consistent and warned young men against the system of "treating " or paying corners." He also asked them to seriously consider whether they could, consistently with their temperance principles, support clubs or other associa- tions which derived revenue from the sale of intoxicants The mission of the temperance movement was not merely to save money or even health, but to save the entire man from physical, moral, and spiritual ruin. (Applause).l The Rev. .T. S. HUGHES ddressed the meeting and said he would be ashamed of himself if he were not a temperance advocate and a total- abstainer in these days when drink was such a curse in our land and so much needed to be done by the church in furtherarrce of truth and temperance, He was proud to say he had been a total abstainer from his boyhood and he believed that if everyone would adopt the same method of living as far as drink was concerned, it would settle a great many questions about which they were very much disturbed. He would say to the Labour party that it would settle the labour question if they adopted the temperance platform. The question of socialism could, he believed,also be settled in a like manner. He was aertainly of the opinion that the vexed fiscal (pies tion would also be settled if the people as a whole adopted temperance principles and lived a temperance life. (Hear, hear.) Twenty-five millions only were spent annually in Christian work, whereas ISO millions were spent in drink in this country. No wonder there was the cry of poverty among the working classes. He appealed to the labour movement, to the socialists, and all who had the interests of the working people at heart to consider the question. Drink, continued the speaker, had also cap- tured the Prime Minister. The last time he (the speaker) addressed a temperance meeting at Wycliffe he was highly elated at the new Licensing Act which had been passed. The measure had not, however, acted quite as well as some of them anticipated. it had not entirely swept our streets of drunkards and the black- list had not such a terror for the habitual drunkard. Now, it seemed to him the Prime Minister was going to counteract all the good of that Act by proposing to have legislative action that was likely to endow the brewing and publican interest, in support of his argument that no compens- ation should be given out of the public funds when a licence was not renewed, the rev, gentleman nointed out that the "Mulberry Tree "inn, Stockton Heath, was recently sold for £6,000 or £7,000. He contended that the house for ordinary purposes was worth only 22,000. and that its value was enhanced to such a great extent simply by the licence. That, he said, was a present which the people of the country made to. the person who held the licence, and yet publicarts demanded, although, they had profited so enormously by their trade, that compensation should be given when a licence was taken away. When they dealt with the question of compensation, let them compensate those , who had been made widows and orphans by drink, the wretched homes that had resulted from it, and the rate- payers who had to pay increased rates and taxes in conse- ' quence of the drinking that went on in the public houses. Continuing the speaker said the only effectual way in which they could cleanse the country from the drink curse washy everyone becoming total abstainers. The trade would then collapse. (Applause,) An enjoyable musical programme was submitted, Pianoforte solos were very creditably executed by Mr. J. A. Jones, songs were rendered in pleasing style by Miss Sumner and Mr. Booth and Messrs. Booth and Monks contributed two excellent duets. Mr. H. A. Roberts was responsible for a flute solo, and Miss M. Stanley gave mandoline solos, both performers acquitting themselves well. Ma. H. A. Roberts was an efficient accompanist. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Chair- man, speaker, and artistes, on the proposition of Mr. FARRAR.

div.head: DISCHARGED COACHMAN'S PATHETIO SUICIDE.
div.p: DISCHARGED COACHMAN'S PATHETIO SUICIDE.

Coroner Dobson held an inquest at Appleton Hall last evening touching the death of William Wilkins aged 38 years, a coachman until recently in the employ of Mr. T. H. Lyon.—The evidence showed that it was recently found necessary to dis- pense with the services of Wilkins and other servants. Deceased left the hall about ten o'clock on Thursday night and nothing was heard of him until Friday morn- ing when another employee on the estate, named John Heywood, recovered his body from a pit in Appleton Park. The hands were fastened together in a noose, and a 401 b dumbell was attached. It appeared that Mrs. Lester, of Stockton Heath, had a conversation with deceased on Thursday night and he was very much depressed at having to leave the estate, as he had been employed there for many years. Deceased was unmarried.
The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind."
Frßr. GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street,Warringion.—Ailvt.

div.head: MOTOR CAR TRANSACTION.
div.p: A MOTOR CAR TRANSACTION.
Interesting Case at the Warrington
County Court.
Amusing Passages.

His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C. heard an action at the Warriugton County Court on Thursday, in which Thomas Ralph Garton, director of the firm of Garton's, Limited, seed merchants &c., Warrington,. sought to recover from the Newton-Pearce Motor Car Company, Ltd., Hulme, Manchester, the sum of £5O, being the balance of the price of a motor car sold to the defendants by the plaintiff. Defendants counter- claimed for the return of the amounts paid by them on =count for the car, totalling £llO and made up of ZGO in cash and :C5O debentures in the defendant com- pany. Defendants claimed that they were entitled to reject the car on the ground that it was not in good rnnning order.--Mr. Acton, barrister, (instructed by Messrs. Browne and Crompton) appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendant company was represented by Mr. Rigby Swift, barrister (instructed by Mr. H. J. Longton). _ _ _ _ . _

Mr. ActO'n said that in June last Mr. Garton was the possessor of a6l h.p. motor car, known as the Darracq. The defendants were in the motor car industry and the manager, Mr. Heyl-Dia, wished to obtain a Darracq car for the purpose of getting patterns from it to use in constructing cars. Accordingly a message was sent to the plaintiff, as a result of which he took the car to Mr. Heyl-Dia,'s house at Stretton. He interviewed Mr. Heyl-Dia in the presence of Mr. Hall. Plaintiff said he would sell the car for ea() (he had in fact been offered £155 for it previously) but Mr. Heyl-Dia at first said that was a great deal too much. After some discussion Mr. Heyl-Dia gave way and agreed to pay the amount asked by the plaintiff. The question of the time and mode of payment then arose and Mr. Heyl-Dia said he knew the plaintiff was inter- ested in motor cars and he would very much like him to have an interest in the company. He asked him to take part payment of the £l6O in shares and suggested that he should receive both debentures and ordinary shares. Plaintiff said he knew nothing about the shares or the company, but he was informed by Mr. Heyl-Dia that there had been a public issue and the shares were worth their face-value—or par—and would almost rcertainly be worth a great deal more before much time had elapsed. It was arranged that there should be a cash payment of £6O, debentures to the extent of £5O, and fifty ordinary £1 shares in the company. The car was delivered to Mr. Heyl-Dia and for three months nothing more was heard about the matter. The ordinary shares were not sent to the plaintiff and on September 7th he received a letter stating that the board had decided not to com- plete the purchase of the car and they had requested Mr. Heyl-Dia to see the plaintiff. Mr. Garton replied to the effect that Mr. Heyl-Dia purchased the car for £l6O, and as the defendants had had possession of it for two Months and part of the purchase money had been paid, he must inform them that unless he received a cheque for £5O by return of post he should place the matter in the hands of his solicitors., The reply from the company was that the car was bought from thelplaintiff on condition that it was in perfect runnin,, order, but an examination at the works had proved that it was not. Mr. Garton again wrote demanding Payment of £5O. Subsequently he received a form of -transfer of sixty fully paid-up shares in the company which, it was stated, would complete the purchase. Mr. Garton was asked to sign the trans- fer and return it along with 10s. for the stamp. It be- came apparent on inquiry that the shares in the com- pany had never been issued to the public. He (Mr. Acton) said with confidence that they were practically owned by Mr. Hdyl-Dia, and he further ventured to say they they were not worth is. each at the present moment. The transfer was accordingly not negotiated; and he contended that plaintiff was entitled to sue for £5O in cash.
Plaintiff gave evidence and said the car was in good condition.

In cross-examination he admitted that there was nothing improper in one man holding the bulk of the shares in a Company. The motor car was placed in charge of Mr. W. H. Bellian, with a view to a sale being effected, and Mr. &Allan gave witness the information that Mr. Heyl-Dia required one. He denied telling Mr. Heyl-Dia that he only wanted £l4O for the car. He was not told by Mr. Heyl-Dia that the value of the shares would depend upon the success of the Company which was a new one. He did not use the car after the date of sale.

Mr. Swift asked witness if previously the car had gone through a hedge into a ploughed field. (Laughter). His Honour: This is a new chapter in the natural history of motor cars. (Laughter.) Plaintiff said the car did not go into the field. It ran against the fence. Mr. Swift: Did'nt you take a doctor for a drive, and drive the car over the hedge into a ploughed field? Witness: No. There was no damage done to the car.
His Honour anpearedamused when Mr. Swift inquired if the" bonnet was damaged. "It covers the engine like a bonnet covers the brain said Mr. Swift.

His Honour: I did'nt know motor cars had come out of their primeval condition and reached a state of civilization. (Laughter.) There were saveral other questions which called forth the remark from his Honour "It is very interesting. We will get to the matinee hat soon." A share register of the defendant company was then producel and plaintiff said it showed that the fully paid-up ordinary shares were issue to the gentlemen who took up debentures. There wefe, he believed, only two shareholders in addition to Mr. Heyl-Dia and em- ployees of the company. By Mr. Swift: He was not aware that the share- holders had entered into agreements with the company which would be a consideration of the issue to them of fully paid-up shares. Mr. W. H. Bellian, 115, Sankey-street, spoke to over- hauling the car at a cost of about £2O. In addition the car was upholstered. It was in running order. After the sale had been effected Mr. Heyl-Dia sent the car to him for slight running-repairs. Judging by its appear- ance witness should say the car had been used a great deal since Mr. Garton took it from his works to sell it. By Mr. Swift: Mr. Heyl-Dia bought a Darracq car from witness several months previously. Witness admitted that on one occasion he said Mr. Garton's car would" kill someone some day." The "clutch was very fierce." Witness was of the opinion that the car was worth £l5O.
Frederick R. Holding, manager for Mr. BeMan. said the car was in good running-order when Mr. Garton took it front the shop. _ _ _

For the defence Mr. Heyl-Dia stated that the com- pany required the car to take measurements from it. The last witness told him plaintiff wanted about £l4O for the car. When plaintiff came to his house he said the car was in absolutely perfect condition. Witness said he understood plaintiff wanted about £l4O for it, but if the Company purchased the car they would not be inclined to pay that amount in cash and some arrange- ment would have tl be made for payment of a certain sum in debentures and shares. It was decided that the Company should pay £6O in cash, £5O in debentures, and that plaintiff should receive GO ordinary shares. Witness told Mr. Garton that the working capital of the company had been formed by the issue of deben- tures and the value of the shares was entirely dependent upon the profits. He did not say there had been a public issue. On going to Mr. Bellian's for the car witness was told that it was out. The car "chucked the passengers about" to such an extent that the com- pany could not possibly use it. - His Honour pointed out that in view of the fact that defendants kept the car for so long without complaint and afterwards sent it to be repaired, he did not think they could convince him in favour of the counter-claim as to repudiation.

The question of payment was then dealt with. Mr. Thomas Hall, director of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. Ltd., who was present when plaintiff interviewed Mr. Heyl-Dia, said Mr. Garton asked for £l6O and was immovable on that point. The arrangement as to shares, &c„ was subsequently agreed upon. He did not hear Mr. Heyl-Dia state that there had been a public issue and that the shares were worth their face value. In the course of further argument on legal points Mr. Acton submitted that plaintiff was entitled to a special allotment of shares and not a transfer.
His.Honour.held_this point was immaterial.
Ultimately his Honor came to the conclusion that plaintiff was entitled to 60 shares in the company with- out costs. He also gave judgm.mt for the plaintiff on the counter-claim with costs.

div.head: HARRIERS.
div.p: HARRIERS.
WARRINGTON HARRIERS v. WINNINGTON PARK.

An inter-club run between the above clubs tookplace from the former's headquarters the Bridge Inn. The hares Messrs. Anderton .and Smith were despatched at 3.30 p.m. the pack consisting of 18 of the home team and 12 of the visitors following 20 minutes later. The course taken was through*Arpley fields to Fiddler's Ferry. Arrived at this point the trail was laid in the direction of Moore by way of Bobs Bridge and then along the Ship Canal to the Stag Bridge where the , pack lined up for a break to headquarters and after a I spirited run arrived in the following order : WA RRIXGTON. WINNINGTON. C. J. Straw ' 1 Frayne C. Dagnall J. Mather 4 Barton S. Parsonage C. Berry J. Stuart .
