div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

WARRINGTON POACHERS SENT TO PRISON. At the Lvmm Police Court on Monday,two Warrington men named Peter Rowson and George Ogden were brought before Messrs T. P. Norris and W. P. Brabazon on a charge of trespassing on enclpsedland in the occu- pation of Mr. John Longshaw,atlLymm,with snares and .a gun, for the purpose of destroying game, early that morning.—John Leigh, gamekeeper for Mr. Fox, stated that at a quarter to two that morning he was near to Mr. Fox's land in company with Col. Legh's keeper, when he heard shots fired. After listening for a while he heard five more reports in Longshavv Wood, near Cherry-lane. He and the other keeper moved towards the wood, and they encountered the two prisoners and another man. They charged them, but no resistance was offered. One man escaped. The pheasant rearing ground was adjacent to Longshaw Wood. Witness took a gun from Rowson and Colonel Legh's keeper took Ogden into custody. At five o'clock -they returned to the wood, and found three bags con- taihing 12 rabbits, three hen pheasants and two long 70-yard nets under a bush about 40 yards from where the prisoners were arrested. In Rowson's possession were 20 loaded cartridges and seven empty ones. The gun was sighted for night firing, a piece of string being wrapped round the nozzle. Several pegs were subse- quently found.—Charles Marchant, Col. Legh's keeper, tendered similar evidence.—The police records showed a number of peevious convictions against the prisoners for game trespass, and the magistrates sent them to gaol for two months' hard labour each, and at the expiration of their term ordered them to find a surety each in 210, •Or two sureties each of £5, or to undergo a further month's imprisonment each. SAD CA.SE OF THEFT.—GIRL SENT TO A HOME. •

A girl of sixteen named Betsy Robinson, residing at 75, Baxter-street, was placed in tie dock at the War- rington Police Court on Tuesday on the charge of steal- ing a quilt, the property of Beryl May Gleave, 86, Bramhall-street.—The Chief Constable said the case was particularly sad because the prisoner was the daughter of an expert thief who was now undergoing nine months' imprisonment for numerous shop robberies. No doubt the girl had been trained in the ways of -robbery and to some extent one might say that her present position was not entirely due to her own fault. It appeared that prisoner had for some time been living with her married sister in BAxter- street, and the house faced the back premises of the prosecutrix's residence. The quilt was hung on a line in the yard and shortly after seven o'clock on Monday evening Mrs. Gleave heard someone drop over the wall into the yard. On going outside she found the quilt had been stolen. Information was given to the police and P.C. Clough made inquiries with the result that it was ascertained that prisoner had attempted to pledge the quilt. On hearing that the police were making in- quiries she became alarmed and concealed it in a passage where it was subSequently found.—After con- siderable persuasion prisoner consented to go into a home for twelve months, and the case was adjourned .sini die.

div.head: STOPPING THE IRISH MAIL.
div.p: STOPPING THE IRISH MAIL.

At Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr. Henry Nield (presiding) and Colonel Ridgway, Ernest Woods, 2, Smith-street, Lower Walton, was summoned for making use of the means of communication be- tween passengers and the company's servants without reasonable or sufficient cause, on a train on the London and North-Western Railway at Kekewick, on Septem- ber 9th.—He pleaded guilty.—Mr. Fenna, solicitor, prosecuted on behalf of the Railway Company and said that on the night in question the defendant was a pas- senger on an Irish mail train, which left Chester for Manchester at 2.30a.m. In the same carriage was an officer in the Bengal Marine Service, who had come down specially from London to give evidence. After the train left Chester the defendant went to Mr. Hopkins, the service officer, and wanted to shake hands with him. Mr. Hopkins saw he was under the influence of drink, and shook hands with him -twice, thinking he would then be quiet. Defend- ant however, wanted to keep on shaking hands, and Mr. Hopkins told him not to bother him. The defendant, .subsequently stood up and got hold of the communica- tion cord, and in spite of the warning of his fellow- passenger, pulled it violently. The result was that the train stopped, and the guard came to the carriage and spoke to the defendant. Defendant did not make any -complaint at that time, but at the next station (War- rington), he said that the officer had tried to rob him of his watch and chain: That was entirely false and Mr.

div.head: TOY PISTOL DANGER. A Warrington Boy Shot.
div.p: THE TOY PISTOL DANGER. A Warrington Boy Shot.

A singular case was heard at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. John Fairclough and others magistrates, when a boy of thirteen named Albert Wakefield, residing in Heath-lane, was charged with using a pistol in Cambria Place on November Ist. The Chief Constable said this was the first information which had been laid in Warrington under the Pistols' Act which became law in August last. The Act was passed for the purpose of restricting the use and sale of toy pistols, principally, and of fire arms generally by unauthorised and improper persons. The section under which the prosecution was in- stituted provided that any person under the age of eighteen (not being exempt by virtue of section 7 of the gun licences act,lB7o) using or carrying a pistol should be liable to a penalty not exceeding 40s. Any person who knowingly sold or delivered a pistol to any person under 18 who was not exempted by the clause named. was liable to a penalty not exceeding £.5. The facts of the case would almost have warranted him charg- ing the prisoner, had he been older, with shooting with intent todo grievous bodily harm On the date in question a boy named David Henry Stanley,(l4) of King street was playing with some companions in Cambria Place whon he heard three reports as if a pistol were being fired. The children ran down a dark entry and prisoner followed them shouting " I can fetch a leg off any of you." He then knelt down, took deliberate aim with a small pistol—a very deadly weapon—and fired at the boys, hitting Stanley on the leg. Stanley fell down suffering from shock and bleed- ing profusely. He was removed to the Infirmary, where he.was detained as an in-patient. The X rays had to be used for the purpose of locating the position of the bullet, which was subsequently extracted. Prisoner , immediately left home and did not return until Tues- day last. In the meantime the pistol and ammuni- tion had been made away with. The by said he bought the pistol at the shop of Mr. Skelton, Sankey-street, together with one or two cartridges, for I about half-a-crown. P.C. Stewart interviewed Mr. 'Skelton in company with the prisoner, and Mr. Skelton frankly said he remembered selling the pistol to the lad but he was entirely ignorant of the law on the point. Prisoner's motherentered the witness-box and said a large air gun which the Chief Constable produced belonged to her son. Questioned as to where the boy obtained his money from, she stated that he told her he found 235. ma hole on the site of the new Post Office. The Chief Constable said the boy had been Convicted of felony and birched. Not long ago the police were searching for him in connection with several robberies perpetrated in the market with theaid of skeleton keys. A fine of 20s. and costs with the option of seven days imprisonment was inflicted. The Chief Constable suggested that prominence should be given to the caseby the press in order that the law on the subject might be more generally known.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 14, 1903
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 14, 1903

A Mrs. Constance Wallace. on Thursday, obtained £25 damages against Major H. F. Woodgate, a former lover, for a libel contained in a novel he wrote, one of the characters of which plaintiff declared had been taken by her friends to be intended as a picture of her. A good and possibly new, story is told of Chauncey Depew. He was riding up Pennsylva.nia•avenue, in Washington, in a street car. A motherly old lady who sat next to hini asked a question. The Senator answered it, and found the old lady was deaf. He repeated his answer in a shout, and the conversation went on until the Senator said: "You are quite deaf, are you not ?" "Yes," she replied," and I haven't been able to do a thing for it." " Have you ever triedelectricity?" asked. the Senator. "Yes," she said, nodding her head vigor- ously. "I was struck by lightning last summer."
ELECTION OF AN ALDERMAN. CONSERVATIVES OPPOSE COUNCILLOR WILLIAM PIERPOINT.

The next business was the appointment of an alder- man to succeed Mr. F. W. Monks, resigned, the new aldermanto continue in office until the 9th day of November, 1904. The MAYOR observed that all the members knew the rule with reference to the election of an alderman. They had all made up their minds, and talking would not alter a single vote. He would thank them to hand up the voting papers. The members did so, and the MAYOR announced that the result was as follows : FOR COUNCILLOR JOHN EVANS. Alderman Smethurst „ Fairclough Hutchinson Franco m b Sutton Heaton Councillor Hulse Rogers „ IVlaginn 1, Wilson—lo

FOR COUNC I LLOR PIERPOINT! Alderman Bennett Councillor Tinnion Burton Wilkinson Ashcroft Barton Lord James Evans Pemberton Ho rrocks Forshaw Peacock Duncan Ellison Davies Dodds •• Roberts-17 The Mavoa then declared Councillor Pierpoint to have been dulyelected an alderman of the borough by 17 votes to 10, and said he congratulated the new Alder- man very much. Councillor William Pierpoint had repeatedly been in anticipation of having the seat, and he was now pleased to know that he was one of them. (Hear, hear.) ALDERMAN SUTTON'S EXPLANATION. Alderman SUTTON said that although he was one who voted against Mr. Pierpoint, he was very wishful at once to be one of the first to congratulate him on his appointment. (Cries of" Oh, oh," and laughter.) What he said he meant. (Hear, hear.) He was not in the habit of saying things in that Council Chamber which he did not believe or mean, so that they might he as sarcastic as they liked. He said without hesitation that there was no one in the Council Chamber he respected more as a personal friend than Mr. Pierpoint, and had it not been for the hints and innuendoes, even almost amounting to threats, that there would probably be a fight between Liberals and Conservatives there would have been no opposition to Mr. Pierpoint. 114 was very pleased inde ed that he had been appointed, because he believed from his past services, and from the length of time he had been in the Council, that he was fully entitled to the. position. He hoped Alderman Pierpoint would understand the position of things, and how it was he did not give him his vote en that occasion. Councillor TiNazioN : I know you are willing to make any excuse. Alderman SUTTON: The only one who— The MAYOR: Don't gentlemen. ALDERMAN PIE3E'OINT'S INTENTION. After making the usual declaration Alderman Pier- point said it was a curious coincidence that his friend the Mayor aad himself 21 years ago that day signed their respective declarations as councillors of the borough—(applause)—and he supposed the unfortunate fact that he (the speaker) happened to belong to the Liberal party of Warrington must account in some measure for another fact, and that was that after he had been a member of the Council for nine years his good friend Alderman Smethurst managed to give him a down-right good beating in • the Town Hall Ward. (Laughter.) Mr. Smethurst and he had been the best of friends ever since, and the beating never did him (Coun- cillor Pierpoint) the least harm, and he had never re- gretted it. After serving the best part of his business life on behalf of the town of Warringtoa it would have been a graceful act at least on the part of his Tory friends if they had allowed this vote to have been aunanimous one. (Hear, hear.) What ever anyone might have said with reference to threats or innuendoes, at all events no one could possibly say that he had ever given the slightest hint of being dissatisfied with anything the Tory party have chile for him. He had always been used to political fighting,and he was used to political knocks; he never objected to them. He was a poor man who could not put his hands up to do his best to protect himself and then go home and thank goodness he had had a grueling which he would be able to get over. (Laughter.) There was one consolation he had,and it was—that the small minority at was against him in the main con- sisted of the ardermen of the borough, with a few exceptions. He belonged to the honourable body now, but he was afraid he should have to stand isolated from them. He should take his own course, and he hoped the opportunity might present itself when he might be able to give one straight" back irom the shoulder for the adverse vote that had been given to him that day. He hoped they would let byegones be byegoaes and he thanked Alderman Sutton for what he had said with reference to him. (Applause.) COUNCILLOR TINNION AND THE QUESTION OF SENIORITY. The Council then proceeded to consider the Standing Orders for the regulation of the proceedings of the Council and for the government of committees. Councillor 'FISSION alluded to Order 48, referrine' to precedence. The order reads as follows :—" For the purpose of determining the seniority of members of the Council, with a view to the allotment of their seats in the Council Chamber and for other purposes a list shall be prepared by the Town Clerk in which shall be inserted in the first place the names of the several aldermen in the order of their respective periods of tenure of that office; and in the next place the names of the several councillors in the order of their re- spective periods of tenure of the office of councillor, provided that the Deputy Mayor shall in all cases take priority next after the Mayor." He said that it would be well to have some understanding as to what the order meant. He did not propose to do so that day,but at some future time he should move a resolution to the effect that they should so alter the order that it could not be misunderstood, and he could not be blamed for wilfully or otherwise misrepresenting the order. He took it that when the order was passed it was the inten- tion that it should apply to both aldermen and coun- cillors. It seemed to him, continued Councillor Tinnion, unfair that he should be charged, as he had been that day, with being the sole cause of the opposition to Mr. Pierpoint. That was not so, and he was inclined to think that the misunderstanding was owing to the vague- ness of the order to which he had referred. He asked the Town Clerk so to draw up the rule that there could in future be no misunderstanding as to what it meant. It was painful to him to be charged with having intro- duced politics into the Council Chamber. He denied the insinuation as strongly as he could. The MAYOR suggested that the Standing Order in question should be brought under the notice of the General Purposes Committee. Councillor TINNION: It would be better if in the meantime the Town Clerk nitered the order so that there can be no misunderstanding. The TOWN CLERK said Mr. William Pierpoint would now take his proper place on the list of aldermen. Councillor TINNION asked who was the senior coun- cillor according to the Standing Orders. The TOWN CLERK : Mr. William. Pierpoint. Alderman SMETHURST did not think the order was quite clear. He suggested that they should leave the matter in the hands of the Town Clerk. (Hear, hear). Alderman SUTTON was in favour of the matter being discussed by the General Purposes Committee. Councillor PEMBERTON said that as this seemed to be a public question he did not think it ought to be dis- cussed by the General Purposes Committee who sat in private. He moved that the words "and for other pur- poses "be left out. It was decided to leave the matter in the hands of the General Purposes Committee and the Town Clerk. THE CONSTITUTION OF COMMITTEES. DUTIES TO BE MORE EVENLY DISTRIBUTED. Councillor DODDS called attention to Rule 29—" The, Mayor shall, ex-officio, be a member of every committee and of every sub-committee." He wanted to add to that order the words "But no other member of the Council shall be appointed to serve upon more than five committees except by special resolution of the Council, neither the General Purposes Committee nor the Education Committee to be deemed one of the com- mittees referred to." There were several gentle- men present on few committees, others were on seven or eight. Some line should be drawn with regard to the matter. In Manchester no member of the Council was allowed to be on more than three committees, and he thought it would be a very good rule to bring the number down to five in Warrington. Councillor WILKINSON seconded. The MAYOR pointed out that if Mr. Dodds' motion , was carried the whole of the committees would have to be remodelled. Councillor DODDS replied that he did not think the alteration would affect more than two or three. 1 The MAYOR: It will mean going through the com- mittees seriatim. 1 Councillor WILKINSON said that those who were serving on many committees could retire while those I serving on a few ought to take their places, and thus 1 the work of the Corporation would be equally divided. I The MAYOR: I offered to retire from several com- mittees. I sent in my resignations but they refused to allow any one of them to take effect. I Councillor PnainEwroN supported Councillor Dodds' proposition, and said that Councillor Horrocks was on no committees at all. He thought they would be fol- lowing a good city if they followed the custom adopted in Manchester.

Councillor ROBERTS said ho was willing to withdraw . from two committees—the Markets and Rivers. Councillor JAMES EVANS suggested that the names appearing on the agenda should be left as they were, and the members who felt they were on too many corn- mittees could afterwards withdraw. He intended to withdtuw from one or two.

Councillor TINNION said that five was the smallest number of committees a member should be on. They would not get full committees unless some members were on more than five committees. He was afraid Councillor Dodds had not thought the matter out suffi- ciently. He (the speaker) was a sinner to the extent of seven committees, but he contended he should be con- sulted as to what committees would be most suitable;to him to attend. The same remark applied to other mem- bers. He quite agreed with Councillor Dodds' prin- ciple, but it was not desirable to deal with the matter that afternoon ; the matter could be dealt with another day.

----6;uncillor SMETHURST was quite prepared to give up any committee if another member could be found to take his place. Councillor DODDS agreed to alter the number of com- mittees to six, and the resolution was carried unani- mously.
THE COMMITTEES. MR. F. MONKS RETIRES FROM THE MUSEUM COMMITTEE.
The following appointments to committees were then submitted to the Council :

Watch.—The Mayor, Aldermen Fairclough, Francomb Heaton, Hutchinson, Smethurst, Sutton, and Pierpoint ; Councillors Burton and John Roberts. Finance and Estate.—Aldermen Bennett and Fairclough Councillors Craik, Dodds Forshaw, Hulse, Lord, Wilkinson] Peacock'and Thornton. _

Simko-17 Works.—Aldermen Bennett and Smethurst ; Councillors Burton, Craik, Duncan, John Evans, Tinnion, Wilkinson Maoinn and Wilson.

Paving and gewerage.—Aldermen Heaton, Hutchin- son and Smethurst; Councillors Burton, Davies, For- shaw, Peraberton, J. Roberts, Rogers and Tinnion. Museam.—Aldermenßennett and Hutchinson; Coun- cillors Barton, Brough, Ellisn, Forshaw, Hulse,Thorn- ton and Pemberton; and the following non-members of the Council, viz.: Messrs. Robert Pierpoint, ma, T.J. Ridgway, Thomas May, F. Monks, J. F. Dutton, A. J. Jolley, and Rev: Morley Stevenson. _ _
Cemeteri.--Cvuncillors Ifarton, Brophy, Brough, Craik, Duncan, James Evans, John Evans, Hulse and Peacock.
Town Hall, Parks. and Baths Committee.—The Mayor Aldermen Bolton, Fairclough, Prancomb, Hutchinson, Smethurst, Sutton and Pierpoint ; Councillors Ellison, John Roberts and Wilkinson.

iklarkets.—AlderMan Hutchinson; Councillors Duncan, James Evans, Hale, Lord, Peacock, John Roberts, Rogers, Ashcroft and Davies. Gas.—Aldermen Balton, Fairclough, Pierpoint and Heaton; Councillors Duncan, Ellison, James Evans, John Evans,. John Roberts and Tinnion.

Rivers,—.Aldermen Bennett, 13,3&n, Fairclough, Hutchinson and Sutton; Councillor James Evans, John Evans, Forshaw, John R oberts and Tinnion. Fire Engine.—Alderman Smethurst, and Councillors Barton, Brophy, Brough, Burton, Duncan, James Evans, Peacock, Wilson and Ashcroft.

Water..—Aldermen Bolton, Francomb, Hutchinson and Smethurst; Councillor Duncan, John Evans, Forshaw, Pemberton, John Roberts and Rogers. Gymnasium.—Councillors Brophy, James Evans, John Evans, Hulse Tinnion, Wilson and Ashcroft; and the following non-members of the Council :—Messrs Hugh Ferguson, Thomas Locker, and A. Mottram. Electricity and Tramways.—Aldermeoßennett, Bolton, Smethurst, Pierpoint and Sutton ; and Conncillors Ellison, John Evans, Pemberton, Tinnion, Wilkinson, Peacock, Craik, Lord, Thornton and Maginn. General Purposes Cominittee.—This committee con- sists of all members of the Council.
The constitution of several committees having been agreed to,

-Councillor DODDS asked if the Council were not now appointing the committees by a special resolution of the Council. If they were, some gentlemen might say : "We are entitledto our seats on certain committees because we have been appointed at a special meeting of the Council."

The M.vvoß said he hoped Councillor Dodds would adopt his suggestion to allow each committee to decide. When the appointment of members of the Museum Committee came up for consideration, Alderman BENNETr read the following letter from Mr. Monks: —"Monks, Hall, and Company, Limited. Warrington, 9th I November,l9o3. Dear Mr. Town Clerk,—l see from the published list of nominations that the Council renominate me as a member of the Museum and Library Committee. I must ask the Council to elect some other ratepayer. I have sat on the committee for a very long time, and been its chairman, for the past 13 years, but I am getting older and less inclined to accept responsi- bilities. Please to thank the members of the Council for their uniform kindness and for again suggesting my name, but the time has come for the younger men to do their share of the work and let the older ones rest and be thankful." Alderman Bennett said they would all feel extremely sorry that Mr. Monks had come to such a decision but they must recognize the fact for many years he Wad been of the greatest possible service to the town in the position he had occupied with so much credit to himself and advantage to the Co uncll.(Hear,hear) Councillor DODOS suggested that the name of Mr. Upson should be added to the committee.
Alderman BENNETT replied that if it was competent for him to add his name to the committee he should be very pleased to do so.
thi; TOWN CLERK said it was competent to fill up the vacancy then. Alderman SUTTON thought the matter should be left to the committee.

Alderman BENNETT said Mr. Upson had rendered great services to the town in the matter of the branch libraries, and they would be only too pleased as a com- mittee to take advantage of his agsistance. (Hear, hear.) There was another vanancy on the committee, and it was decided to fill it up by adding the name of Coun- cillor Horrocks.
When the minutes of the Gymnasium Committee came up for consideration, Councillor JAMES EVANS said he was already a member of seven committees.

The MAYOR: Leave it over. When the names of the members of the Electricity and Tramway Committee were read, Alderman BENNETT: and Pierpoint expressed their willingness to retire. The Alxvoit : That will ba borne in mind at the next committee meeting. Councillor Horrocks was appointed a member of the Cemetery Committee.
The constitution of the committees was then agreed to with the additions named.
THE COUNCIL MEETINGS.

It was unanimously Iresolved "that there shall be three following quarterly meetings of the:Council in the year for the transaction of general business, to be holden at six o'clock on each day, that is to say : On the first Tuesday in February, 1904, on the first Tuesday in May, 1904, on the first Tuesday in August, 1904," and "That a monthly meeting of the Council be held on the first Tuesday in each month (excepting the months of February, May, and August), at six o'clock in the evening, and that an additional meeting be held on the last Tuesday in October, at the same hour. PRESIDING ALDERMEN.

On the motion of Councillor ROGERS, it was decided that the following be appointed the •presiding alder- men :—TownHale Ward, Alderman Smethurst; White Cross Ward, Alderman Pierpoint ; Bewsey Ward, Alder- man Fairclough ; Orford Ward, Alderman Sutton ; Fairfield Ward, Alderman Heaton; Howley Ward, Alder- man Francomb : St. Austin's Ward, Alderman Bennett;. Latchford Ward, Alderman Bolton. APPOINTMENT OF REPRESENTATIVES.

Alderman Sutton and Councillor Maginn were ap- pointed the two representative members of the Educa- tion Committee,Alderman Francomb the representative of the Council on the Lancashire Asylums Board,Alder- man Heaton on the Lancashire Inebriates Acts' Board, and Councillor Dadds on the County Rate Joint Com- mittee.
COUNCILLOR DODDS AND COMMITTEE WORK. Councillor DODDS expressed a wish to retire from the Education Committee.

AldQrman SMETHURST did not think it right that Councillor Dodds who was a member of only two com- mittees should wish to retire from one of them. Councillor DODDS said he did not know whether Alderman Smethurst was angry with him or not. but when he (Councillor Dodds) was elected he put it to the ratepayers of the ward he represented that he cauld not give the time that other members were.able to give to serve on ninny committees. The NIA von. : You are out of order.
Alderman SNIET If URST : Why do y9n complain about other people being on so many committees if you can- not attend yourself? The discussion then dropped. • THE LATE MR. SHAW GREEN. -,lm.

The MAYOR, after the conclusion of the ordinary business, said it was his painful duty formally to announce to the Council the death of Mr. Joseph Shaw Green, formally an Alderman of the borough, and for many years a member of the Council. Mr. Shaw Green was a very earnest and useful member of the Council, and the best of his labours were given in the interests of the town. He occupied a very high position among the members of the Council, and filled with great credit the.7several important positions which were entrusted to him. The state of his health a few months ago com- pelled his retirement from the Council, and a universal opinion was then expressed of the serious loss of his public services which the town then suffered. His death unfortenately followed his retirement in a very brief space of time, and now they had to mourn the loss of him as a fellow townsman. He was sure their sympathy would go out to his widow and children with the earnest hope that they would find solace in the high estimation and warm regard which were felt and shown to his memory by the members of the Council and the inhabitants at large. div.head: DOCTORS WERE BAFFLED. Liver complaint and Constipation.
div.p: DOCTORS WERE BAFFLED. Liver complaint and Constipation.
BILE BEANS CURED BOTH.

Mrs. Ann Maria Jeffs, of Frankley. (Worcester). tells an experience which is sufficiently interesting to justify repetition. Here it is:—" About three years ago I began to suffer with liver complaint and constipation. The first symptoms were those of lassitude, and later, overpowering drowsiness. These feelings were followed by giddiness and occasional attacks of fainting weak- ness which would cause me to stagger and reel. I also had indigestion. , "After taking any food whatever, I experienced most acute pain. This was at times so very bad that I actually pined myself rather than pass through itjand I have gone as long as three days without breaking my fast. "My tongue was coated with a yellow* 'substance as thick as half-a-crown. Added to this I supred acutely from constipation, and experienced the dffll, heavy feel ing which that ailment gives—the headache and awfu- depression. A local doctor was consulted, but I ob-I tamed no results from his medicines, and continued to get worse. My condition eventually became so critical that my husband and friends thought my days were numbered. "Nothing would stay on my stomach—not even a drop of beef tea or a little boiled milk; .and as no nourishment could be put into my system, I wasted away to a mere shadow. "My husband heard of Charles Forde's bile beans, and as a last hope we got a supply. I persevered with them, and the fact that they were going to cure me son became clear. Soon after beginning to take them I passed two great gall stones. The passing of these gave me great pain, but when the pains subsided my bowels became easier and the constipation left me altogether. Every week I got better, the ailments I had suffered from disappeared, and in the end I was completely restored to health. . "I met my doctor while the cure was in progress. He asked the cause of my improvement, and when I told him he said: 'lf bile beans have made this wonderful change in you, by all means continue them.' Another day I was stopped by our minister, who, on hearing what had cured me, said: 'The change is so wonderful it is your duty to write to the Bile Bean Co., and thank them. Bile beans are now our family medicine." Every local sufferer should benefit by hearing Mrs. Jeffs' experience. It need only be added that the remedy which she so extols may now be obtained from all chemists at is. id. or 2s. 9d. per box.

LIBERAL AND LABOUR. President of the Trades Council Replies to Mr. Osborne.

Before the commencement of the ordinary busines! at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Trade Labour Council on Tuesday evening, the President' (Mr. J. Podmore) said he wished to make a few rfr marks concerning an article which appeared in rl "Examiner." They would recollect that at the las„, meeting he called attention to a Mr. Osborne wire wrote an article and to the statements which he nia in regard to the Trades Council. Mr. Osborne ,ha another contribution_ in last week's" Examiner ' titled" Liberal and Labour." div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S OFFER TO
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S OFFER TO
LABOUR.

Corrupt PraCt'''c IT has long 0)...J been found out that the present law as to Corrupt Practices at elections is quite insufficient to prevent a wealthy candi- date from committing wholesale bribery under the gentle name of charity. The Corrupt Practices Act needs stringent amendment. It is a pity that the corrupt practice of making wholesale and reckless promises to the electors cannot also be made illegal. It is perfectly clear that Mr. Chamberlain means to promise anything, so long as he can secure support for Protection. To every trade which asks for special consideration he replies that he will carefully consider their interests. And as Mr. Winston Churchill wrote recently, should this scheme be adopted,

every dirty little monopolist in the island will have his own society to push his special trade, and for each and all the watchword will 15e, "Scratch my back," and the countersign, "I will scratch yours." Every election Will turn on tariff.

We have already the revolting sight of one of our great parties in the State being bound hand and foot to the liquor trade. What would be the moral condition of the country if every trade became a monopoly whose motto was "Our trade, our politics" F. But even this prospect falls into comparative insignificance before the great bribe which Mr. Chamberlain is offering to Labour in connection with his ,scheme. He informs us that:

I am going to tell every meeting I address in which working men predominate that they should address themselves'mainly and chiefly to the ques- tion whether or not ~the proposals I make will increase their employment.

Later on, in the same speech, he answered his own question about the increase in employ- ment by saying: "I say that if you follow me I believe you may have more employment." In °there of his speeches he has promised higher wages. In the House of Commons last May he promised to draw up a table showing how much the increase of wages would be. This patent Protectionist ready-reckoner for workmen's wages has not yet appeared. Why this delay ?
Promising- Imp

THE proba. iie reasou for the delay in pro- ducing this scale of wages is that it is impossible to draw up any scheme of Protec- tion which would ensure an increase of wages all round. There are dozens of occupations where the wages of workmen and workwomen could not possibly be increased by any scheme of Protection yet devised by man. There are vast armies of civil servants. Government employees, whose earnings would be in no way affected. On the other hand, there are thousands of men and women now employed in the handling and sale of foreign goods who would be thrown out of employment if Mr. Chamberlain had his way. The fact of it is, so far from increasing employment and wages, Mr. Chamberlain's scheme would have the opposite effect. A few special trades would probably increase their plant, employees, ali4 output. But when we come to compare till number of these trades with the rest of the community, we immediately see that, while a few would benefit, the whole nation would suffer. The cost of living would be increased for every man, woman, and child in the land.

The Prosperous Foreigner. IN order to prop up his rickety cause, Mr. Chamberlain has had to make two absolutely opposite statements respecting the condition of foreign Protectionist countries. This is one which he has repeated over and over again : If Protection inevitably brought with it destitu- tion and Misery and starvation, and if .Eree Trade inevitably brought with it prosperity and progress, how do our opponents account for the fact that every foreign country without excep- tion that has adopted Protection has, in recent years at any rate, progressed much more rapidly and in much greater proportion than we ? Birmingham, November 3rd. The above is Mr. Chamberlain's chief stock argument in favour of Protection--the amazing prosperity of Protectionist countries.

The Sweated, Depressed Foreigner. BUT when Mr. Chamberlain appeals to labour, he tells quite another story. Foreign labour, he says, is cheap, sweated, unpro- tected by factory laws, and industry in protected countries is so depressed that they sell us their goods at less than cost price. Let us quote again:

Dumping only takes place seriouslywhen the country that has ' recourse to it . is in a state of depression.—Liverpool, October 7th. They have not done this by what is called fair competition. not because they make things better than we de, or cheaper than we do, but they have done it, owing partly to the advantage given by their Fiscal system, owing to the trusts which they have created, owing to the fact that as to many of them they have not adopted our humanitarian views about the position of work- ing men, and accordingly they have been able to produce more cheaply, because they have got their labour at a lower price.—Tynemouth. October 21st. What is the good, I ask in the name of common sense, of prohibiting sweating in. this country if you allow sweated goods to come in from foreign countries. If you insist upon limitation of hours, and upon precaution of security, all these things add to the cost of pro., duction. . . . Everybody knows that there are countries in which labour is very much

cheaPer-th-ansit is here.—Liverpool, Oct°lier 27th. Now Mr. Chamberlain cannot have it both ways. He cannot argue that (1) Protectionist countries have been prosperous, therefore it would be a good thing for the British work- man, increase his employment and wages, if we followed their example; and then go on to say that (2) Protectionist countries have been depressed, their goods made by cheap, sweated labour, and their workmen unpro- tected by factory legislation. As Sir William Harcourt says, Mr. clifkmberlain qnswers his own arguments in the course of the same speech. Free Traders, on the other hand, are beset by none of these delusions. We have argued all along that our trade, as the figures shew, is far ahead of our rivals, while our workmen work less hours than the Con- tinental, earn better wages, and can buy more with their money. On his own showing, Mr. Chamberlain's great bribe of more work and more wages, as a result of Protection, is complete fraud.

div.head: "RECENT RESEARCH IN CRETE."
div.p: "RECENT RESEARCH IN CRETE."
Paper by the Rev. R. S. Efoxon, M.A.

This subject was capably handled by the Rev. R. S. Moxon, M.A. one of the assistant masters at the Grammar school, at a meeting of the Literary and. Philosophical Society on Monday evening. The Presi- dent (Mr. F. G. Ruddock) presided. The lecturer has recently paid a visit to Crete and was able to give first hand information of the remains of the enormous palace of King Minos that has. been unearthed there. He illustrated his subject with a numberof original photo- graphs, which were shown on the screen by, Mr. H. Parkinson. In discussing the discoveries made by Dr. Evan* the lecturer pointed out that the remains of the palace of King Minos at Knossus which had been un- earthed were not merely a bare outline and vague views that ,needed the expert's eye to make anyihing of, but whole rooms, staircases, ,•frescoes, pottery, and relics innumerable had been and still were being dug out of the earth : and Dr, Evans hoped, by a careful process of restoration .and reconstruction, to ascertain in time not only the style of architecture, but the manners, customs, and even language of a prehistoric civilization, one that came to an end .ages before that of Greece began. All evidences showed that this civilization was the result of a long period of pettceful presperty. There wag nothing at Knossus suggestive of strife or a sense of insecurity. All relics discovered were indicative of peace, culture and wealth. The palace was unfortified, the frescoes were of peaceful scenes. It was true that one frieze showed a group of armed men, but they appeared to be connected with some ceremonial rite. There were pro- cessions of richly dressed men; groups of women with very slim waists and decidedly modern skirts—all in - a very fragmentary condition of course. There were also architectural designs and fixtures that no Greek or Roman buildings had hitherto shown. Staircases of a modern type rising one flight Over another with balustrading at the ends of the steps were a very noticeable feature. Here, too, was a water supply upon most scientific principles, and a system of sanitation and drainage that all succeeding ages had never attained to, so far as we can discover, till we began it in our own country no more than 50 years ago. The maze-like building was not so very mazy after all when intelligently studied. It would then be found to be carefully and conveniently planned with a skilful eye for the pucposes proper to each part. ' But all these wonderful discoveries might ultimately prove much less important than the treasures found in the archive chambers. ArchEeologists before this had picked up here and there among the people of Crete some curious clay tablets inscribed in unknown characters,and these were properly looked upon as valuable. Dr. Evans obtained one here and there throughout his wanderings in Crete and longed to discover some at Knossus. He had, indeed, found them not by twos or threes, but by hundreds, deposited in a most orderly and systematic way in their own chambers, which leads them 'to hope , that he had here found the rolls office of prehistoric Crete.—The lecturer was thanked for his services on the proposition of Mr. CHARLES WHITE, seconded by Mr. MAY.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
A Sr. HELENS BREWER'S WILL.

Mr. William Richardson, J. P., formerly owner of the Rainford Brewery, who died at his residence, Rainford House, Rainford, St. Helens, on September 30th, left property which is valued by the widow at £39,002 2s 2d gross, and £36,167 12s 3d net.

div.head: HELENS' NEW MAYOR.
div.p: HELENS' NEW MAYOR.

Mr. Alderman Joseph Massey, who had been elected Mayor of St. Helens, was presented on Saturday night, with an illuminated address together with a gold brace- let set with diamonds for Mrs. Massey, in recognition of his services to the Conservative party in the borough, of which he has practically been the leader for some years.

div.head: ST. HELENS GLASSIVORKERS' WAGES.
div.p: ST. HELENS GLASSIVORKERS' WAGES.

On Saturday most sections of the glassworkers em- ployed by Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, glass manufac- turers, St. Helens, receivedrseven days' notice of a reduction in their wages amounting to 5 per cent. The men principally•affected will be the plate-glass, rolled plate, cathedral glass, and sheet-glass makers. The firm employ some 8,000 hands, but not all of these will be affected, as a great number of them are merely labourers whose wages will not be reduced. It is understood that the sheet-glass workers are organised, but there is no mention of any resistance to the reduction.
THE LIABILITIES 01' COTTAGE PROPERTY OWNERS

At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday _before his Honour Judge Shand and a jury, a claim for £5O damages came up for trial a second time. The case was brought by a Mrs. Stott, who lived at 4, Church row, Whiston, near Prescot, in a house belonging to Mrs. Eleanor Molyneux. The house was occupied by them in October 1901, and in July 1902 the staircase, which it was alleged had been complainedabout, gave way under Mrs. Stott, and her leg was seriously injured. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for plaintiff, and 'Mr. Rigby Smith defended. The jury found that although it was usual for these repairs to be done by the landlord, he had not been notified in this case, and there had been no agree- ment on his part to do them. The judge thereupon gave judgment for the defendant, judgment to carry the cost of the hearing in the Divisional Court and of all the proceedings.

div.head: BETTING AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: BETTING AT EARLESTOWN.
Fifty-Three Prosecutions, CLEVER POLICE RUSE,

At Newton-le-Willows Police Court on Thursday the list contained fifty-three cases of betting at Earlestown. There were five charges of bookmaking against Matthew Seton, four each against Walter • Waterman, Benjamin Howarth, James Lee and Frank Dale, three charges of aiding and abetting against Thomas Wyatt, Joseph Healor, William Boughey, Owen Morris, and Eliza Audley, two charges against Thomas Taylor and Frank Dale Jun., and one each against John Burgess, Thomas Maley, William Turton, Albert Graham, John E. Close, Thomas Astley, John Neary, George Allison, Robert SaliEbury, Charles Forshaw, Thomas Holgate, Thomas Donoghue, and Mary Lewis. Mr. A. Browne prosecuted for the police, and Mx. J. W. Knowles defended in fifty- one of the cases, _ _

Mr. Browne stated that as Seton was a very clever man, inspector Foster and his men had to adopt in- genious methods to catch the defendants. The police got a fancy box van, in the front of which were a num- ber of boxes, behind which Sergeant Barrowand Police- constable Lennie were secreted. The driver, who was not a policeman, drove up to the front of the Griffin Hotel, in Earle-street,Earlestown, on each of the dates. He fed the horse and left it. standing in front of the hotel. The police saw that went on. _ _ _ _ _

In conside.ration of the defendants pleading guilty, a compromise was arrived at. Seton was fined £5 and costs in two cases, and three guineas solicitor's fees, and ss. including costs in the remaining three cases; Watermnn was fined £5 and costs and three guineas advocate's fee in one case, and ss. including costs in three others, Howarth, Lee, and Dale being similarly dealt with. In all the other cases defendants, for aid- ing and abetting,',were mulcted in ss. including costs. A case against Zachariah Clough was withdrawn, his explanation being considered satisfactory by the pro- secuting solicitor.

div.head: PEN KETH.
div.p: PEN KETH.

AN UNUSITAL SlGHT.—Although not within the Penketh boundary, the operations carried out during the last few days along the canal, have been witnessed by many interested spectators from Penketh and Widnes. The water in the canal, from Messrs. Tomlinson and Heywood's works at Penketh, to Messrs. -Sullivan's works at Widnes, has been drawn off, to allow the con- tractors to lay the huge water pipes beneath the bed of the canal. This is part of the new Liverpool Corpora- tion water supply. Operations have been carried on night and day, and on Sunday last many hundreds of people visited the spot to watch the work in progress. The contractors, Messrs.. Holme and King, bad all pro- vision for the men on the ground, living and sleeping, tents being erected there, and the temporary village was the source of much interest to the spectators. div.p: The Examiner, Saturday November 14, 1903.
MEMORIAL TO FALLEN SOLDIERS'

On Saturday next, the 21st inst., the Bishop of Liver- pool will unveil the screen and tablet which have been erected at the west end of the Boteler Chapel in the Warrington Parish Church by the officers, non-coin- missioned officers and men, past and present, of the 3rd South Lancashire Regiment, to the memory of their comrades who lost their lives in the South African war during the year 1900-1901. Late pprpendicular in style, the screen is of English oak throughout aid is divided into seven bays; a large central one forming the entrance into the chapel, flanked by three small ones on either side, the upper portions of which hre filled with wrought iron grilles and the lower with carved " linen " panels. The bays are all richly traceried and have overhanging canopies springing from small octagonal shafts with caps and bases. Surmount- ing these is a carved cornice divided up by crocketed pinnacles, each bearing a shield with the cyphers 1.H.5." and" St. E." alternately. On the Chapel side the shields are carved with emblems of the Passion. Crowning the central canopy is a figure of an angel representing Victory, carrying in the right hand an uplifted sword and in the left a wreath of bays. On either side of these are smaller figures of angels also carrying wreaths, and below the centre figure is a shield bearing the arms of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. On the adjoining wall is placed a brass respousse tablet in oak frame bearing the names of the officers and men who lost their lives in South Africa.

div.head: HAYMAKING IN NOVEMBER.
div.p: HAYMAKING IN NOVEMBER.

A curious sound at Martinmas is the hum of the reaper in the cornfields, but this year it is. all too com- mon up in Westmorland. A still more curious pheno- menon is that during this week haymaking operations have been general in the neighbourhood of Tebay. On Tebay Fell the occasion was further signalised by the factltbat several veterans wore at work amongst the hay. Mr. Anthony Cowperthwaite, of Busk, 84 years of age, was particularly noticeable. He said it was 20 years since he made hay before in November.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possiblemot later than Thursday. [Correspondence on the objects of the National Ser- vice League must now cease.—Eo. "Es."]
Mr. A. H. Crosfield and Mr. Dodds.

Sir,—l do not know what passage in the correspond- ence I had with Mr. Dodds last year has struck him as being disparaging to the Non-Traders. I have, how- ever, referred to that correspondence, and if Mr. Dodds insinuates that this is the tone of it, then he is again (inadvertently, no doubt) leading people to believe what as contrary to fact. The attitude taken up by the President of our Asso- ciation and myself at that time was one of perfeCt impartiality, and therefore with regard to my remarks at the Liberal Club Mr. Dodds must understand they were as strictly accurate, as his remark about myself was inaccurate. I think it as well there should be no mistake about these facts, and having stated them I shall not argue the matter further with Mr. Dodds. It has always seemed to me a mistake to argue with a man suffering from what is graphically described in America as a "swelled head," and to everyone excepting himself it has been perfectly evident for a long time past that Mr. Dodds has been suffering from an acute attack of this grievous malady. I believe that he verily considers himself a Dathelcome to judgment on everything and everybody in the town, lock, stock and barrel; so how can the Liberal Party and those connected with it hope to escape? When he has recovered the piens sana incorpore sauo we may perhaps-be able to discuss matters further with some profit and advantage. And I think there are now hopes for his recovery. Mr. Birchall's weighty and important letter—to which I ventured to draw attention at the Liberal Club—a letter which is both unanswered and unanswerable, was bound to have a salutary effect, and has I think , more than anything else helped to prick the bubble of egregious vanity.—Yours etc.. 'London, Nov. 12th, 1903. A. If. CROSFIELD.

div.head: Macedonian Relief Fund.
div.p: The Macedonian Relief Fund.

Sir,—May I ask you agtiin to favour me by granting me space for this brief note? It has already been intimated that in accordance with the request of the Parr Hall meeting on the sth instant, a Mayor's Fund in aid of relief for Macedonian refugees has been opened at our local banks. A considerable numb* of circulars from the London Committee have been sent out, but so far the responses have been but few. A gentleman made the remark to me the other day that .this is a case which does not appeal to people. I replied that its appeal could only fail With any people who are humane and Christian through their not realising the actual need .of the case. Mr. Arthur 'Crosfield, enclosing a cheque for a donation which is explained as a second response he has made to the Fund, states that Mr. Brailsford, who has gone out to Macedonia to administer the relief, has written him to say that at least £lOO,OOO is absolutely re- quired if these unhappy refugees are to be 'provided with the merest necessities of life during the winter. Towards this, so far, only a very few thousands have been contributed. Surely when it is properly apprehended that thousands of families have had their homes and properties utterly 'destroyed by the Turkish soldiery; that we in this kingdom are so supremely responsible for the anarchy whichhas reigned in Macedonia ; and that these people thus suffering are not only" our own flesh and blood" as fellow beings, but, also as Christians,—there will be forthcoming a more generous and general sympathy and help. I venture very strongly to appeal to the Christian people of Warrington3who are readers of your paper, to consider this urgent case of need, and to promptly accord contributions that may be worthy of the cause, and worthy of the reputation for generosity which our town has so frequently deserved.—Yeurs faithfully, JOHN YONGE. 19, Wilson-Patten-street, November 13th, 1903. The Non-Trading Movement: A Suggestion. • Sir,—The hitch which has taken place in the inquiry into the immoral trading with the Corporation by some of its own members mayhave had something to do with the repulse sustained by the movement at the elections on the 2nd inst. But why should there be a hitch at all unless the Commissioners are divided into two factions, one trying to screen the traders and the other to expose -them? The talk about the time and enormous cost of the inquiry is misleading and out of place. it neves was intended that the inquiry should resolve itself into an exhaustive audit of the whole of the books and documents of the Corporation for seven years. Such an audit would indeed involve so much time and labour -that very few of our competent citizens would be willing to undertake it. What the rate- payers want, and are determined to have, is an 1 investigation that shall prove who the Alderin'en and Town Councillors are who have been trading with the Corporation for the period named, and -the amount of the town's money they have respectively received. Now with all deference to the six Commis- sioners, who seem to look upon their task as an enormous one, I venture to say that such an inquiry might be accomplished by regular and diligent effort in a few weeks, and at very little expense indeed. When a merchant desires to know the volume of trade any of his customers has done with him for a given period he does not commence by ransacking his letters, orders and sales journals. He goes direct to his ledgers, and there he finds, without much trouble, not only the value of the business done but also the amount of cash he has received for it. Could not this simple method be adopted in dealing with the traders' business with the -Corporation, and with equally satisfactory results? The books of account of the Corporation are regularly audited by qualified accountants who certify that they are in order. Might not then a start be made with the Limited Liability Company, who are alleged to have been the largest dealers with the Corporation during the time under review? A reference to the Corporation ledgers would or should show the extent to which this Company and its sub- contractors have been engaged in supplying the wants of the Corporation during that period. Having settled and duly noted this important point, the Commissioners would then have a free and experienced hand to devote to the minor traders neon the same principle. And when thg required information in all cases had been extracted from the ledgers it would be a comparatively easy matter to tabulate the results in an intelligent form, showing the names of the traders and their res- pective drawings from the Corporation coffers. The information would be both interesting and instruc- tive, and its value might be enhanced by such explanatory notes as the Commissioners in their wisdom might deem desirable to add in the interest of their clients—the ratepayers. An investigation of the merchant's method would, I venture to assume, meet the wishes of the Non-Traders and their friends, while at the same time it would do no injustice to any present or ex-member of the Council. And as the Commissioners are to receive no pay for their services the expense would be limited to the cost of printing and publishing a few thousand copies of their dulysigned report which, with the schedule of the traders and explanatory notes, should not exceed more than six pages of foolscap. The offers of financial assistance towards the expenses from outsiders are quite uncalled for. The inquiry iis a matter which concerns the whole body of ratepayers who will lam sure, be willing to pay for the publica- tion of" the findings "of the Commissioners.—Yours truly, November 1903.
lON A.

;mint, splendid education and extraordinary progress in industiy to the rest of the world, it is the proudest privilege of every citizen to give a short span of his life to the service of his country. The institution of personal service which, as with us dates from the earliest times, is enthusiastically 6herished by the Swiss, and receives the loyal support of men—and women—of every party, class and religion. Turning to some other points in Miss Robinson's speech, I note that she hinted that continental nations did not have full-blown conscription at once." In this, as in the rest of her remarks she showed an ignor- ance, perfectly pardonable in a lady, but hardly to be excused in one engaged in a denunciation of a proposal; she has avowedly not taken the trouble to examine. The fact is ,that all these continental nations did have full-blown" conscription," in the worst sense of the word, from the moment that the feudal system broke down with them and when in this country its place was taken up ,by a national militia,founded upon the obliga- tory personal service of every citizen. Eventually, indeed, these nations, one by one, adopted the great principle of universal service. But in every instance the term originallyadopted was very much longer than that which now prevails. In every instance the period of service has been reduced from 8,5, and 3, to 2 years, landthe whole tendency of modern civilization is in the 'same direction—the abolition of standing armies and compolsory training of all for a short time. Of course a speech in denunciation of compulsory ser- vice could not pass without the expression of a fear that the" liberty :and freedom which have been so much valued in this country "would be interfered with. Here again I would point out, in the first place, that by a perfectly logical process, which I cannot develop here, the march of liberty, civil and religious, has been unexampled in the history of the world since the adoption in the last 40 or 50 years of the principle of universal service by all civilised countries including Japan. I would commend this thought to the able and sincere speaker. fAtthe same:time I would ask her, does she think that true freedom consists simply in each man doing what he likes without thought or-refer- ence to duty, society -or national responsibility? If her, answer is in the affirmative, I must admit that any system of national service would be disastrous to such liberty. But if liberty is given us in order to develop our powers usefully to ourselves and to the State, then think that a training in discipline, self-control, obedi- ence and methodic work are necessary adjuncts to that liberty, lest it should degenerate into th 3 licence, under the name of liberty, which Milton condemns : "Licence they mean when they cry Liberty." One word more. Miss Robinson evidently spoke with sincerity and convict ion. But I fear that those of her audience who value liberty of mind must have been somewhat disconcerted to hear her confess, by implica- tion, that she had not read anything which stated the case of those she was opposing. I trust the ladies who heard her very able speech will not follow her example in this matter, but will show that they are liberal and enlightened enough to examine the case for themselves. —I have the honour to be your obedient servant, GEORGE TIGHE, Secretary. The National Service League, Dacre House, Victoria- street, S.W. November 11th, 1903.

div.head: ST. MARY'S AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
div.p: ST. MARY'S AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
Performance of" Lady Clancarty."

For several years now, the members of the St. Mary's Amateur Dramatic Society have rendered assistance to the funds of the Warrington District Nursing Associa- tion by giving performances in aid of that deserving institution. Four such .performances have been given by the Society this week in the Parr Hall. The drama chosen for representation was "Lady Clancarty" written by the late Mr, Tom Taylor, M.A. Considering the numerous attractions which have been placed before the Warrington public during the past few weeks, the attendance has been satisfactory. Of the performance itself, we cannot speak in terms of unqualified praise: The denominational character of the society neces- sarily limits the cast, and in attempting such a difficult piece as "Lady Clancarty," in which a strong dramatic persona is essential for its successful performance, the members were too ambitious. Last year's ,omedy "A Bird in the Hand' was much more suited' b the capabilities of the members than either "The Courier of Lyons "or "Lady Clancarty," which have both been attempted with only qualified success. It would, of course, be ungenerous and unjust to expect an amateur dramatic society, with its limited resources, to produce a play with the same exactitude and power as a professional company, but there are many pieces which the St. Mary's Society could do fuller justice to than has been the case with "LadyClancarty." A political plot, with its intrigues and subterfuges, generally requires a greater display of histrionic] ability than is at the command of a young amateur society, if the situations are to be made the most of and not lost upon the audience. The heavy nature of the cast will be seen from a recital of the dramatic persona King William 111 Mr. M. Cunningham The Earl of Portland \lr. C. J. Newton Lord Woodstock \lr. W. Courtiers. Soldiers, Smugglers, Ste, by the Company. The curtain rises on a smuggler's house of call on Romney Marsh, but the performance in this first act was disappointing. There was plenty of movement and colour, but it was difficult to divinewhat was taking place, owing to a lack of clear enunciation, which was usually followed by some rather forced laughter. The second act, in which Earl Clancarty, under an assumed name meets Lady Clancarty after a long absence as a political exile, was much better, the principals rising to the occasion and doing justice to their respec- tive roles. Perhaps the preittiest scene is that which takes place in Lady Clanca,rty's boudoir,the scenery and effects being artistically arranged. As Lady Clancarty, Miss Agnes Kilduff had many opportunities of showing her abilities and at times she was intensely dramatic. The scenes in which she and her brother, Mr. W. Kilduff, as Earl Clancarty, were associated were especially good. Members of the Kilduff family have on previous occasions shown that they possess histrionic ability and in this performance they more than maintained their reputation ; in fact it would be difficult to conceive of the St. Mary's Dramatic Society without them. A third member of • the family Mr. A. Kilduff gave a rather lively portrayal of "Clink," although it must be observed that he makes rather a diminutive gaolor. Mr. M. Cunningham played the role of King William 111. with dignity and regal grace' his commanding presence and pleasing voice serving him in good stead. Mr. S. Ryan infuses the necessary villainy into his play as Lord Spencer and was seen at his best in his altercation with Lady Clancarty. One of the surprises of the performance was the excellent part played by Mr. C. J. Newton as the Earl of Port land. His demeanour and enunciation were all that could be desired.
