Of Mr. Wilkie's early political work, it may be stated that in 1884 he wat; a member of a deputation that waited upon the late Mr. Gladstone at the Foreign Office with reference to the extension of the franchise to the counties. There were three speakers on behalf of the deputation, namely Mr. Wilson (for the miners), Mr. Joseph Arch (for the agricultural labourers) and Mr. Wilkie. Mr. Wilkie informed Mr. Gladstone that the ship building.yards which were being started down the Clyde were causing the workers to leave the urban areas and go further afield with the result that they were being disfranchised through no fault of their own. Mr. Gladstone used this as an argument for extending the franchise to the counties.

Asked for his' views on the political program:ne, Mr. Wilkie said he stood for measures not party. "In seeking a seat in Parliament," he continued, "I have no personal axe to grind whatever. lam simply a standard-bearer for the workers on whose behalf I stand. We want a solid group of labour men in Parlia- ment, not to vote independently but to vote as a group on behalf of the workers. Isolation will not succeed. The programme of the Labour Representation Committee is clear and emphatic. The first item is 'To promote immediate and effective legislation defining our Trade Union rights and securing absolute protection for the funds of the various trade organizations.' I referred to that at the meeting last night and also spoke upon the housing question and old age pensions. There are other items in our programme of equal importance to the workers of the country. There is a direct issue for labour and we will accept help and work from those who are willing to help us." "What is your ?pinion on the fiscal controversy?"

"I stand fol:' free fOod.There may be particular trades which have been hard hit by the protectionist poliu of other countries but this is no argument. If I become the labour candidate for Warrington I shall take an early opportunity of stating my views on this question." In the course of further conversation, *Mr. Wilkie said "I am not only a politician, but I think I can claim to be a labour statesman by the practical work I have done for our own trade and labour generally. I have been in the labour movement for over 30 years and I think I know what the workers want. If you look at the composition of Parliament you find the capitalists well represented, the legal profession and the army service also strongly represented. We want a fair share. of labour representatives, trained in the ranks of labour, who know the wants of the workers and the wants of the constituency as a whole. We stand not for class legislation but for the great bulk of the. nation. Not only do we stand for industrial peace, but for , national and international peace. The communications which we have constantly with the labour, leaders and labour organisations on the Continent and in America are as gossamer lines or wireless telegraphy, binding the workers of the world into a harmonious whole. Our programme can be carried out without doing any harm to any class of the community. There are ways and means hy which the condition of the masses of the people can be ameliorated without injuring anybody."

div.head: MR. WILKIE, OF NEWCASTLE, INVITED TO STAND.
div.p: MR. WILKIE, OF NEWCASTLE, INVITED TO STAND.
INTERVIEW WITH THE CANDIDATE.

Since Warrington first returned a representative to Parliament in 1832, the elections have always been fought solely on political lines. Now, however. there is a prospect that at the next general election a labour candidate will contest the seat.. The local branch of the National Labov Representation Commiteee have had the matter under consideration, and the outcome was that on Thursday evening a conference of representatives of the various trade union branches was held. in Bold-street Wesleyan schools to decide definitely whether the borough should be contested in the labour interest. Mr. J. Podmore, jun., presided and there was a large attend- ance, all the principal societies being repre- sented. The proceedings were conducted in private but the Press ropresentatives were afterwards in- formed that Mr. Alexander Wilkie, DE Newcastle-on- Tyne, general secretary of the Associated Shipwrights' Society, attended and set forth his views on various labour questions. It was unanimously resolved "That this Confer- ence of Trade Unionists recognising the importance and necessity of direct Labour Representation in the House of Commons, views with satisfaction the pros- pect of a Labour Candidate for Warrington." The following resolution was also unanimously, adopted :—" This Conference heartily and unani- mously invites Mr. Alexander Wilkie to become the Labour candidate for Warrington, at the next Parlia- mentary election; and pledges itself to actively work for, and use every legitimnte means to ensure his return to Imperial,Parlia,ment."
The invitation will be forwardezl to the Secretary of the Shipwrights' Society and will be considered at an early date.

div.head: MR. WILKIE INTERVIEWED.
div.p: MR. WILKIE INTERVIEWED.
His Career in the Labour World.

LABOUR REPRESENTATION PROSPECTS. A reporter of "The Examiner" yesterday sought an interview with Mr. Wilkie, with the object of gaining some particulars of his career as a labour leader and an. expression of his views on labour matters generally. The reporter found Mr. Wilkie at the Patten Arms Hotel, and had a long chat with him in the smoke room. Mr. Wilkie is of rather Short but bulky build, with aoleasing open countenance. He has passed his half-century and his hair is turning grey, but he ha S an abundance of that energy and enthusiasm so necessary for a successful labour leader.

Our reporter found him very ready to talk on matters affectinc, Trades Unions and particularly those connected with the Associated Shipwrights' Society, of which he is the general secretary, but a natural modesty asserted itself when the reporter endeavoured to shift the conversation to Mr. Wilkie's own personality and the part he himself has played in the movement. By dint of steady application a few main facts and opinions were however, gleaned, and these shall be set down in due order and place.

Mr. Wilkie is a man who has risen from- the ranks. A. Scotchman by birth, he commenced life as .an apprentice shipwright in a yard on the Clyde. On completing his apprenticeship, in accordance with.the practice of shipwrights, he attached hinaself to a ship and voyaged to various parts of the world. Some time afterwards he took up a position in a yard on the Clyde, and took an active part in the organisa- tion of the trade. " A bit of a ferment," as Mr. Wilkie called it, arose, and he was appointed to state the views of the men. Subsequently he was elected secre- tary of the local branch of the society and so dis- tinguished himself in that capacity, that on the secre- taryship of the Associated Shipwrights' Association of Scotland becoming vacant, he was elected to the office. In 1877, a long dispute took place betvteen the shipwrights and thew employers. The matter was submitted to arbitration. At the close, Lord Afoncrieff, the arbitrator, highly complimented Mr. Wilkie on the manner in which he had fought the case for the men, remarking that it could not have been done better by a paid advocate. At this time the shipwrights had separate and inde- pendent unions in the various shipbuilding centres, each acting independently of the other. Mr. Wilkie conceived the idea of amalgamating these scattered branches into one complete whole and in 1881 he had the satisfaction of realising his object. The Associated Shipwtights' Society was organised by him and it started in 1881 with 1,750 members from 11 branches. Under the reconstituted scheme, the general rules of the association, the contributions and the benefits were made uniform, whilst each local branch retained its own 'autonomy as regards bye-laws and regulations of the trade. The progress of the society since the recon- struction took place may be judged from the fact that the society has nearly 20,000 members and 150 branches, with a reserve fund of £127,000. The reserve fund is so well invested that the interest obtained pays all the central working expenses. The general offices for the first seven or eight years were situated at Glasgow, but they are now situated at Wilkie Chambers, Eldon-square, Newcastle-on-Tyne. "Like many trades unions," said Mr. WrrAclE. "we are showing how it is possible to have a practical scheme of Old Age Pensions. We have started a superannuation fund for all over 55 years of age who are unable to work at the trade, but who, have been members of the Union for 20 years. We are also helping to solve the housing problem by advancing money to our members whereby they • can purchase their own honses. The money is advanced on better terms than building societies can offer. These benefits are in addition to the usual friendly benefits, such as advances for tools, unemployed pay, sick and accident relief, medical advice and funeral funds. Most of our disputes with employers," continued Mr. Wilkie"have been settled Ina friendly manner across the conference table and the percentage of our income spent on disputes is very small. Whilst our expenditure since 1882 has been £257,320, our expenses on disputes have only amounted to £10,253. Since the'institution of our association, the wages of the trade have been the highest known, the hours of labour have been shorter and the conditions of employment better. I believe in meeting the employers and settling our griev- ances by reason rather than force." in reply to questions as to the attitude of the Ship- wrights' Society on the questions of labour representa- tion, Mr. Wilkie observed that the Society had decided to place two caddidates in the field at the forthcoming general election. "One of our candidates"he continued, "is Alderman John Jenkins, the Mayor of Cardiff, who is likely to contest Chatham and the other is myself." %And what opinion have you formed of the Warring- ton invitation?

"Well, I must say that I was pleased with last night's meeting. Mr. Podmore, who presided, handled the meeting in a calm and judicial spirit, and the tone of the speeches augurs well for the success of the labour movement in Warrington. There are, I believe, about 3,000 trades unionists in the town and if they will take off their coats and work'they can have a representative of their own in Parliament. With re- gard to the Invitation that was extended to me to con- test the Borough in the labour interest, that invitation ,wtll have to be laid before the executive of my society before a decision is come to. I have had several invita- tions from other sources.elsewhere. but personallynone have pleased me better than the Warrington one." At this point it may be well to refer to Mr. Wilkie's work as a trades unionist outside his own particular organisation. He has represented his Society at many Trades Union Congresses and in September, 1896 he was returned at the top of the poll for the Parliamentary Committee. • He has tilled all the offices open to him at the congress, including Oat of president, and presided at the Swansea Congress. In 1899 he was appointed one of the fraternal delegates of the Congress to attend the meetings of the American Federa- tion of Labour held at Detroit, Michiiv'an. Since then he has paid another visit to America, wken he went as a member of the Mosely Commission. His reports on that occasion have been printed, and are valued by members of his trade. Some of his most valuable work in connection with the tirades Union Con- gress has been performed whilst a member, of its most important committees. He helped to draw up the scheme whereby all the trades unions assist any par- ticular trad•l naion in time of difficulty with an bmployer. and he was also a member of the committee which brought into being the Labour Representation Committee. He has been a member of the Central Com- mittee ever since.

Going further afield, Mr. Wilkie was a member of the late School Board in Newcastle, and at the present time is a member of the new Education Committee in Newcastle. He is also an earnest co- operator, more estmially with regard to productive co- operation, by which means the workers become their own employers. in this connection Mr. Wilkie is a member of the Board having the • control of the large Co-operative printing establishments in London, New- I castle and Manchester. He also takes a considerable interest in the Friendly Society movement,and has held offices in connection with the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, of which he is a member. Furthermore he is a life member of a Freemasons' lodge. At the last general election he contested Sunderland in the labour interest. He was unsuccessful but polled 8,842 votes, which is the largest. number of votes polled by a labour cnndidate in any election. with the one exception of Mr. Broadhurst, at Leicester.

div.head: THE" SUNNY SOUTH" BAZAAR. Children's Opening Ceremony.
div.p: THE" SUNNY SOUTH" BAZAAR. Children's Opening Ceremony.

The successful" Sunny South" bazaar in aid of the new Workingmen's Mission Chapel %Building Fund was brought to a close on Saturday. Sunday school chil- dren played a prominent part in the final opening cere- mony, which was gracefully performed by Miss Bessie Dutton. Miss Lily Kendrick was escorted to the chair by two little pages (Masters Tom Tanner and Alfred Burton) and delivered a neat little speech in which she explained that the scholars had, by selling "penny bricks "raised about £5 in aid of the bazaar. They had also obtained numerous articles which were on sale at the Sunday school stall. The scholars marched into the room in procession, and handed statements of each child's effort to Miss Dutton. An appropriate chorus was rendered by the children, after which Mr. N. Hough engaged in prayer. In opening the bazaar Miss Dutton spoke of the influence, the beauty and simplicity of child life, and pointed out how the works of Dickens in which child life was described dwelt in the mind of the tender. She commended the object of the bazaar and said there was a fesling of honour and respect in the town for those who were engaged in the useful work of the mission. She hoped that God would bless their efforts and that they would go forward extending their operation s She trusted that the Sunday school children would grow up to be a great help to the mission; and she asked the parents to take care of them especially when they were in their teens; as that was the time when tempations came very thickly. In conclusion she urged the importance of aggressive Christian work and expressed the great pleasure which it afforded her to declare the bazaar open. _

'Money prizes were then presented to Lily Kendrick and Tom Tanner, who had collected 9s. and 15s. id. re- sPectively in aid of the bazaar. Miss Dutton was cordially thanked for her presence and business was proceeded with. The orchestra, which played selections during each day of the bazaar, was composed as follows :—Mr. Hr ry Roberts, conductor; let violins„ Messrs. R. Gs t (leader), W. Brough, W. Taylor, S. Dark, L. E wards; 2nd violins, Mr. F. Taylor, Mr. J. J. Pritch- ard, Miss E. Ward, Miss E. Osborne; 'cello, Mr. Vane; double bass, Mr. T. Clarke; oboes, Messrs. Joseph Stanley and G. Clarke; clarionet, Mr. W. Ford; flute, Mx. H. Osborne; cornet Mr. J. Booth; pianist, Mr. H. Roberts.

During the evening the WarringtonMale Voice Choir, under the conductorship of Me. S. Hassan rendered selections in highly creditable style. The proceeds for Saturday amounted to R6l 7s. 9d., making a total for the three days of £247 9s. 6id. At the conclusion of the day's proceedings Mr. T. Dale moved, and Mr. T. Ashley seconded a vote of thanks, which was cordially passed, to the orchestra, artistes nnd others who had assisted in various ways. A similar compliment was paid to Mr. A. Tilling, jun., for his untiring efforts.

div.head: ORFORD WARD ELECTION. Mr. F. Stott and the Non-Traders.
div.p: ORFORD WARD ELECTION. Mr. F. Stott and the Non-Traders.

Mr. F. Stott's defeat in the recent contest in Orford Ward and his candidature at the forthcoming bye-elec- tion 'were commented upon at the monthly meeting of the Trades and Labour Council on Tuesday evening. The CHAIRMAN (Mr. J. Podmore) 'expressed the hope that Mr. Stott would be successful in his renewed efforts. From what he could gather there was a dead set against him in the town owing to the principles that he held, and he (the speaker) believedthat some of those organizations which had been in the habit of ruling Warrington in election work were determined to keep a man of .Mr. Stott's stamp out of the Council. He thoughtLa.bour ought to be equally determined that Mr. Stott should be elected. (Hear, hear.) If every man 'would put his shoulder to the wheel their candi- date would stand a good chance whoever his opponent might be. I Mr. P. STOTT wished to correct a statement which he ' made inhis speech after the declaration of the poll. He said he was under the impression that the Non- Trading association was being controlled by the Property Owners' Association. On making further inquiries he found that the Property Owners' Association as an Association had nothing at all to do with the Non- Trading Association. Of course there was a very large proportion of property owners on the Non-Trading Association who were connected with the other organiza- tion. Many of his friends and sympathisers in the election belonged to the Non-Trading Association, and some of them had pointed out to him that they felt rather hurt at his remarks. They, however, were entirely opposed to the attitude of the Non-Trading Association in the election. He believed his candidature was opposed owing to the Non-Traders' Association being controlled by the property-owning section of that body. It was his firm conviction that it was owing to his stand in regard to municipal reform, and especially the housing ques- tion, that he was opposed by the majority of the Non- Trading Association. Under the circumstances he thought he did magnificently and he hoped with the assistance of trade unionists to be able to achieve a great victory for labour in the coming election. Mr. BUCKLEY referred to the statements in Council- lor Dodds' letter published last week as to the "ques- tionable tactics" adopted in the election and saidthat if questionable methods were brought to bear in the future an inquiry would be necessary and the Labour party would demand it. The political bodies must act fairly or they would have to look out for squalls. The CHAIRMAN passed severe strictures on the methods which he said were adopted.
THE CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE. At a meeting orthe Conservative Ward Committee on Wednesday evening Mr. .1. A. Rushworth, licensee of the " Horse and Jockey" Inn was selected to oppose Mr. Stott.
THE BEWSEIr WARD VACANCY.
MR. HENRY ROBERTS AND THE ELECTION.

A vacancy has arisen in Rewsey Ward through the elevation of Councillor Pierpoint to an Aldermanic seat. We understand that Mr. Henry Roberts was asked to allow himself to be nominated, but declined, pre- ferring to wait until the inquiry had been held and his character vindicated before again seeking the suffrages of the electors. Mr. Thomas Pemberton. secretary of the Liberal Club and a resident in the Ward. has been mentioned as it possible eandidate.Mr.Edwin Plinston is also mentioned as a Labour Candidate,and there is every likelihood of Mr. Owen Toole also entering the field.

The ease in which Mr. John Meiklejohn sought to recover damages from Major Arthur Griffiths and Messrs. Cassell and Company, for alleged libel contained in the Major's book, "Mysteries of Police anderime, was Con- chided on Thursday when the jury returned a verdict for the defendants, and judgment was entered accord- ingly.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Baptist Church, Colborne Street.

On Sunday evening, the Pastor replied to letters and questions relating to his recent address on Protestantism Statements he had made in connection with the Roman Catholic Church and also the Anglican Church had been criticised, and were further explained by the preacher. All Saints' Mission Church.

There were large congregations at this mission on Sunday when the harvest thanksgiving services were continued. At the .rnorning, service the Rev. Clement J. Ethvard3 occupied the pulpit. The Rev. D. R. James curate of St. 1 Peter's, addressed the Sunday sahool children in the aftbrnoon on "Faith and Promise." In the evening the special preacher was the Rev. A. S. W. Smith, M.A., curate at St. Mary's, Widnes. The musi- cal portions of the services were well rendered by the choir, Mr..Lilley presiding at the organ. The solos'in the anthems were ably given by Miss A. Jones, Miss Cruikshank, and Mr. .Albert Poole. The collections, which were on behalf of the Mission Church expenses, amounted to 6s. 41d.

div.head: New Minister of Cairo-street Chapel.
div.p: The New Minister of Cairo-street Chapel.

The Rev. Charles Hargrove, the eminent minister of Mile Hill Chapel, Leeds, says in a provincial letter to the "Londo,n Inquirer :" Holbeck is sore at losing the Rev. Charles Harvey Cook, who has been called up' higher. .He has left us to take the responsible post of minister of Cairo-street Chapel, Warrington, which has been filled by so may men distinguished among u'a for their zeal and learning. But his late congregatton will not suffer alone. Mr. Cook was one who had the in- terest .of all our churches much at heart. He was an active worker for the union and always willing to do anything and go anywhere in the service of our com- mon cause. The members of the Mile Hill Social Union, to whom he )vas well known, took the oppor- tunity of a meeting falling on the eve of his departure to bid him farewell, and presented him with "Mr. Morley's Life of Gladstone ' as a small token of the sincerity of the regard and goad wishes which were ex- pressed for him and Mrs. Cook. We hope Holbeck- will soon find a worthy- successor to console them for their loss.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

Mr. J. Owen was the chairman at the meeting on Sunday and spoke of the pleasure it gave him to help on the work of the P.S.A.—The Rev. H. Dunnico spoke upon the higher life of man, his present and future destiny. Evolutionists,he said were not all agreed as to where we came from; theologians were not all agreed as to where we were going to. But both evolutionists and theologians were agreed as to where we are. The speaker then dwelt upon the work of man. All work was secular, or spiritual according to what a man put into it. He looked upon every day work, as work that ought to be done in the highest sense for God—a working together for the good of the labour Master, and himself, and to the Glory of God. We ought to see God everywhere. We had too many Esaus who could not see God, we wanted to get into closer touch with God, and consecrate our lives to God. Life was very uncertain • time was short there- fore let us be in earnest, and take a stand for God, self and men.—Mr. Farrar (hon. secretary) said they were pleased to have Mr. Dunnico amongstthern for the first time and they hoped for a second visit. He also referred to the death of a brother, also the death of a brother's wife. He also welcomed one new member. The meeting was also taken part in by Mr. J. Bailey and the Rev. John Yonge.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church. .
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church. .

The Sunday school anniversary services were held in this Church on Sunday. At the morning service at 10.30 the Rev. J. L. Milne, occupied the pulpit, and preached from the words, "Jesus took them up in His arms, and blessed them, laying His hands upon them." The preacher dwelt on the loving care which Christ always showed for children, and contrasted it with the lack of interest shown by so many members of their churches in the welfare of the young in the Sunday schools. In Vole afternoon the Rev. Benjamin Bell, of Withington, conducted a children's service and gave an account of a visit he had recently paid to the Holy Land, describing Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and other places. There was a fairly large attendance at the evening service when the Rev. Benjamin Bell preached from the teat, "But this I say brethren the time is short." How highly important it was to theta, said the preacher, if they wanted to spend their life worthily, that they should have this conviction of the shortness Of opportunity thoroughly rubbed into them. The fuller and busier their life was, the shorter it would seem to them. It was the idle and pleasure-loving who found life weary and tedious. When they remembered that time was short they should not harbour revengeful feelings against their neighbours when they thought they had been wronged, but should bear in mind' that they needed forgiveness themselves every day, both from God and from man. Life was too short for bear- ing grudges. During the evening services the choir sang the anthem "Lift up your. hea-ls. Oh ye gates ! " while the solo" Angels ever bright and fair," was sung y Mrs. H. P. Brown.

div.head: Morley's " Gladstone." Sermon by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees.
div.p: Morley's " Gladstone." Sermon by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees.

Last Sunday evening the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees Velivered a very striking sermon, at Bewsey-road Wes- leyan Church, on the "Life of Mr. Gladstone," and during the course of it he threw several sidelights on the religious character of Mr. John Morley, Mr. Glad- stone's biographer. The sermon, though far exceeding the usual length, was listened to with wrapt attention to the end. The preacher said that it was generally acknowledged (that Mr. Gladstone •possessed a tran- scendent intellect, a power of oratory rarely equalled and probably never surpassed, a magnetic attractive- ness well-nigh irresistible, find an unmatched influence over the men of his time—that his were the essentials of a superb genius. But undoubtedly the Marquis of Salisbury had voiced the best feeling of the day when he had said that Mr. Gladstone would be long remem- bered as a great example, to which history hardly furnished a parallel, of a great Chris- tian man. For that reason, and that reason alone, did he venture then to l refer to Mr. Glad- stone. There in a Christian assembly they acknow- ledged above all the depths of Mr. Gladstone's religious faith and the grace of his Christian charaeter. And generations still 'to come would look, as Lord Rosebery had once eloquently said, for encouragement in labour, , for fortitude in adversity, for the example of a splendid Christianity,with constalithope and constant encourage- ment, to the pure, splendid, and dauntless figure of William Ewa,rt Gladstone. His rare genius, his Con- summate ability extorted our wonder, but his nag goodness, his nobility of character • won our homage and our love. The preacher then referred to the grave doubts that had been expressed in many quarters when' it had become known that Mr. John Morley was to write Mr. Gladstone's life. Mr. Morley was a man of letters of magnificent gifts, but he had seemed to lack certain indispensable qualities for the work for which he had thus been chosen. In every direction it had been asked how could a man declared to be an unbeliever write with sympathy concerning a man with such a dominant religious life ? No man's life bore clearer witness than Mr. Gladstone's to the truth that faith and unfaith could never be equal powers. And to him both the State and the Church were divine. As Mr. Morley admitted Mr. Gladstone cared as much for the Church as he cared for the State; helthought of the Church as the soul of.the State, he believed the attainment by the magistrate of the ends of Government to depend upon religion, and he was sure that the strength of a State correspoaded to the religious strength and soundness of the community of which the State is the civil organ. He not only accepted the doctrines of Christianity, but strove to apply the noblest -4. moralities to the affairs both of his own nation and of the commonwealth of nations. His political life was only a part of his religious life. In this region of faith and morals Mr. Qtadstone towered above contemporary statesmen. Would there not then, it was asked, be some shortcom- ings, at, least, in the strength and truth of Mr. Morley's presentment of Mr. Gladstone in supreruey important respects, since the key of Mr. Gladstone's life and character lay inc. faith which Mr. Morley did not share? Those who really knew Mr. Morley could not, however, have anticipated any insnnerable difficulty. Hypocrisy, rather than religionz had incurred his strong and bitter criticism. He had shown a fine and just sense of the highest elements in human life, and confidence in him as Ir.Otadstone's biographer had been amply justified by the great result. Even a leading high churchman had declared that no one, however deeply steeped in the Christian dogma, could have touched Mr. Gladstone's religious life with fuller sympathy, more tender rever- ence, or keener insight into the spiritual forces which swayed those seventy years of strenuous conflict for the right. Mr. Rees did not attempt to hide his regret that amen so exalted and reverent as Mr. Morley undoubtedly was, should feel himself unable to accept the terms of the Christian Gospel, but no dogmatic orthodoxy should blind them to the religiousness of Mr. Morley's spirit. His attitude was perhaps best described in his own declaration that a man might dis- believe religiously as he might religiously believe. Then the preacher proceeded td show, by several extremely interesting but scarcely known incidents in Mr. Morley'slife, how Mr. Morley had frequently, in a most beautiful and reverent manner, identified himself with the spirit that lay behind our Christian beliefs. This part of the discourse, with its references to Mr. Morley's Methodist associations and other unfamiliar particulars, abounded in surprises. There might not seem to be much, said the preacher, in some of the incidents he narrated, but their value lay in the man himself, and all personal knowledge of Mr. Morley indicated his thorough honesty and sincerity, with an entire absence of sham. The preacher proceeded to indicate certain points of intense religious interest in the remarkable biography Mr. Morley had written. , He said that all he could hope to do was to thrust forth here and there a fact in regard to Mr. Gladstone that 'might be pondered long and earnestly to the best advantage by every member of that congregation. Sympathetic reference was then made to Mr. Gladstone's school days, and especially his life at Oxford. when in practice his great aim was that the love of God might become the habit of his soul, and he realised the ,

ncreasel importance and necessityand benefit of prayer and of the life of obedience and self-sacrifice. Occasional glimpses of Mr. Gladstone as the years sped on were also given, and allusion was made to his fearless work among the unfortunate ministers to the great sin of great cities; his systematic and generous giving to the purposes of charity and religion; his belief in prayer and his constant practice therein; and his reverence for the Lord's Day, the Bible, and various means of grace in connection with the Church of Christ. In closing, Mr. Rees impressively referred to Mr. Gladstone's clos- ing days, when he endured heroically a martyrdom of pain, and then summarised the lessons of the noble life which that evening had been passed under review. He urged his hearers in Mr. Gladstone's own words, as quoted by Mr. Morley, to be inspired with the belief that life was a great ani noble calling, not a mean and grovelling thing, that we were to struggle through as best we could, but an elevated and a lofty destiny.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Fo3tb3ll.
By " Ovalist."

In thn.es Wm-chi-4ton have f r3quently had all the game and none of the points, but in recent years they have generally won or lost on their merits. Last Saturday, however, they lost the Oldham match after beating the visitors all over the field. The reason is not far to 5;945:... Warrington had Fish away and consequmtly lac!red sooi•ing p)wer. Had he been oh the side, the homesters must have won comfort- ably, but the left-winger was playing the role of spectator instead of player, in consequence of neglecting work. Of this more an m. The fact was patent to everybody that Fish's absence made all the difference between winning and losing on Saturday. Neither the players nor the crowd were in anything like a good humour after the match, for two valuable points had been sacrificed, and all through the shortcomings of one man.

Oldham were delighted at the turn of events, as well they might be, for victory put them at the head of the League, and they were distinctly lucky to get there. There was only a try between the teams, and that was obtained in a very fluky manner, though the individual effort of the scorer was very smart. Still, had the referee's whistle sounded at the inception of the movement it would only have been a correct ruling in the opinim of the majority. It's no use repining however, though I for oite, would rather have seen the home team well beaten than see them lose under such circumstances. Warrington had their chances, but they let them slip and failed to reap the due reward for getting the better of the . Oldhamers at nearly all points. .

' The biggest gate of the se.tson assembled, and the crowd had its money's worth in excitetnent and good football. Oldham have always played a ,good back game, and though the lights of other days have gone, the men sporting the red and white hoops can yet give a smart exposition. They endeavoured to beat Warrington at theit own tactics, but never looked like doing it, for, with the single exception of Edmunds, Fish's substitute, the home men were too quick and too strong for them. From the commencement the Oldhamers were fairly bustled. Warrington seemed to be all over them at times, and " Dicky " Thomas had as warm a spell of defensive work as he is likely to get for a while. Warrington should have been credited with a try, for smart passing on the line left Oldham standing. Dickenson and Harris had the line at their mercy, but the former held a shade too long, gave the wing man a poor pass, and a glorious chance was bungled. • Warrington never had such another golden opportunity, and the match would probably have ended in a draw but for Tyson's sensational run-away try.

Oldham are reputed to share with Salford the honour of having the best pack in Lancashire but they had to play second fiddle on Saturday. The Warrington forwards played a magnificent game and fairly controlled the scrummages. Davies and Mahoney were also very smut and often got the better of Lees and Dixon, whae the three-quarters on each side found themselves well in itclred. Oldham were perhaps, the more dangerous in this departrnent, but this was entirely owing to the fact that Isher- wood's best work was wasted on Edmund.s. Poor " Tich" was helpless on the wing, and the Committee made a blunder in not selecting a stronger player for the vacancy. Hallam again put up a great display, and quite outclassed Thomas. He has this season, well merited the honour of ,being chosen reserve for Lancashire, and I. hope to sea him selected yet. Were he a bit faster "Jack" Hallam would have no superior in the Northern Union.

On the Oldham side tees, Phil Thoraas, and Spottis- wood were the best men, while a word of praise is due to that fine forward, Fergusson, who was always prominent. Dixon, the half back, appears to me much below the class usually associated with Oldham.

Warrington did not make the bet use of their chances, as I have already indicated. Harris was the man who should have been worked for, and I think if Dickenson had played with the sole idea of getting his wing man in, Warrington would havt obtained something tangible. He has still to mend his ways/ cinsiderably before he is a successful centre.

Warrington's failure has quite spoiled their League record, and they are now sixth from the top. Salford have come back to brm again, and there fs bound to be a keen struggle, for the first half-dozen clubs are all well in the running for honours. Warrington have the worst ell'ance, for tliey are not a great scoring team, but they should finish well up.

The great County match,Lancashire v.Yorkshire,t4es place at Headingly to-day, under 12-aside conditions. Lancashire will be without Fish—which is a-big loss —for there is no other left-winger of any class. The vacancy will be filled by Dickenson, who, though not a wing player, should uphold the honour of his cluh and_county. There won't be a more certain trier— of that lam sure. If Hallam and Boardman happen to be called upon, Warrington will be supplying a quarter of the Colirity team.. In any case Lancashire should retain the honours.

Fish has been in hot water of late, as the foregoing notes show. It is a great pity so fine a player does not recognise his responsibilities, and give the club the service it is entitled to. I never knew the War- ringtan crowd to be more " raw " than last Saturday wheti they found Fish absent, and lost the match for that reason.. The Opinion that he 'should be suspen- ded was general, and the Committee have taken that unpleasant course. Fish will therefore not play until November 28th at Bradford. He has merited the punishment, and I hope he will mend his ways, otherwise his popularity will soon wane. The crowd will not support a man who treats his club as Fish has done lately.

In the meantime Warrington play Seaton and Hudclersaeld. The former club are met to-day and should give Warrington an interesting game. It is not long since they were the cracks of Cumberland. In the days of Tom Fletcher, Seaton were a team to be feared, and they possess some good men yet.

The Warrington team has beea selected as follows: Hallam, full back; Harris, Hockenhall, Isherwood and Kenyon, threequarters ; Dwies and Mahoney, half- backs; Morrison, Thomas, Cook, Jolly, Swift, Lunt, Naylor and Harmer, forwards. •

div.head: R. A. NAYLOR, HYMNSTER
div.p: R. A. NAYLOR, HYMNSTER
ANOTHER "MORNING LEADER "
SKIT.
Monday's "Morning I, icier contained a second skit by S.L.H., this ,time on Mr. R. A. Naylor's hymns. It reads as follows :

"A friendly correspondent has rebuked me for admir- ing a cartoon by Mr. F. C. Goald in which certain lines from a famous hymn by Newman were applied to the political situation. He says such an application of the words is desecration. If so, I suppose the original blame belongs to Earl Percy—a serious young man— who was the first to apply the words "One step enough for me "to the fiscal outlook, and to Sir Edward Grey,. who suggested that " Remember not past years" was, a fitting aspiration for the Government. So far as I am concerned I cannot recognize any sanctity in hymns, and if they lend themselves to happy quotations'for political hits I think they should be so quoted. Let me ask my correspondent this—Are all hymns to be protected in the way he suggests? If not, who is to decide which may be used lightly and which may not ?' I cart scarcely suppose that m3r correspondent will claim. that all hymns are to be regarded as sacred for I have a volume before me now which will hardly sustain such a contention. They are by Mr. R. A. Naylor, the Union- ist candidate who wishes to capture the seat now held by Mr. Lloyd George. A few days ago I noticed some of this gentleman's secular verse, and it is to that little review that I owe the privilege of having received these specimens of Mr. Naylor's sacred muse.. Here is a verse in a hymn addressed to mothers. The writer is dealing with the fact that the sons of a good mother arise up and call her blessed, and this is how be puts that truth: Then, as tly.?y grow to man's estate, They bless you while you stay, But they arise and bless you more When you have gone away. Now, am I to be told that it is wicked to laugh at that? The lines seem more appropriate to the case of a. mother-in-Law who, having looked in for a week-end, has stayed for six months. Yet, if the theory that hymns are sacred be accepted we must all regard the stanza quoted as above criticism.- It will not do to say that Newman's hymn is a gem and that the other one is an outrage, for these are matters of opinion. It may be that Mr. Naylor would reverse such a judgment. In another of Mr. Naylor's hymns we have a lesson, taught in simple language, which may be used with effect at political meetings. One often hears at suth places reminders that it is useless to come to meetings and to applaud unless that assent is followed up by work and voting. This helpful truth is crystallised by the hymnist in this way: For just to simply listen Without more special heed • Seen afterwards in actions Is foolishness indeed. We may pardon the split infinitive because of the happr manner in which a useful political maxim is impressed upon a careless and thoughtless generation. Now the " desecration " theory would hinder the public from employing this valuable reminder at a public meeting, and that would be a pity.
It is possible that Aft:. Chamberlain might object to one or two of Mr. Naylor's teachings. For instance, there is an unnecessary raking up of old grievances in. this:

The storms of life may be severe, And make sometimes a cruel raid. The bad impression made by that suggestion will very likely be deepened by the fact that in another place a hymn, which isheaded, "Tune—' Kruger," begins: A good man wise and prudent. Mr. Naylor must be careful. Men have been written down as traitors and Little Englanders for far less than this and he may find himself on the black list along with Lord Goschen, Sir Michael Hicks Beach, and the Duke of Devonshire.

On the other hand,Mr. chamberlain, who never tires of telling us that he is an optimist, will probably hail these lines with rapture: If thy gift be a merry heart, Thou hast a blessing king's might crave, For thy bright face and cheery smile, Works well from cradle to the grave. Why the word "kings "is printed " king's" cannot explain. Perhaps it is poetical license. The word "works "is singular in a double sense. In any case these lines are home made, they are manufactured by an Englishman. The notion of a man's bright face working well from cradle to grave has the imprint of original- ity. ___

-It will not do to take all the assertions one sees in a man's hymns as being plain statements of fact. For instance, in the following lines, which are to be stmg to the tune, "Safe Home,' Mr. Naylor is no doubt ex- pressing in a general way the views of the repentant sinner, and is not describing his own experiences.
I wandered far away, From virtue's-peaceful track, And though I knew 'twas wrong,

Refused ti; come back. It would be just as unfair to hold Mr. Naylor to the statements here set forth as it would have been to accept ina literal sense the confesiion of the music-hall singer who sang: Oh, if ever there was an old scamp, I flatter myself I am he, From William the Norman, To Brigham the Mormon, - They can't hold a candle to me. In each case the songster is indulging in modest self" depreciation, but he does not mean all he says, any more than people who with complacent equanimity des- cribe themselves in church as " miserable offenders." A parliamentary candidate must often be impresse with the untrustworthiness of applause, and alas ! of promises made to canvassers. When two candidates are standing it sometimes happens that each of then/ has the solemn promise of three-quarters of the voters. Such experiences may well make candidates alive to the unreality of electoral enthusiasm. Mr. Naylor hits this • off very happily: _ _ _ _

• ifew:tre of adulation, , And do not stand among The double-hearted people Who flatter with the tongue ; Yield not then to these charmers, For better blame severe, And friendly admonition Then a deceitful cheer. The electors of the Carnarvon Boroughs may learn front this that Mr. Naylor does not like adulation or flattery, and that he prefers friendly admonition and even severe blame to deceitful cheers. I hope the electors will be polite enough to see that he gets what he likes. We have seen that Mr. Naylor is conscious of the advantages of a merry heart and a smiling face, but no one can mix in the rough and tumble of politics with- out sometimes feeling inclined to strike the lyre in minor key—l hope the expression is correct, but lam no musician. The good candidate may have been think- ing of the Government when he, wrote :

Few men are indefec‘ible,— Or even can approach That state of perfect excellence Which is above reproach. Mr. Naylor is right again. Indeed, Ido not know one indefectible gentleman in the Government—with the possible exception of Mr. Walter Long. The minor key is perceptible again in the lines:
Ho' sad the closing,of the day When we have nothing done. He may, perhaps, hum these words after the declarationv of the poll." S.L.H.

Addressing the Council, Browne, solicitor, Warrington, warrants were granted he said he thanked them for the great honour they had for the apprehension of two men named Isaac Smith conferred upon him by, electing him 'Mayor of the and Richard Hughes, of Warrington, who were sum- Borough for the ensuing year. It was the greatest monad for game trespass. honour they had to give and as such he respected it. He accepted the honour knowing that he should have the unanimous support of the whole of the Council. His predecessor Mr. J. Charlton Parr, had made a model chairman—(hear, hearl—and proved to the Council that he had the welfare of his town at heart when he presented the Corporation with the noble and handsome bust of his most Gracious Majesty King Edward VII. (Applause.) In the great responsibility that would fall upon him as chief magistrate of the borough he would do his utmost to fulfil faithfully and to the best or his ability his duties. The present year might not be a light one as there were signs of Parliamentary work in connection with the River Diversion and Ship Canal Bills. There were also several other things, such as Bridge-street improvements, electric light works, and Stockton Heath tramways,that would be advanced a stage further, and he only hoped that the inquiry proceedings would in some manner be brought to a satisfactoryconclusion and end the matter if possible. (Hear, hear.) He again thanked them for the honour conferred upon him. (Hear, hear). 1 THE MAYOR AND MR. PARR'S RETIREMENT. 1 The MAYOR said they could not allow Mr. Parr to 'retire from the Council Without again thanking him 1 for the generous manner in which he had filled the ; office—a manner which had given satisfaction to every one in the town. In Mr. Parr he hoped they had made I a friend whom they would never forget and who would 1 never forget them. (Hear, hear.) He was sure the 1 Council would do what they could if occasion offered, 1 to further the interests of Mr. Parr and his family. He ' hoped the Council would express their appreciation of ' Mr. Parr's services in the usual way. (Loud applause.) 1 Mr.PARR,in acknowledging the compliment, thanked !them very much for the kind expression of feeling. He I Could not tell them with what very great satisfaction he saw such a worthy representative in the place he ' had just vacated. (Hear, hear.) , THE DEPUTY MAYOR AND MAYOR'S CHAPLAIN. ALDERMAN FAIRCLOUGH SUGGESTS THAT THE INQUIRY BE DROPPED. The MAYOR appointed Alderman Fairclough as the Deputy Mayor and the Rev. Canon Wijlis as his chaplain. Alderman FAIRCLOUGH said he had been hoping that I the Mayor would have appointed someone else as his , deputy, but as he had been appointed he would do his best. At the same time he should like to inform the Council that it had been his intention to resign his , office of alderman, but after the result of the recent elections he had changed his views. (Laughter.) To his mind it was a great pity they could not let this in- quiry drop. It had been carried on quite far enough and if they went on with it they would only create more bitter feeling amongst each other. Why not give the present Mayor a clean bill of health? He was sure they would save the ratepayers' money by doing so, and he advised them all to bury the hatchet. (Hear, hear.) I The MAYOR said they thanked the Deputy Mayor for the very sympathetic manner in which he had expressed his willingness to serve the Council again as deputy mayor. (Laughter.) 1 i
